#3097. Terra (NKLR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Procurement shifts to funded production as the first reactor nears manufacturing.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 18, 2026 at 4:09PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Terra (NKLR +4.44%) reported a transition from engineering preparation to industrial execution during the third quarter of 2026. Management stated that the company is currently procuring equipment for its first microreactor, establishing supply chain partnerships, and advancing customer opportunities toward commercial deployment. The company reported that its current cost estimates for the first-of-a-kind reactor remain aligned with forecasts established 1.5 years ago due to the use of off-the-shelf components. CFO Katherine Williams confirmed that existing cash reserves are sufficient to complete the first reactor deployment in Rock City and prove the design's operational capability.

Operator: [Audio Gap] 3Q 2026 Business Update Webinar. I'll be operator for today. Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that today's webinar is being recorded and will be made available on Terra's website following the event. [Operator Instructions] It's my pleasure now to hand the call over to Giordano Morichi, Founding Partner and Managing Director of Global Business Development and Investor Relations. Giordano, please begin.

Giordano Morichi: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone, and welcome. Joining me today are Alessandro Petruzzi, our Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer; and Katherine Williams, our Chief Financial Officer. On Monday, November 16, Terra Innovatum filed its quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, and issued its quarterly financial results and business update. This morning, we also posted our Q3 2026 business update presentation, which we'll refer to during today's call and webcast. All these materials are available in the Investor Relations section of Terra Innovatum's website.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind everyone that today's discussion will include forward-looking statements concerning our business, financial outlook, licensing activities, equipment procurement, manufacturing preparations, potential customer deployments, and commercialization plans. These statements reflect current expectations and assumptions and involve risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our earnings release, most recent Form 10-Q, and other SEC filings for a discussion of these risks. We undertake no obligation to update forward-looking statements, except as required by law. Today, we will discuss progress during the third quarter and subsequent developments through the date of our earnings release.

Our discussion will focus on 3 connected priorities: executing the work required for the first SOLO reactor, advancing qualified customer opportunities toward commercial deployment, and managing capital against defined milestones. With that, please turn to Slide 1 of the presentation. Alessandro, over to you.

Alessandro Petruzzi: Thank you, Giordano, and thank you, everyone, for joining us today. The fundamental message we want to share with you today is that Terra Innovatum is moving from preparation towards execution. We are, in fact, procuring equipment for our first reactor, preparing manufacturing and assembly processes, and advancing customer opportunities towards commercial deployment. Our objective is to build a scalable, profitable business around SOLO. Our first reactor is a foundational technical and regulatory step, while the supplier relationships, manufacturing processes, and customer relationships we established today are intended to support subsequent commercial installations tomorrow. During the quarter, we entered into a procurement agreement with Turboden for steam turbine and generator equipment.

We also advanced NRC pre-application readiness activities and entered into a nonbinding commercial letter of intent with Waiken Group for potential data center deployment in Latin America. Subsequent to the quarter end, we progressed the manufacturing preparation with ATB Riva Calzoni, reported procurement and down payments for major reactor components, and completed sharing all 18 draft preliminary safety analysis report chapters with the NRC for its readiness review. We remain completely focused on technical execution and continue to target our first-of-a-kind reactor deployment in 2027 with commercial deployments beginning 2028, subject to the regulatory approvals and execution milestones. Our priority today is to ensure these work streams advance in parallel.

So, we need to align regulatory and technical milestones, supply chain execution, and customer commitments to support a coordinated and scalable SOLO deployment strategy. Moving now to Slide 2. Our industrial strategy is built around established supply and manufacturing partners. We are working with companies that bring relevant equipment fabrication and industrial capability to the SOLO program. This approach allows us to concentrate our resources on engineering activities, licensing integration, and deployment while drawing on existing manufacturing infrastructure. During the third quarter, our agreement with Turboden advanced procurement of steam turbine and generator equipment for the first SOLO and potential subsequent units.

Following quarter end, we reported that procurement had commenced, and down payments had been made for graphite components from Mersen, turbine and steam generator equipment from Turboden, and air-cooled condenser from SPG Dry Cooling. These steps mark a shift from supplier planning into funded equipment procurement. We are committing capital to critical components and supporting the manufacturing and delivery activities required to build our first SOLO reactor. These are not simply expressions of intent, but actual financial commitments supporting equipment production, supply delivery schedules, and our target FOAK deployment. In October, we progressed the assembly planning, manufacturing procedures, and evaluation of dedicated factory space at ATB Riva Calzoni.

That work supports both the first reactor and the development of repeatable manufacturing processes for future units. We also progressed the equipment testing with Boldrocchi -- helium circulator of the same design intended for SOLO completed a 4-hour hot running test successfully. Two additional helium blowers were being acquired and prepared for nonnuclear system testing and interface evaluation. And this testing helps us evaluate equipment performance and interface ahead of integration into our first reactor. Alongside this commitment, we are also in advancing discussion on the remaining major equipment packages. Each component has its own specification, production requirements, and delivery schedules today.

Our next priority is to coordinate procurement and delivery with the testing and assembling activities required for the first reactor deployment. Please now turn to Slide 3. And, obviously, licensing remains a central part of the development program. During the third quarter, following our July request, the NRC began its initial pre-application readiness assessment. The initial scope included the environmental report and 9 draft preliminary safety analysis report chapters. This process provides an opportunity to receive feedback and identify information needs as we prepare for our formal construction permit application. Subsequent to the quarter end, as planned, we completed sharing all 18 draft PSAR chapters with the NRC for readiness review, announcing these important milestones in early November.

The PSAR is a core element of our planned construction permit application, and completing these chapters represents substantial engineering and safety analysis work for us. This is not NRC approval or acceptance of a formal application, but this is a milestone we have achieved as publicly announced 1 year ago. Our focus now is to address feedback, continue readiness review engagement, and advance the application material required for the next stage. And our engineering and execution team are coordinating this application preparation with the equipment specifications, manufacturing plans, and site requirements. Moving on to Slide 4. We are approaching the first SOLO reactor with subsequent customer deployments in mind.

That means working with suppliers on repeatable manufacturing processes, coordinating equipment specifications and assembly requirements, and evaluating customer opportunities against our delivery capabilities as we prepare for commercial deployment. Our first reactor established a technical regulatory foundation, but our commercial work is focused on converting customer demand into definitive agreements and executable deployment plans. The 2 work streams inform each other. Customer requirements help shape deployment planning, while the progress on licensing, the procurement, and manufacturing help us define credible delivery plans. Across the business, we are advancing 3 near-term priorities in parallel.

First, advancing NRC readiness review work and construction permit application preparation; second, progress major equipment procurement, delivery planning, testing, and assembly preparation; and third, advancing qualified customer opportunities towards definitive agreements with the deployment requirements aligned to our execution capabilities. These are the steps we will use to measure and communicate our progress towards deployment. I will now turn the call over to Kathy to discuss our financial results and the capital allocation.

Katherine Williams: Thank you, Alessandro, and good morning, everyone. I'll ask you to now please refer to Slide 5 of the presentation. Terra Innovatum reported $61 million in net income for the third quarter of 2026, and we ended September 30, 2026, with $82.4 million in cash and cash equivalents compared with the $91.1 million at June 30, 2026. Our financial focus is on managing that capital against the activities that are required to bring the first SOLO reactor into operation. Those activities include licensing, engineering, equipment procurement, supplier commitments, and manufacturing readiness alongside the people and public company infrastructure that's needed to execute our program. As procurement progresses, the timing of supplier payments and equipment deliveries will influence quarterly cash usage.

We are managing those expenditures against the contractual requirements and execution milestones with continued focus on overhead and organizational costs. Advances to suppliers totaled $2.6 million as of September 30, representing advance payments to third-party engineering and component suppliers under the SOLO development agreements. Our total operating expenses were $7.1 million during the third quarter, including $1.7 million of development costs and $5.4 million of general and administrative expenses. As noted, net income was $61 million or $0.55 per basic and diluted share. This included $67.5 million of noncash gains from changes in the fair value of settled contingent warrant liabilities. Our industrial model relies on working with established manufacturing partners.

That allows us to direct capital towards our reactor program, equipment integration activities, while leveraging the existing industrial capabilities. Looking ahead, our priorities are disciplined capital allocation, clear reporting, and maintaining the financial resources needed to support the next stage of execution. With that, I'll turn the call back to Giordano for our commercial update.

Giordano Morichi: Thank you, Kathy. And I'd like everyone now to please turn to Slide 6. Our commercial strategy is focused on moving beyond expressions of interest and translating qualified customer demand into binding reactor purchase agreements and executable SOLO deployment plans. This requires aligning customer power requirements with site readiness, regulatory pathways, technical specifications, and delivery schedules while establishing clear commercial commitments and financial milestones. During the third quarter, we advanced our international commercial pipeline through the nonbinding LOI agreement with Waiken ILW for the potential deployment of up to 8 megawatt electric for the behind-the-meter SOLO capacity supporting DIRECTV Latin America and SKY Brasil data center infrastructure in Argentina and Brazil. Moving to Slide 7, please.

More broadly, the commercial priorities are evolving beyond, again, traditional letters of intent, the LOIs, and the memorandums of understanding, the MOUs, toward structured commercial frameworks that establish the foundation for definitive reactor purchase agreements. These frameworks are designed to define reactor quantities, deployment schedules, contractual responsibilities, payment structures, potentially including upfront reactor reservation deposits and milestone-based payments. As we progress toward the definitive agreements, that we believe this approach can strengthen customer commitment, improve revenue visibility and support future deployments.

Our U.S. commercial platform remains central to the strategy, supporting customer engagement, strategic partnerships, and deployment planning while we continue advancing qualified international opportunities across data center, industrial infrastructure, defense, health care, especially for the radioisotope production and other energy-intensive applications. Ultimately, our objective is not simply to expand the pipeline, but to convert qualified commercial demand into tangible binding orders, secure customer commitments, and predictable deployment schedules. We will continue to provide updates as material commercial milestones are achieved. With that, we move to the questions.

Giordano Morichi: I already see some of the questions from H.C. Wainwright, StoneX, and B. Riley. I will take them as they come in. Thank you, Sameer, for joining us. I'll run it through the first one and continue with the rest. Does the fact that you are making upfront payments as listed on Slide 2 indicate the completeness of the engineering design? Do you expect any change to design that could affect this agreement? So Alessandro?

Alessandro Petruzzi: Actually, all our technical activities are following the schedule and the road map we established 1.5 years ago. So far, the design of the graphite and stainless steel vessel are really in the end phase, very close to the manufacturing drawings, what is called manufacturing drawings. We do not expect any major change in the next few weeks. Our intention is to complete those steps by the end of the year and to start the real work for the manufacturing of those components at the beginning of next year. Minor changes may be still expected on the layout of the plant.

We are still working and cooperating, in particular, with the company that will support us for the site application in Rock City at Admiral Parkway. But no one of them, in our view, is affecting the costs that we foresaw 1.5 years ago. And this, I think -- we think is one of the big achievements we have realized in this 1.5 years.

We -- not only we submit the construction permit in just less than 14 months as announced -- but thanks to the fact that our reactor is made of the off-the-shelf components and the supply chain as is today, our estimation of costs made 1.5 years ago are very in line with the real cost we are now supporting today for procuring those materials and components.

Giordano Morichi: Second question from Sameer, H.C. Wainwright. It still regards the NRC licensing. Nature of commitments, lessons learned, can we leverage the commitments done so far? And there has been any items that take longer than expected? How quickly do we respond to the NRC?

Alessandro Petruzzi: We have a continuous relation with U.S. NRC, at least 2, 3 meetings per week. Unluckily, I can attend only one while my team is attending all, and I would like to attend more. But -- the situation is very fluid. We are now entering a very hectic period because we submit all these -- we advance for the submission those 18 chapters. We should receive the readiness review in the upcoming few weeks in order to stay in line with our construction permit next year. The project itself, the simplicity of the project, the low power, the very limited number of components made the process definitely easy from the technical point of view, from the safety point of view.

But this is just a part of the licensing process. There is additional part of the licensing process, which involve also the construction, the siting and the oversight of the work. This is -- there are topics that we are now really discussing with U.S. NRC -- but again, so far, there is no evidence of any event that may cause a delay in our application. And in particular, this is because, again, our reactor is strongly based on fundamental safety principles of physics, which made the application at the end more straightforward than other reactors.

Giordano Morichi: And then last from Sameer of H.C. Wainwright. Imagine it is December 2028, what would you expect to see at the first-of-a-kind site?

Alessandro Petruzzi: Sorry, Gio, can you repeat, please?

Giordano Morichi: Imagine it is December 2028, what do you expect to see at the first-of-a-kind site in Rock City...

Alessandro Petruzzi: December 2028, we would hope that will be even before December 2028 since we are working really actively to do by end of 2027. This is our goal to bring the reactor in the United States from the factory in Italy and to start the deployment of the reactor in 2027, beginning of 2028 with the operating licensing application. I think this will be a big event for everybody. It will be the first microreactor that is immediately connected to an industrial application because this is also important to outline. The Rock City Admiral Parkway is an industrial site. They need power and our reactor, our first of a kind will provide reactor to this.

So I would imagine a very great day for us for -- and very important because, anyway, we fully understand that the execution is fundamental for the success of this project. We are working very hard, as Giordano say, for the commercial application. We will continue. But from the other side, we understand that the realization of the first-of-a-kind Rock City will be a sort of cliff edge effect for our marketing.

Giordano Morichi: Thank you, Ale. Subash Chandra, StoneX, thank you for joining. Has the second phase of the readiness review started, Alessandro?

Alessandro Petruzzi: The second phase of readiness review will start immediately after it is complete, and we expect that will occur before the end of this year. So we are, again, continuously having meetings with the U.S. NRC. There is complete continuous feedback and answers to this feedback. All our team is involved in this. This is the priority of our team today or the technical team to complete the readiness review. So immediately after this, we will start, and we will continue, I have to say, the work on the operating license, which has been already started.

So the next step, obviously, is to continue in the next 6 months of the year from January to June, July next year to support U.S. NRC for getting the construction permit application.

Giordano Morichi: Perfect. And then one for Kathy, still from Subash. Of the $70 million first-of-a-kind budget, how has the budget been spent so far?

Katherine Williams: So out of the $70 million for the first of a kind, that is where our expenditures have been reflected in the 10-Q because that is all that we're working on right now is the first of a kind. So what you will see is that we began 2026 with a little over $100 million in the bank. At this point, we have the $82 million of cash still in the bank. All of the expenditures, again, have gone for the first of a kind. So for the $70 million, which is 2026 and 2027, we have spent about 1/3 of it. We're still on track with all of our planned expenditures.

And right now, it looks like with the agreements we have with suppliers, we will come in right on budget for the $70 million. And we will still have between $20 million and $30 million remaining to help us with the commercialization efforts.

Giordano Morichi: And part of the regulatory cost of this question related to this, Kathy?

Katherine Williams: I'm sorry, Gio, can you...

Giordano Morichi: How much would it be the regulatory cost within those $70 million?

Katherine Williams: The regulatory cost of that. So we have budgeted around $15 million.

Giordano Morichi: Thank you. We have a few still from Subash on 80% list of material suppliers secured. What is the left 20%? There's a question related to the fuel and the EPC, if it's been secured and is NKLR the EPC. Alessandro?

Alessandro Petruzzi: Fuel is definitely the most important element in the reactor. We are actively finalizing the procurement of the fuel. And for that, the specification for the fuel have been already submitted to our fuel vendor. So we are interacting. As you know, our fuel is low enriched uranium fuel. And the amount of fuel that we need is not a concern for any fuel vendor. The amount that we need is something that the current industry can produce easily in less than 1 day. So there is no problem of getting the fuel. We are obviously interacting with the fuel vendor because -- the focus is the FOAK, but the focus is also the commercialization as well.

So it's a larger discussion that we are having, and this should be completed in the few weeks, I would say, starting from the beginning of year 2028. I don't know the second part. Can you remind me the second part of the question, Giordano?

Giordano Morichi: Regarding the EPC secured.

Alessandro Petruzzi: EPC, we are -- we have started work in Rock City at Admiral Parkway. We have done boreholes. We are started the analysis, the geographical analysis with the analysis of the soil. We are interacting with our EPC for organizing the work on site. And this work is something that is going to grow up in the next, again, a few weeks. We will move from the technical activities related with the construction permit to the activities that are more engineering based related with the siting.

Giordano Morichi: And related to what you just said, Alessandro, does the Rock City require separate site permitting? Or is it part of the construction permit?

Alessandro Petruzzi: No, it's part of the construction permit. We already submitted the environmental safety analysis. We are proceeding. We needed to add elements to this coming from the analysis of the soil, which has been done recently in just a few days ago with positive results. So you will see upcoming news in respect to this very, very soon for the site.

Giordano Morichi: We have one from Ryan Pfingst. Thank you so much for joining from B. Riley. As we're working with the NRC and come closer to submitting the construction permit application, has the NRC given you an indication of a potential review timeline?

Alessandro Petruzzi: Officially, no. Formally, we are having this discussion with U.S. NRC since the engagement -- since the first engagement. We know that our reactor is a very simple design. We know that the reactors which were much more complex than ours terminated the construction permit in less than 18 months, even in 12 months. So even though formally, there is no everything -- definitely no engagement from U.S.

NRC to commit any date, there is a lot of elements, the simplicity of the design, our full support to this activity, our experience in doing licensing that help to understand that we are still on track to get the construction permit in 2027 in the second half of 2027 as it is our goal.

Giordano Morichi: There's a second side to the question. Maybe I can answer that. When do you think customers will be able and move comfortably toward the binding order and when they will likely wait on -- or would they likely wait on completion for the first of a kind? I think having secured, again, 80% of the supply chain progressing constantly with the U.S. NRC has a big advantage for us in terms of the commercialization. All of our customers have been vetted in terms of KYCs and so forth. So the main point is really moving again from the LOIs and the MOUs, which are preliminary contracts. They are nonbinding in nature. They do define the scope, but they're broad.

They are a few pages long. We're getting to a much more robust framework agreement where, again, showcases the timeline, the execution, what happens in case of delivery delays. And I think this is very important. We cannot confirm on how comfortable the customers are moving forward. What we can say is that we have been working thoroughly for the past year. We have a very good engagement with all of our customers and definitely having advanced our licensing and the supply chain securement puts them in a good position to proceed with the next steps of the framework, which will then lead to the binding agreement.

We've planned to have a portfolio in mid-2027 to end of 2027 for the future supply chain demand and growth for the commercialization, but we're working very hard to execute if possible before that. One more question from George Gianarikas from Canaccord Genuity. Thank you for joining. Can you please discuss your updated business model and cost structure per the 10-Q? Kathy?

Katherine Williams: Definitely, we can. So per the 10-Q, our cost structure is progressing to keep our overheads at the lowest level possible since we are planning that everything will be manufactured by someone else. We are not doing any vertical integration of all the supply chain. And we're using existing suppliers, existing manufacturing capabilities. So with that, we keep our overheads lower. The focus getting to the first of a kind is with getting the right engineering and the right supplier contracts in place. That is why we're confident we'll stay within the $70 million that has been reported for the first of a kind.

As we move forward after the first of a kind into commercialization, we still will have money to begin the commercialization, but that's where we'll need to have the firm contracts in place in order to have the advance payments to suppliers and where we have talked about the potential maybe for another capital raise. But that will not happen as a result of first of a kind. We have the cash in hand to complete the first of a kind in Rock City and prove that the design works.

Giordano Morichi: And then can you please discuss the projected cash burn for 2027?

Alessandro Petruzzi: If I may add, sorry, Giordano. So far, the positive aspect of this project, we think is stay in the estimation of the cost because the supply chain exists today. So this gives us an uncertainty of the -- gave us an uncertainty on this estimation, which was very narrow, and we confirmed a lot of them during this 1 year. What I'm going to say is that the $70 million obviously included not only the reactor construction, but all the work for licensing, as Kathy say, and also the work that the people for the Safety Analysis Group and licensing group has to perform, including the site.

The estimation we have for the first -- for the first of commercial reactor are today still aligned with our forecast done time ago, 2 years ago. And because we base those estimation on those costs provided by the supplier. This is to say that in our business model, as we think that we will not integrate the supply chain, at least during the first phase of the commercialization up to 2030, 2031, up to we don't reach a very high number of units per year.

And second, as the costs are today almost known to us -- and third, as we intend to go in the deployment phase with advance payment, as Kathy said, this means that, basically, our business model will be such that we will not be in loss in the first phase of commercialization. This is our goal.

Giordano Morichi: Thank you, Ale. Bear with me. Can we please discuss the mechanics of coordination with Part 57 year-end 2026? And do you expect to get this pushed into 2027?

Alessandro Petruzzi: This is -- this will be a nice gift for us and for all the nuclear microreactor ecosystem. Part 57 now has been, as far as I understand, moved to be effective in February 2027. The process in Part 57 starts to become clear, more clear to everybody. And the time to get the license under Part 57, as you know, is 12 months. So this is a very important point of internal discussion inside the team because whenever the Part 57 will become executive, several options will be available to us, definitely continuing the licensing under Part 50, but also the evaluation of to start in parallel a Part 57 commercial license.

This is what we are also organizing internally, creating a team that already have as goal, the activity related with Part 57 more than the Part 50.

Giordano Morichi: And one more from George, Canaccord, for Kathy, a little bit more in depth on the cash burn for 2027 on the...

Katherine Williams: Certainly. The expected cash burn for 2027 is between $30 million and $35 million. It's primarily directed now at -- for 2027 with the suppliers to have the deliveries of the equipment that's needed.

Giordano Morichi: We have a couple of more questions, and I believe this will conclude the Q&A. We have one from Graham Tanaka. "Which specific milestones are needed to achieve actual binding orders, and what size of advance payments could come from customers on receiving those binding orders?" What today we're discussing is 25% to 30% down payments on the estimated cost of the reactor, which we have announced throughout the year. These are the numbers we're working through. Of course, these are the stages where we're negotiating those framework agreements. They are very detailed documents as discussed. We'll be able to provide more information when there's advancements on those. On Richard Longgreen, Goldman Sachs, "Great progress, congratulations." Thank you very much.

What is the current -- currently the biggest bottleneck preventing Terra Innovatum from transitioning from the promising technology platform to a commercially deployable and revenue-generating business? So bottleneck on execution and what is the realistic timeline to resolve it? I will leave this to Alessandro to start.

Alessandro Petruzzi: Yes. I may start, and then everybody, Kathy and Gio, can comment. I think this is part of the innovation. Yesterday night, I was discussing with some of people that you need to go back maybe to the time when there was the big cell phone, the huge one and who can get this? Rich people or only people that really can need this reactor, but this cell phone. And -- but for nuclear, for a nuclear product, maybe the situation is a little even more complicated than this because it's nuclear. So there is still something -- some elements more.

It's problematic because you cannot sell the reactor to everybody because to sell the reactor, you need to have end user statement for what you are going to use. You cannot sell just to the first person in the street. So there is some elements that make this market a little more complex than any other market. This is to say what that advancing the work and watching the steps that we are executing in terms of safety analysis report, in terms of supply chain is something that can create confidence in the market to arrive at the end to the final stage of transforming the nonbinding and binding, but it's an evolution process.

We are confident of our work, and we will continue to work as much as we can to transform those nonbinding in binding. But from the other side, I think it is the execution itself is the realization of the FOAK on site. It's the time when the FOAK will reach the site in Illinois or even when the vessel will be ready at ATB that will be a sort of cliff edge in the behavior of the customer. And in terms of timelines -- we are still on our timelines. We want to become commercial by 2028.

Giordano Morichi: Kathy, any remarks on this? Any bottlenecks that you see on your front? And how do we get to this revenue-generating?

Katherine Williams: That will certainly be an exciting day for all of us when we get there. The only bottleneck would be having the customers believe in the product, getting their agreement that, yes, this is what they want and where we will go forward. And of course, we're continuing to do that every month as we advance with the process with the NRC and that we will get the licensing in place, everything that's required, and it will perform the way that we have said that it will perform, which is why the first of a kind at Rock City is so important.

A lot of the discussions we are having with potential customers is focusing now on, okay, how do we structure a contract that will allow us to go ahead and say, we want this product. But we also want some assurance that if this gets delayed or this gets delayed, recognizing we're dealing with a government regulation, that this will be what the secured price still is. And it's getting more favorable with every discussion we have because we have stuck to our plan. We have delivered exactly what we said we were going to deliver and met all the milestones.

As Alessandro says, we have good security in what the cost of the reactor is going to be at this point. We have placed the majority of contracts needed with suppliers. So we know what the price is. Again, it has been secured. So it's working with the customers to get their confidence that now is the time to place the order. And that's part of our big focus, as you know, Gio, that we're trying to secure those orders for proof that we are commercially ready.

Giordano Morichi: And I think if I can detail what Kathy said, one item that I really would like the company -- sorry, the investors and the analysts to focus on, and I think you appreciated being part of this call is the fact that Terra went to the market with the R&D done with a very strong engineering background. We're a crawl-walk approach company. We're very reliable in terms of deliveries on the U.S. NRC as we've demonstrated -- what we said we would do, we have done, we're excelling at.

And thanks to that, thanks to the technology that is the underlying element of the whole structure of the whole machine, we're able to get to these framework agreements, as Kathy explained, and we're able to discuss some of the preliminary details, which would then lead to the binding aspect. So I think we're in a strong position to continue this process with the customers that have been vetted again. And hopefully, we'll give some good news soon. But we're working very diligently on these items. And I think this is the end of the Q&A with all the questions. I would really like to thank everyone joining the call today, investors, analysts, and all of the Terra family.

Again, thank you, operator, and I will turn now to Alessandro for the closing remarks.

Alessandro Petruzzi: Thank you, Gio. So please turn to Slide 8. As a summary, during the quarter and subsequent weeks, we advanced the licensing preparation, equipment procurement, manufacturing readiness, and defined potential customer opportunity with Waiken ILW. From here, the milestones to track are basically 3. First, the readiness review feedback with the advancement of our construction permit application as well as the initial preparation for our operating licensing application; second, the procurement of remaining major equipment and site readiness work; and third, the conversion of qualified customer opportunities into binding reactor purchase agreements with the reservation deposits and milestone-based payment.

Together, these milestones will demonstrate progress on 2 connected objectives: bringing our first SOLO reactor towards deployment; and, second, establishing the industrial and commercial foundation for a scalable business. So, we will continue to manage capital against these priorities and communicate material progress as it occurs. Thank you so much for your continued interest in Terra Innovatum for joining us today. And with that, operator, we conclude the call.

Operator: Thank you, everybody. Thank you, Terra team, for joining us today. Thank you, audience, for joining us as well. This concludes today's webinar, and you may disconnect at your convenience. Thank you. Have a great day.

#3096. Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Underground brokers are selling access to hijacked enterprise AI accounts, with companies footing the usage bill, Google reports.

In just a few years, businesses have adopted AI and large language models (LLMs) to manage everything from calendar invites to data analysis and programming. Bad actors steal credentials for those models through LLMjacking — and the marketplace is evolving.

Google’s latest report on AI threats, the Q4 AI Threat Tracker from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), found that gateways called LLM Mixers are selling access for cents on the dollar.

Also: 6 essential strategies to defend against AI-powered threat actors

Organizations have poured billions of dollars into AI development and deployment, although the amount they spend on AI tokens every month varies. According to Ramp AI index data, among firms paying for AI, the top 1% spent over $10,000 per employee per month, compared with around $16 for the median firm. When employees have access to AI models, companies may introduce spending caps, but smaller outfits may overlook them.

LLMjacking is the theft of AI-related credentials, including usernames and passwords, or API keys, used to access AI models. This gives cybercriminals the opportunity to use tokens and AI resources belonging to a victim organization (or individual), typically with usage-based billing or subscriptions with no fixed cap.

With these credentials, an unauthorized user could run high-resource computing tasks, manage their own malicious AI deployments, extract and steal corporate data from the AI’s memory, or even poison training data. To add insult to injury, if demand outstrips the limits of the victim’s subscription, cybercriminals can rack up high usage costs that the victim is then on the hook for.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

John Hultquist, chief analyst for GTIG, previously said the cybersecurity unit has seen a “major increase” in LLMjacking over 2026, so we can assume this trend will likely continue into 2027 and beyond.

AI access is now a lucrative illegal business in its own right, leading to what Google calls LLM Mixers: “illicit storefronts” that provide unauthorized access to AI services and underlying proxy infrastructure.

After analyzing LLMJacking vendor advertisements on Russian- and Chinese-language marketplaces, GTIG researchers found that most offer access not only to frontier models from AI labs, but also to jailbroken models marketed as suitable for malicious purposes.

However, it doesn’t seem that many of these cybercriminal groups can agree on “reasonable” pricing, with prices swinging wildly depending on the models offered and the credentials available.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac – with Claude Code standing guard

Free trial credentials fetch far less than enterprise credentials, as you would expect. Token prices for business use ranged from $0.10 to $25, and one vendor, APIMart, increased its token price fivefold once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens. Other vendors offer subscription-based pricing.

This might not seem like much at the lower tiers, but Sysdig estimates LLMJacking could cost around $46,000 based on earlier models, and even over $100,000 per day on cutting-edge models. Mandiant research published earlier this month recorded incidents with illicit AI usage exceeding $100,000 in only 24 hours, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million before access was revoked.

While direct credentials can be sold, the infrastructure element is also an interesting service offering. Google’s threat team said in the report that the sale of LLM infrastructure “routes buyer traffic through a pool of stolen credentials and compute instances to ensure reliable access, while also offering the ability to spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce the likelihood of detection.”

LLM Mixers look similar to the rest of the cybercriminal underground economy, in which traders tend to specialize in one or two parts of an attack chain. For example, an LLM Mixer offers the access and infrastructure needed to exploit an enterprise AI model, while its partners might break into victim networks to secure initial access or buy stolen credentials from operators of infostealer malware.

Avoid LLMjacking and having your organization’s AI added to a Mixer’s menu similarly to how you would prevent intrusions into SaaS applications and cloud setups: managing access, monitoring, and imposing restrictions.

Usage and spending are the first areas to tackle. By setting limits on how many tokens can be issued and used across every AI service and account, and by alerting when usage suddenly spikes, organizations can limit damage if an account is compromised and stop massive bills before they rack up.

Organizations should also try to prevent their keys from ending up in the hands of cyberattackers in the first place. Google recommends using a secrets manager that securely stores and frequently rotates API keys, and running audits to detect quiet probing, misconfigurations, or shadow accounts.

It’s also advisable, across the board, to implement phishing protections and multi-factor authentication (MFA) to make the business of stealing credentials or compromising your accounts and networks more difficult in the first place.

#3095. Google’s Xreal Aura, Reviewed: The Weird Evolution of VR Into Glasses Is Already Underway

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Computing > Gadgets > VR/AR Productivity

The most fascinating and frustrating device I've used in a long time pushes at the edges of where headsets are heading, and glasses are evolving.

Let me tell you about a strange, fascinating and rough tweener product called Xreal Aura.

There are VR headsets, and there are smart glasses. And there’s a new class of devices that’s falling right in between. What do we call these things? I have no idea. The category includes the Meta VR Glasses coming next year and now the Aura, a collaboration by Google and Xreal.

The Xreal Aura shoots for the moon, aiming to bridge glasses and VR, and to shrink everything down on the go. It’s often fascinating, and more often frustrating. At times, it almost feels like a VR headset. At other times it feels like a superpowered version of the tethered display glasses that Xreal and several others already make, that act like wearable monitors for your phone or laptop or almost anything else.

I think it’s actually an experimental bridge to a future where phones will play nicer with advanced smart glasses. Those future glasses could create floating displays and workspaces all around you, if you wish. Consider the Aura, in a way, Google’s early attempt to get there.

Emphasis on early. Right now, the Xreal Aura’s features, OS and especially inputs feel rough to use at times and sometimes hard to get into a natural flow with. But it shows what something of this size could be capable of with more software and input-flow tweaks. And when it does work, it feels wildly like a portable VR/AR headset in a way I’ve never really seen before.

The Aura aspires to be a shrunk-down version of last year’s Samsung Galaxy XR, an expensive mixed-reality headset similar to Apple’s Vision Pro. Like the Galaxy XR, the Aura runs Android XR, a variant of Android that floats apps all around. It even runs VR apps. At times it gets close. Other times, it’s not nearly close enough.

What’s wild about the Aura is that it folds down into a case that’s truly small enough to slide into my bag. But setting up and using the Aura often involves patience and experimentation. When it works, it’s a heck of a peek at a future that’s likely around the corner. But the hoops you have to jump through to make it happen sometimes make me want to hop out.

Android XR is Google’s OS for AR/VR/AI devices and wearables, and aims to connect glasses and headsets of all shapes and sizes to Google and Gemini services and apps. The Samsung Galaxy XR, released last year, was the first. Coming up next, in just a few weeks, are Google and Samsung’s Warby Parker- and Gentle Monster-designed AI smart glasses.

The Xreal Aura is more Galaxy XR than smart glasses, in concept: It’s an AR/VR headset that you can take on the go. The glasses connect with a USB-C cable to an included processor puck that runs Android XR. It can display Android apps in both 2D and immersive 3D.

The Aura supports hand tracking and can allow full spatial movement to place floating 3D objects or play immersive games. It can float apps all around you, and you can navigate apps at the same time. You can use hand tracking to open or tap those apps, or a trackpad that’s built into the top of the processor puck. You can also pair a Bluetooth keyboard, or game controller, or a mouse, like I’m doing.

The kit tucks into an included carry case that’s smaller than the one I carry my Nintendo Switch 2 in. It’s easy to pack away for travel. I love this part of the Aura so, so much.

It’s $1,279 for the version with 256GB of storage and 12GB RAM or $1,499 for 512GB/16GB, but it’s on sale until the end of the year for $1,099/$1,299. That onboard storage is all you get, though. There’s no expandable microSD card slot. I reviewed the 256GB version.

The display tech in the Aura is an enhanced version of what’s already on Xreal’s other tethered display glasses, and similar to what Viture and TCL RayNeo use. The twin micro OLED displays are impressively bright and crisp, projected via prisms to look like they’re floating in the room with you. The “birdbath” display tech means the lenses are chunky and odd-looking, but they’re also a lot bigger and better-looking than what’s possible on display-enabled wireless glasses like Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays.

They have a 70-degree field of view, something that beats out previous generations of AR glasses like Magic Leap or the upcoming Snap Specs. The fidelity, although capping at 1,920×1,200 pixels per eye, is also really crisp and great for movie watching or games (up to 120Hz refresh). It’s enough to feel like a big movie screen is projected across the room or to lay out a virtual computer monitor, but there are clear edges where the image is still cut off compared to VR headsets (which tend to have 90 degree or better fields of view).

When running VR apps, which this can shockingly do, the graphics look sharp but narrowly framed. It’s good enough to use VR in a pinch, though: I floated through 3D Immersive Google Maps, dragging and scrolling with my fingers in the air, or played the VR role-playing game Demeo, exploring a tabletop board game dungeon, or played back 360-degree videos on YouTube. But the limits of the viewing field become a lot more stark in these modes, making me wish I had a VR headset instead. Then again, I never travel with VR headsets, and I’d travel with this.

The display’s visuals seemed to tear a few times while playing YouTube videos. Tracking, using the built-in cameras, also sometimes drifted. Mostly, the displays stayed where I put them, but sometimes they’d shift slightly out of alignment.

The processor puck means the Xreal Aura can open up most Android and Chrome-based apps I can think of, but not all of them. The Qualcommm Snapdragon Reality Elite chip on the puck seems more than zippy enough to handle whatever multiple games and apps (even VR ones) I throw at it, but not all Android apps are available: Developers can choose not to opt in, as with Netflix and Disney Plus, but they can be loaded up in-browser.

Other apps aren’t necessarily optimized for the fluid way the Aura can open an app in any size. I watched a Jets game on Paramount Plus on the Aura, and it stayed in a fixed window size. I could move closer or further away, but it wouldn’t enlarge.

The whole Aura interface feels new-ish, even if you’ve used VR. The glasses enable hand tracking that’s surprisingly OK: Tapping and pinching works, and an extended pointer can reach at a distance and click and drag or adjust windows. When my hand passes in front of the Aura’s display, it even gets overlaid with a virtual hand mapped onto mine, like VR.

There’s no eye tracking, though, something Apple Vision Pro, Samsung Galaxy XR and Meta VR Glasses do. Eye tracking is helpful: It means you can lock into something and click it without lifting your hand. Here, I found I had to lift and aim my hand a lot, like an interactive remote. Hand tracking does work somewhat below the display’s field of view, but you often won’t know if you’re interacting until that hand’s lifted up higher. This is where the Aura’s smaller-than-VR viewing area becomes a problem.

It’s particularly an issue when playing some VR games. I tried Synth Riders, a popular fitness music movement game that’s also on Android XR. I could see what was further off in front of me, but the limited viewing area meant my hands were out of sight when in my peripheral vision, so I couldn’t reach for targets near me or off to the sides.

There’s a second way to control Aura: The processor puck itself has a touchpad across its whole top. Hold it and it’s a touch remote: I can drag my finger and touch-click. On a table next to a paired keyboard, it’s a trackpad.

That’s super clever, but the trackpad’s performance ranged from OK to poor depending on the apps I ran. There are some multitouch elements too, but it still felt less effective as a headset control than I wanted.

The puck has discrete volume controls and a power button with a fingerprint sensor for secure logins. But the side button wasn’t always in an easy place to press, depending on how I held the puck.

You could also just use voice to control things: Saying “Hey Google” or launching live Gemini can open apps, handle dictation and feel like a control system of sorts. But Gemini can’t always do things in apps. It’s more of a launcher.

There aren’t a ton of unique immersive Android XR experiences, unfortunately, even a year after the Samsung Galaxy XR debuted. The Aura can technically run almost all of those same apps, including many 2D ones that show up on the Google Play store in-headset. On the plus side, VR apps working at all on glasses this small feels like magic, despite some limits.

Demeo, one of several VR games I found that run on these glasses, looks great and is surprisingly playable. I can cast up a virtual tabletop RPG game in front of me, and my hands bring up cards that I can pick and play on the field. An included Galapagos immersive 3D documentary app looks lovely.

YouTube and Google Maps are once again stars of Android XR, just like they were on Galaxy XR when I reviewed it last year. YouTube has plenty of 3D and 360-degree videos you can view, and Google Maps’ immersive 3D earth modes and, occasionally, 3D scanned interior locations are still great to browse on the Aura’s smaller screens.

I fell in love with a demo of Sock Puppet Superstar, too. It’s a hand-puppet-singing VR game that works well on the Aura.

Mixed reality VR experiences that try to project a few simple things into a room work best, effectively turning the glasses into augmented reality. Cubism, a hand-tracking enabled puzzle game I’ve played on other VR headsets, works well here too. The accuracy of the hand tracking isn’t always great for precision gripping the corners of the virtual floating blocks, though.

The refresh rate on these VR apps isn’t as ultrasmooth as on Quest 3 or Steam Frame, but they do look sharp. Except, as I said before, the viewing area ends up clipped more narrowly, so immersion feels blindered.

Some VR apps didn’t run at all, though. A VR air hockey game on Android XR wouldn’t let me use my hands to control the pucks, for some reason. I know this is a prelaunch review of the Aura, but expect some apps to act oddly. You can sideload APKs of other VR apps, which is great. Google’s AI Studio tools also work in spatial 3D in these glasses, which means you could vibecode experiences on them.

Think of the Aura as a pair of super-powered Xreal glasses with a better viewing area and an included processor puck. Xreal’s existing line of other display glasses float microOLED displays via a USB-C tether in a similar way. The Aura glasses have similar Xreal controls on the arm, but they’re modified to Android XR interface controls that are a little different. There are volume buttons, a button that changes the dimming level of the electrochromic lenses from clear to nearly full black, and a top button that brings up the home app grid when clicked once, or launches live Gemini when held.

There’s also an array of three built-in cameras that handle room tracking, visual awareness for Gemini and hand tracking. Two are in the corners of the frame, one’s above the nose. Xreal’s other glasses, for the most part, are camera-free unless you buy a snap-in module.

The prism-like lenses that reflect the microOLED displays from the top of the frame are flatter like the Xreal One Pro line, and prescription lens inserts snap in the same way – I used the ones from the Pro and they work fine.

The display’s field of view, at 70 degrees, is bigger than Xreal’s largest size on the One Pro (57 degrees), and it feels like a larger projected display in front of me. The resolution is still just the same as Xreal’s other recent glasses, but things still look crisp, even for reading.

Sizewise, they’re like many other tethered glasses: bulkier and weirder than normal glasses, but a lot lighter than any VR headset. Three sets of nosepads are included for fit adjustment, and the arms bend at several angles, too.

I’m writing this review now in the Aura, at my dining room table, with a separately sold folding wireless keyboard made by Xreal. The keyboard performance in Chrome and Docs is fantastic. The trackpad, not quite as much. But I really feel like I can write on this.

Navigating Chrome and work apps also is possible: Logged into my office’s Google-based system, I’ve been handling emails and chats and little needs fine.

Getting files on and off the Aura is the trick. I’m Mac- and iPhone-based, so I’d need to put things in Drive and Google apps to triangulate more easily.

But what’s also impressive is that I can plug in other devices, including my MacBook, and use the Aura as a virtual screen. I can float my MacBook and the Aura apps side by side.

Here’s the catch: My MacBook keyboard only controls my Mac, and the Aura’s keyboard and hand tracking only work for the Aura apps. So I need two keyboards side by side to multitask.

To be clear, no one’s handled handing off of peripherals between connected devices well, not even Apple. But it points to the biggest thorn in Aura’s device-bridging dreams.

Connecting to lots of other devices via the Xreal Aura is a wild experience. You just need to cable in with a DisplayPort-ready USB-C cable to do it. The second cable included in the Aura box won’t do it; oddly, that’s just a charging cable.

Right now, I’m connecting the new iPad Mini and casting a second display up in the air. I’m typing on a Logitech keyboard and mouse paired to the iPad, because the Xreal inputs won’t control it. But the point, mainly, is that it connects. And Gemini can still give me feedback on what it sees on my iPad’s virtual screen.

Whatever you plug in can cast a virtual monitor in-glasses: MacBook, iPhone, Steam Deck. Shockingly, even a Nintendo Switch 2 works, something Xreal’s team has been excited about. There are caveats: The Switch 2 goes into docked mode and needs the Joy-Cons detached, and only certain higher-fidelity DisplayPort USB-C cables work. I played Ocarina of Time on the Aura’s screen and it looked great, but the framerate was a bit lower than what I get on the Switch 2 normally. But again, I can ask Gemini questions about the game as I’m playing, and it sees and gives me answers, provided I’ve clicked a little on-screen toggle to share my screen with Gemini’s visual mode.

Bridging between devices is exciting to me, but it’s really just limited to treating the input like a video-in that pops on a second screen in-glasses. Meta’s VR Glasses will do this too. It’s a great bonus addition, but having to cable both my glasses and my other device to the Aura puck means too many cables for my comfort.

The glasses also work on their own without the puck, defaulting to standard Xreal glasses firmware and controls. That’s great if I want to use them with my laptop/phone/etc on the fly without needing the Aura puck, at least.

Turning on Gemini Live with a press of the top button on Aura’s glasses means you can have Gemini in your life constantly, if you wish. Toggle a little upward-arrow icon to share your camera feed and on-screen apps, and suddenly Gemini can also describe YouTube videos for you, or read what you’re writing, or tell you what’s in your hand.

It’s an all-seeing assistant that can even work with Google’s circle-to-search, although that feature’s hard to trigger (press and hold my fingers and click to bring it up, it seems). But I can then circle something in front of me, capture it, and Google AI search brings up results instantly (a book I’m holding, a freezeframe on TV or something on one of my virtual screens).

This is a step beyond the type of live, camera-enabled AI modes in smart glasses. It can see the world via its cameras and all the virtual apps that get conjured.

That being said, it’s hit or miss. The video feed quality isn’t great, so the AI can’t always read things at a distance. But I wore the Xreal Aura across my kitchen, making coffee while floating a YouTube window in front of me and talking to Gemini, and it felt like some sort of cyberpunk future I’d only experienced in bits and pieces before. It’s something you could walk around with, technically, but not a device I’d wear all day (nor is it designed to be).

Xreal promises four hours of battery life on the Aura, which is more than most VR headset claims of 2 to 3 hours. In practice, it feels good. I can use it for several hours and still have a fair amount of battery left, which seems promising. I’ve only been testing for a week, though.

But the processor puck can overheat. The puck has venting fans that can pump very warm air, and it’s not meant to be put in a pocket, even though that’s exactly what I want to do with it when I’m wearing Aura on my face. Instead, there’s an included belt clip. I tried putting it in my pocket, and pretty soon I got an overheating warning pop-up message. Don’t put it in your pocket.

I don’t think I’ve ever been as fascinated and borderline overwhelmed as I have with the Xreal Aura. It points in all sorts of directions for where phones, AI assistants and glasses can be heading. Could this little tweener device be my portable workstation eventually?

Right now it’s more of an experiment with fascinating side benefits. It can’t replace a standard VR headset, though parts come close.

The Xreal Aura tested even my new-device tolerance, although I see amazing glimmers. It’s coming with me on my next trips for sure, and I’ll let you know what happens when I do. But it’s not yet the true fusion solution I’m waiting for. And yet, I’m still convinced that the concept, remixed and refined, will be.

#3093. Lost or stolen Windows laptop? IT can lock it down without wiping it now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The Intune-enabled feature will allow admins to remotely lock down any compromised Windows device.

Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets IT admins instantly lock down your lost or stolen device via remote connection, protecting your work projects and personal data from theft and unauthorized access.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now

The new remote lock feature is designed to work in tandem with other Microsoft services, such as Intune and BitLocker, to manage a fleet of devices both in-office and remotely across the globe.

Once a device is reported missing or stolen, an admin can disable login access from anywhere without having to fully wipe the laptop or smartphone. Microsoft reports that the lockdown will persist across restarts, even if the device is disconnected from Wi-Fi networks, and can only be lifted by an admin. This means that thieves can’t use your passwords, PINs, or biometric data to circumvent the lock.

While the new feature allows IT admins to respond quickly when a laptop or phone is reported missing, there are still security gaps that other Windows controls must address. The new lock feature doesn’t erase your data or wipe your device if it can’t be recovered, nor does it isolate the missing device from corporate networks. Therefore, IT admins will still need to access those controls via the Intune and Microsoft Entra dashboards.

Also: You can now restore Windows 11 even if it can’t boot up

The remote lock feature also doesn’t change your Microsoft account credentials, so you can use your log-ins on other devices to recover your data, change passwords, and temporarily disable permissions. Finally, Remote lock doesn’t block the device from being booted in Safe Mode, from a USB, in Windows Recovery Mode, or if the storage drive is reimaged; Microsoft highly recommends keeping BitLocker enabled until the device can be wiped or recovered.

Setting up the remote lock is a straightforward process: Log into the Intune management center, then go to Devices > Windows > Configuration > Create > New Policy > Windows 10 and later > Templates > Custom. This lets admins create a profile for each network-connected device and a device group reserved for lockdown. Locking down a device is as simple as adding it to the group. To unlock, create a second profile and device group, and move the locked device to the new unlock category.

#3090. Microsoft blames major outage on a July update defect – and two other factors

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

A surprise defect took more than 80% of Microsoft's servers out at the outage's peak. Here's what happened.

Microsoft has released new information explaining the massive outage that started Thursday morning and affected Microsoft 365, Copilot, and Outlook access in 74 countries, according to Downdetector.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, posted early Monday morning that the outage was due to three factors, including a “latent defect” from a July update to Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Low server capacity and peak traffic in the US brought the defect out of hiding, despite no prior reported issues.

“A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. This was due to lock contention inside an internal process which caused the machine to become unavailable,” Lamanna said, noting that the update was deployed safely worldwide without any issues for over three months.

He said Microsoft didn’t find the issue in testing due to “the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs,” because “our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.”

Also: Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited

Two other factors made matters worse, and left servers useless in less than two hours.

“A surge in load increased the likelihood for the networking gateways to encounter the contention,” Lamanna said, explaining that Microsoft 365 maintains two gateway systems. Before the outage started, Teams failed from one to the other, which “changed its traffic patterns.” Simultaneously, he added, “nearly 14% of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service due to an unrelated issue from the previous day.”

Those two conditions collided and “caused the network gateway to encounter the latent bug from July,” Lamanna concluded. Requests eventually overloaded servers, at which point they stopped responding. At the outage’s low point, over 80% of its servers weren’t responding.

“When servers lose connectivity, our traffic management systems automatically route users to other healthy endpoints,” Lamanna said. “However, the redirected traffic increased the likelihood for the same problem to occur on the remaining endpoints. This caused a cascading failure from server to server as the same amount of load was spread across fewer servers.”

Also: AI finds zero-day flaws for just $4 now – even mediocre hackers can cash in

Before Microsoft issued an explanation, some suspected the outage may have been the result of a cyberattack, which both Lamanna and Microsoft’s status account denied.

It’s unclear how many people the outage affected, though Microsoft’s own numbers from January say Microsoft 365 “exceeds 450 million commercial paid seats,” illustrating the scale of the issue. Microsoft deployed an update to fix the outage and gradually applied it to groups of servers. Lamanna said Microsoft would publish a full post-incident review with more details later this week.

Service might be restored, but customers aren’t happy about having lost nearly two full workdays. One think tank told CNN it estimated the outage — which lasted through close of business on Friday for some — resulted in $7 billion in losses, due to many businesses and organizations being unable to access their everyday systems.

Also: If the November Windows update fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do

The fact that Microsoft’s testing couldn’t find the July issue ahead of time may leave customers wondering when the next dormant defect will strike, and whether the company is prepared.

Organizations across Europe have been leaving Microsoft in recent years, opting instead for locally-controlled, open-source alternatives. The former CEO of Github launched a decentralized alternative called Entire earlier this year, citing developers’ need for something more reliable, as Github has similarly been plagued with outages.

For many, Teams was barely offline over the two-day period, or was the first service to come back online.

“Several services like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure. That is why those services were restored earlier, with Teams chats and meetings functioning without issue for most of the outage,” Lamanna explained. Other services like Exchange Online can’t fail out.

He added that fixing the outage was slow because waiting traffic hit servers as soon as they came back, rendering them unresponsive just as quickly.

“Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state,” Lamanna said. “Additionally, since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to quickly revert the change.”

On Thursday morning, people began reporting issues with Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, according to Downdetector. By 1 p.m. ET, the number of reported Outlook outages was nearly 83,000 but had fallen to just under 75,000 by 2:38 p.m. ET. Teams and Copilot reports started dropping significantly by Thursday evening, but many individuals were still reporting issues accessing systems well into Friday morning on X and Reddit. Even Microsoft’s status page was down until around 3 p.m. ET Thursday.

Also: If the November Windows update fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do

As late as Friday afternoon, the company didn’t yet have an ETA of when the outage would be fully solved.
