It seems like one of those could reverse if Marmaxx was a pull-forward of some kind or one-time-ish. Could you help me just clarify that a little?

John Klinger: Yeah. I mean, just to clarify, yeah. Marmaxx was deleveraged 110 basis points, and HomeGoods leveraged 60 basis points. I think that's the question you're asking, right?

John Klinger: Yeah. It was a number of things. Both Marmaxx and HomeGoods were both impacted by higher freight and fuel costs. Like I said to the last question, Marmaxx did expedite inventory receipts late in the quarter, which did increase their freight costs. HomeGoods had a higher year-over-year tariff savings. The timing of markdowns at HomeGoods also benefited them in the quarter. Finally, when HomeGoods did a five, I mean, they leveraged on the five, Marmaxx deleveraged a bit on the two comp. Those are the main differentials that kind of speaks to that basis point differential.

Michael Binetti: Should we think that Marmaxx operationally is at a place where we wouldn't see that kind of potential for accelerated freight that weighing on the margin in that business? Is that how you guys contemplated the build to the margins in fourth quarter?

John Klinger: Yeah. I mean, everything we're seeing right now as far as freight costs is baked into our forecast. The expediting of inventory, we don't expect that in the fourth quarter. Like I said, everything that we see happening, we've put in our forecast.

Michael Binetti: Okay. Appreciate it, guys. Thank you so much.

Operator: Our next question comes from Mark Altschwager from Baird. Your line is open.

Mark Altschwager: Good morning. Thanks for taking the question. Wanted to ask on the competitive backdrop. First, with full price and mass retailers reinvesting in price, how are you measuring the value gap today, and are you seeing it narrow in any particular categories? Then off-price peers stepping up marketing and store investment, can you speak to what you're seeing in markets where you have the most overlap with your off-price competitors as well? Thank you.

Ernie Herrman: Sure. Mark, on the comp shop, on the full price gap value that we show versus competition, let me tell you, and I think we talked about this before, our merchants are extremely diligent on comp shopping all competitors. Again, it's not just off-price. They comp all competitors on the out-the-door retail. So promotional retails at department stores or online players, whatever we think is the out-the-door retail, we will make sure and ensure that we are the lowest price there. If there is even something like a wholesale club, which can sometimes, we can get caught where they might, on a certain item, show up at a low price, we will make sure we are not undersold.

That applies across the board. When you ask any pressure we've seen, we haven't seen any more pressure, I'd say, over the last six months, but there's been pressure, obviously, in this environment with the economy for us to be very diligent on it. We react to, again, the out-the-door price at all these other retails. There have been certain categories where some competition has lowered, and we, by the same token, have lowered our retails in those cases to provide the same value gap that we always have. So, there has been some that I'm aware of, and we react to it.

Just like there were times a couple of years ago when things went up, and prices went up, our retails moved then. The likelihood here, to your point, is prices are to come down, and we will do the same in those cases, without me giving any specifics about where that was. Marketing, off-price peer competition, et cetera, we are very aware of what everyone is doing in terms of competition there.

I would tell you that when it comes to any of the analyses that you might read about in terms of what's going on with the market share that's up for grabs, where some's going to us or away from us or to other retailers versus a competitor of theirs, we just execute our model. We've seen over time that there's plenty of market share up for grabs. When we had the one comp last quarter, that was just us not taking advantage of all the market share that's up for grabs. We believe we will start going back to that as we have started to show in Q3, and we'll show even more so in Q4.

Really, that's how we—because it's too difficult to read and it's a little gray out there as to who's doing what with who, we've always just focused on taking the market share that's up for grabs.

Operator: Our next question comes from Alex Straton from Morgan Stanley. Your line is open.

Alex Straton: Perfect. Thanks so much for taking my questions. I had one on Marmaxx and then one quick one, I promise, and then just one on HomeGoods. On Marmaxx, just thinking about that further improvement in the fourth quarter, outside of weather getting a little bit better and gifting, is there something else you are doing that is going to unlock that is different than this quarter? On HomeGoods, just the margin path continuing to move higher even with some of these freight headwinds, can you just walk through structural drivers there and how you think about the medium-term profitability potential of that banner? Thanks so much.

Ernie Herrman: Yeah, sure, Alex. On Marmaxx, it is really many things that we think will continue the improvement with. One is, when you take into account all that we have identified in some of the execution in those areas, we have made improvement and positioned those specific areas much better for Q4. I know I have built-in improvement there over where I was trending before. We have our gift-giving setups, which, as I mentioned before, we are so, I think, dominant in how we do that relative to the overall market competition, which is why we tend to over-index in December.

I love our marketing campaigns, which I think are unusually creative and will have breakthrough even more than we have in the past, that I think are going to really help drive additional traffic on those that are maybe not frequent shoppers of us or those who are thinking about shopping with us. For example, in TJ Maxx, we have the Never Uniform, Always You campaign, which I think is just terrific because it speaks to how unique and that a woman will not have to wear the same thing that she finds in other retailers.

We have the Marshalls Holiday Hustlers campaign, which we ran last year, extremely successful, which talks to how our merchants work so hard to provide amazing value and price to the consumers on quality and brand. We have HomeGoods, which is the Never Shop the Same, which, as you think about it, HomeGoods is the ultimate in the inventory changing weekly across the banners, which nobody else does it to the degree that we do in HomeGoods. I think that is going to be a powerful campaign. We are fresh flowing, which I haven't talked about this before.

Part of our success in a number of years is fresh flowing a lot of our most recent deals and outstanding value later into December than just about any other brick-and-mortar retailer. We create an opportunity for a consumer that doesn't want to go online and wants something fresh when a lot of stores are picked over, they can come into TJ Maxx or Marshalls and find something there that is just landing 10 days before Christmas, which I think is really groundbreaking in terms of the approach from what other retailers do.

I'm talking a significant amount of merchandise versus some retailers do it, they just don't do it to the impact level that we do and to the quantity we do. Lastly, the Marmaxx inventory level and open-to-buy, the fact that we're still out there buying goods right now because we're so flexible and our supply chain network allows us to do that and land goods just in time, which also adds to that last 10 days before Christmas flow, I think are all advantages that I think a lot of other retailers can't compete with. John?

John Klinger: On your question on HomeGoods, on a full-year basis, we're extremely pleased with the performance of HomeGoods. They're looking to leverage in our forecast 120 basis points on the year, and it really comes down to a number of things. Obviously, the strong execution on the top line is one of the biggest levers we have to leverage any business, and they're forecasted to do a six comp for the year. That along with some of the lower tariff costs that they've experienced and then operational efficiencies that they've also been able to achieve there have really been the drivers of their leverage year-over-year.

Operator: Our next question comes from Ike Boruchow from Wells Fargo. Your line is open.

Ike Boruchow: Hey. Excuse me. Morning, everyone.

Ike Boruchow: Morning, Ernie. Maybe to ask this, I don't know if this got asked, but I know people kind of dug into the Marmaxx on the 3Q and the 4Q plan. Just maybe, could you help bridge the quarter-to-date trends at Marmaxx against the confidence you have in your fourth quarter outlook? And I guess I'm trying to understand, have comps remained positive so far in the quarter? And from the current run rate, how much acceleration is embedded in your plan for the balance of Q4? Because I know you're betting big on gifting. Just trying to understand those dynamics a bit more.

Ernie Herrman: Yeah. I guess, when I was answering this in different ways on a couple of the other questions, we have so many advantages going for Q4 versus Q3 in terms of our balanced execution on the areas where we had our executions. Those are largely behind us as we go into Q4, and we think they'll be very behind us as we end Q4. And again, this is things I was talking about a little bit before, is the marketing positioning we have with the campaigns.

The flow of merchandise, which I think is one of our skill sets, our planning allocation has tied in with our merchant flow as we get later into the season, into December, I think is something strategically we do better than most. And we really are putting a lot of We believe there's a lot of confidence in that. Buying later, our inventories are in great shape. We have liquidity. We're able to chase deals in the market. The markets are flooded, by the way.

And the vendor community, still to this day, we are, in most cases, the first call for vendors for closeout opportunities, of which we've been seeing more and more across almost all the families of business in our stores. So that has ramped up even more than it would have been heading into Q3. Heading into Q4, we feel that's a huge step in a further right direction to drive comp sales in Marmaxx specifically.

Operator: Our next question comes from Simeon Siegel from Guggenheim Securities. Your line is open.

Dana Telsey: Hey, good morning. This is Dan on for Simeon. Thanks for taking my question. As you think about the new store expansion, how is your new store productivity showing? Is there anything different that you're seeing in new Marmaxx and HomeGoods cohorts? Thank you.

John Klinger: No, we're seeing continued strong performance of our new and non-comp stores. Really, we're just seeing continued strong store openings. Again, that's not only in the U.S., that's in Canada and in Europe.

Speaker 12: Thanks. If we can, internationally, what's been driving the comp strength and acceleration abroad there? Is it ticket transactions, the mix of both? Anything there would be helpful.

John Klinger: It's mostly transactions that's driving the comp. Again, it just comes down to excellent execution. They haven't had the weather impacts that North America has had. Ernie, you can probably talk to that.

Ernie Herrman: Yeah. Well, Europe and Canada and Australia have all executed very balanced, high-value mixes across the board. Again, not a ticket thing. No ticket was dictated from above. It's just very balanced values, good, better, best across many mixes. Fundamental control of the open-to-buy in markets that have had a lot of goods, as in Europe. Our Europe business has been extremely strong, and they are taking advantage of so many market opportunities there. As John said, this happens every now and then. They've actually had, more recently, some favorable weather versus maybe what you'd hear about here. So it works both ways sometimes, so that's been a help.

I would say the root of their business is their execution has been superior. Canada as well, and we don't talk about it, but Australia, we are performing extremely well also.

Speaker 12: All right. Thank you for the color. Best of luck.

Operator: Our next question comes from Dana Telsey from Telsey Group. Your line is open.

Dana Telsey: Hi, good morning, everyone. As you think about marketing,—

Dana Telsey: —I believe, Ernie. Hi. As you speak about marketing,—

Dana Telsey: —you mentioned earlier, you are excited about fourth quarter marketing. How is the spend this year versus last year, and how are you thinking about it by banner, perhaps, for example, on HomeGoods? The other thing, you have been mentioning a lot about good, better, best. Any updates on the state of the consumer in terms of household income levels and where you are seeing any differences with good, better, best, and where you are adjusting the mix to good, better, or best? Thank you.

Ernie Herrman: Sure, Dana. First of all, on the spend, our spend, I will not give you the exact number, but it is up this year to last year in terms of the total year. A decent amount. Again, we do not give that number. I will tell you, we are playing offense with that, playing offense with our marketing approach, as witnessed by some of the campaigns which I just talked to you about. The question about good, better, best, I would tell you, is we have not seen a dramatic shift in terms of our sales trend by income group. They are all performing balanced to where they would have been a year ago.

I think some slight tweaks, but nothing of substance across the board. Having said that, we have one of the questions earlier, we have been ultra-sensitive to making sure our values in this situation where some of the competition out there lowered retails in a few categories, which I mentioned earlier on one of the questions, we addressed those right away. So we have, in some areas, addressed lowered retails in some categories, not under the heading of good, better, best, just in terms of competitive retail value.

We think that is still our biggest differentiator for us, is to have the balanced mix of good, better, best, relative to almost any other retailer out there, which really doesn't do it. They don't do branded goods, upstairs brands across good, better, best. Most retailers are kind of leaning into either good and better or best or better, best. One of the things that we never want to lose track of is our balance of keeping all three of those and selling everybody.

I think I say it all the time, we want to sell everybody, whatever income level and whatever age, whether they're fashion or traditional or updated traditional in their fashion approach, we would like to sell everybody.

Operator: Our next question comes from Aneesha Sherman from Bernstein. Your line is open.

Aneesha Sherman: Thank you so much. Hi, Ernie and John.

Aneesha Sherman: Hi. Taking a step back and looking at Marmaxx, the comp has been extremely high the last three years in 4%-6% range, well above the market, and driven by both growth in ticket and growth in traffic or transactions. If you look back over these last couple years, what do you think has driven that outsized Marmaxx comp for three years in a row? I know you're not guiding specifically next year, but broadly, do you expect Marmaxx comp to settle back towards the algo of low single digits going forward, or do you think this three-year trend represents something longer term for the banner? Then a quick follow-up.

You mentioned adding brands online, and the press release noted more gift-giving merchandise flowing online. Is there any change to your e-commerce strategy and how you're flowing online versus stores? Thank you.

Ernie Herrman: Okay. Aneesha, on the, first of all, let's go to this past quarter. We ran a two on a six, which, to your point, is kind of an average of a four, right? If you think about the way we've typically gone, those are some of the outside comps you were seeing, which we run in that 3%-5%, kind of 4%-5% is, I think, what you're referring to. We always plan conservatively, so I won't get out over my skis as I talk forward, but you know when we plan Marmaxx at a 2% or a 3%, we're not satisfied with that, and our expectation is that we are going to strive to beat those plans.

Without me committing to a certain number, our expectation is not to comp lower than we have in the past. Let me say that. Our expectation is to plan conservatively, and our goal is to beat our plans. I know you'd like a more specific on that, but that's kind of the way we like to talk about it. E-commerce, yeah, so the brands on e-commerce, we have not changed anything fundamental there in terms of our outlook. We also are trying to do good, better, best across ranges of brands there, and we're always trying to open new brands in e-commerce.

Again, you know it's complementary to our total, so we by no means are going after our e-commerce business in terms of a huge investment or in terms of people and funding. We do it as complementary to the TJ Maxx brand, and we've been happy with the performance. Sierra is something that we are growing a little more aggressively because of the brick-and-mortar nature of it. Even though we have an online piece of that business, which we do also from a fashion and brand perspective, we're always looking to improve there and on marmaxx.com. But in total, it's complementary to our Marshalls and Maxx businesses.

Aneesha Sherman: Okay, helpful color. Thank you.

Ernie Herrman: Okay. Yep. Thank you, Aneesha.

Operator: Our final question of the day comes from Marni Shapiro from Retail Tracker. Your line is open.

Marni Shapiro: Hey, guys. Congratulations on the improvements and your gorgeous—

Marni Shapiro: —holiday. Can we just talk a little bit about two things? Number one is, I am curious if you are seeing traffic increases that you can match back to the data you are seeing from social media and the traction that you are getting there. And the other thing is also traffic-related. You had a beautiful fall set, a fantastic Halloween set. Your holiday sets are even bigger and better than I recall. Are you seeing these holidays drive traffic to the store? I understand when somebody comes in, they pick up more product, but are customers—is there any way to quantify customers are coming to your stores for these holiday events?

Because you continue to magnify them more and more each year.

Ernie Herrman: Thank you, Marni. Okay, I totally get the very good question. Here is what I can give you directionally. On the social media, difficult for us to track, however, from the, I would say, off-to-the-side analysis that we are able to see, we do believe it drives traffic to our stores. And the social media, which in many times is not funded by us, including, you have some of the—

Ernie Herrman: There is a name for it, the influencers, and then the—

Ernie Herrman: There's a name for the other group that aren't influencers. Yes, that's it.

Ernie Herrman: The creators are creating traffic for us, because we can see it, because it's so instantaneous when they find an amazing item or value in our store. There's no way we would believe that isn't driving traffic to our stores. We love that. It does speak to, and I think you and I have spoken about this before, it speaks to helping our gift-giving destination lure, and it speaks to our coolness factor of it makes us appeal to that younger demographic. I think that is an advantage we've had versus others. We continue to think that's great. Yes, very bullish on that. The seasonal sets, like you're talking about Halloween, we talk a lot about this.

There's Halloween, there's harvest, there's Christmas. We believe that over time, yes, that creates a bit of a destination for us because we do such an expanded job in it. But one of the other things I think you've heard from us, which probably drives equally more traffic and more frequent traffic, is some of the areas that we call consumables. Whether it's food or candles or things like that are regular stock-up items in our stores.

Ernie Herrman: Beauty absolutely would be in that. That's an open book, and I have no problem saying that because it's so obvious. Beauty is a big part of that. There's other categories, I just don't want to give them all publicly.

Ernie Herrman: Our consumables, along with the seasonal, and I'll give you another thing, along with our European influx, how we bring in a lot of goods from Europe that other retailers, whether off-price or traditional retailers, do not do that. So made in Italy, made in Portugal, et cetera. That is also, I think, a differentiator, just like the seasonal things you're talking about, the consumables. Europe for us over time, I think creates an ambiance of quality. Even though sometimes you don't know the brand, you know it's made in Italy.

Ernie Herrman: I think that by the way, our new entrance into Spain, we are hoping will yield even more goods out of some of those countries, and Spain specifically.

Marni Shapiro: Can I just follow up on the Italy thing? You guys ran an event, I think it was last week, but it could have been two weeks ago. It was a made in Italy event. You ran it online.

Marni Shapiro: Can you quantify, if you are running something like that online, you are sending out the information to your customers, are you seeing the traffic in stores at the same time? Is the online event also driving in-store?

Ernie Herrman: We cannot give you that information, but it is a good question. It is a good question. Yeah.

Marni Shapiro: Have a great Thanksgiving.

Ernie Herrman: Thank you, Marni. I would like to thank all of you for joining us today, and we look forward to updating you again on our fourth quarter earnings call in February. Thank you, everybody.

Operator: Thank you, ladies and gentlemen. That concludes your conference call for today. You may all disconnect. Thank you for participating.

#3032. Your Wear OS smartwatch just got a new way to save battery life

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

It could make your Pixel Watch or Samsung Galaxy Watch more power efficient.

Some of the most popular Android smartwatches just got a battery-saving update. Google released an updated version of Google Play Services on Tuesday that can help extend the battery life of a Wear OS smartwatch.

The v26.45 update concerns location tracking during outdoor workouts. Wear OS smartwatch users can now use their phone’s Global Navigation Satellite System to track their location during an outdoor workout, which can conserve battery life by outsourcing the smartwatch’s energy to the smartphone when it isn’t in Battery Saver mode.

Also: Pixel Watch 4 vs. Watch 5: Is Google’s new model worth it?

Constantly communicating with satellites during an outdoor workout can be a battery drain, and every minute of battery life counts when you use your smartwatch for communication, workout tracking, and health monitoring. GPS services, a bright, always-on display, and continuous health sensors like SpO2 can squeeze the most juice out of your smartwatch.

Wear OS software is used by many of the most popular smartwatch brands, including Google, Samsung, and OnePlus. Both the Google Pixel Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch’s largest batteries last approximately 40 hours. That’s nearly two days of use from two top Android smartwatches, but you’d be surprised how quickly it can drain.

Also: Galaxy Watch 9 review: Health data overload, but built for the future

The update improves battery life without users having to take any action or change any settings — the Google Play Services version 26.45 works quietly under the hood.

That’s not the only Google Play Services update that Wear OS smartwatch users can take advantage of. Another recent update lets users view on their phone a larger preview of any watch face they want to install on their smartwatch.

#3031. Amid AI Industry Chaos, Microsoft and OpenAI Drop New Models for Coding and Work

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

While Nvidia and Anthropic are under the spotlight, OpenAI and Microsoft dropped several new models this week.

It has been a wild week for AI, and it’s only Wednesday. Aside from outages, cheating scandals and upcoming IPOs, there are several new models available now. Microsoft dropped seven new versions of its MAI models at its Ignite conference, and OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, the next step forward for its flagship models.

First, Microsoft: At its Ignite developer conference on Tuesday, Microsoft introduced seven new AI models. They include MAI Cyber 2 Flash, MAI Code 2, MAI Image 2.7 and Dragon Copilot Transcribe — models meant to help with tasks in cybersecurity, coding, image generation and transcription.

It’s clear from Microsoft’s marketing that it is aiming to position its new tech as a cheaper alternative to OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s leading models, with many of these significantly cheaper to run at the enterprise level. That, plus its new licensed weight program, which lets companies customize the new AI models for their purposes, highlights how Microsoft is continuing to pitch its AI tech to the workplace.

While these new models might be useful for AI power users, they are far from most of the AI industry’s mind this week. During Tuesday’s earnings call, new interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress tried to assure investors that everything was “business as usual” after weeks of turmoil inside the company rocked the global economy. Nvidia cofounder and now-former CEO Jensen Huang’s multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence, threw the company into chaos and have attracted the attention of the Securities and Exchange Commission and both chambers of Congress, where Huang has agreed to testify.

And let’s not forget about Anthropic, the Claude maker plans to become a public company this week, with the possible biggest-ever IPO slated for Thursday. Anthropic’s reportedly seeking an opening price of $78 per share, for a total valuation of $1.4 trillion — narrowly beating the other largest-ever IPO earlier this year, Elon’s Musk mega-conglomerate, SpaceX (including now SpaceXSI, because President Trump said so).

The Nvidia scandal caused a drastic 14% dip in its stock price during its first week and wiped out $1 trillion in the company’s value, but Anthropic investors don’t seem to be worried. At least, not publicly.

If nothing else, Anthropic’s IPO and the new models from OpenAI and Microsoft are stark reminders that the tech industry is nowhere near ready to slow down on AI. Even as financial, environmental and legal concerns mount — and arguably hit a fever pitch during the midterm elections — Big Tech is plowing ahead with generative AI.

#3030. 74% of shoppers trust AI agents for buying advice – but checkout is another story

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Shoppers who use AI agents spend 8% more than the average buyer and purchase 23% more items per order.

Twenty percent of holiday shoppers are using AI agents as their first stop for research and advice, but they are not ready to have agents make purchases, according to the latest Salesforce research.

Also: What to know about early Black Friday sales

Salesforce surveyed more than 2,500 shoppers in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia and found that 74% of shoppers trust recommendations from AI agents. Salesforce research forecasts AI-driven shopping recommendations to drive $75.8 billion in Cyber Week spending, up 13% from 2025.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer

Brands are also being noticed by AI agents, with 30% of shoppers saying they were first introduced to a new brand via AI. And most importantly, 1 in 10 (11%) shoppers would avoid a brand if an AI agent told them to.

Here are some of the key findings from the 2026 holiday shopping research.

Retailers that use AI shopping agents are seeing bigger orders and more loyal customers. The survey found that shoppers who use AI agent referrals are twice as likely to make a purchase. In addition, 39% of shoppers have used AI agents on an e-commerce site, and 80% had a positive experience, while 75% felt more loyal to the brand as a result of the AI agent experience.

Shoppers who use AI agents spend 8% more than the average buyer and purchase 23% more items per order. Brands that use AI agents are seeing seven times faster sales growth than brands without them.

1 in 3 consumers has used an AI agent, including the widely adopted Meta Muse, now used by 12% of all consumers. Grok Bot is also in high demand.

The survey found that 28% of consumers give their agents multiple tasks per day. The most common use of AI agents is price comparisons, product reviews, and brainstorming for gift items. Brand discovery is a major benefit of AI agent use cases.

Agents as advisors are growing, but agents are not buying products yet, with only 19% of personal agent users using logic to check out. Only 9% of consumers allow their personal AI agents to have unrestricted access to their financial details, and 36% have set up a separate credit card for their AI agents.

Also: ZDNET’s favorite tech devices for 2026

The majority of consumers (73%) are not comfortable giving personal AI agents their payment information, and 49% are not interested in agents making purchases on their behalf. Consumers do not want to share their purchase history or personal data that could potentially lead to unwanted charges. Shoppers will abandon an AI agent after 2-3 mistakes. If an AI agent makes a bad recommendation, 1 in 3 consumers will blame the AI.

Retailers must adopt AI shopping agents in order to compete. Retailers must be able to service and respond to shopper agents. The ability to detect intent, buying signals, sources of dissatisfaction, and other consumer-related buying patterns at machine scale (significantly faster and higher volume than human scale) will require retailers to invest in AI agentic engagement capabilities.

Also: 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Today, AI agents advise consumers on their holiday shopping journeys, but in the very near future, they will autonomously make purchasing decisions with little to no involvement from their human counterparts. The future of shopping will be more autonomous, highly personalized, and nearly frictionless. Brands that invest in agentic AI will garner the most loyalty and future business.

#3029. Giving the iPhone Duo a Spin at the Apple Store? Be Sure to Test These Things Out

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Want to test out the iPhone Duo? Here are six things you need to try with it.

Now that the iPhone Duo is in stores, there are plenty of people who are curious about Apple’s first folding device. Foldables are hardly a new sector in the smartphone world, with Samsung leading the charge, but Apple’s entry into the market is a big deal, and the iPhone Duo is a stunner.

If you’re planning on checking out the iPhone Duo at the Apple store, it might be easy to just marvel at how cool it looks, but if you’re considering making this your new phone that’ll be in your pocket all of the time, you’ll probably want to get an idea of how it will be living with this new design. After all, you should be in love with all aspects of the device if you’re going to drop $2,000-plus on it.

Below, we’ve listed a handful of features and things to try out when you’re test-driving the Apple iPhone Duo in the store.

When the Duo was first revealed, Apple showed off a very intriguing animation when you unfold it. Leave it to Apple to make a function so simple look so aesthetically pleasing.

It’ll likely be the first thing you notice when you first open the Duo up to see its inner display, and there’s a good chance you’ll continue to open and close the device to see the effect. At the end of the day, it’s a parlor trick — but a very good one, adding delight to ordinary use.

Read more: The iPhone Duo Crossed 517,000 Folds and Counting in Our Custom Machine

Foldables, well, fold, and they typically come with creases. The Duo has a minimal crease and a matte display, both of which are wins. That said, even the most noticeable creases tend to “disappear” when you’re viewing content — you just get used to them while watching TV shows or YouTube videos. The Duo’s minimal crease should be even easier to ignore.

And let’s not forget about the matte screen. Several foldables ship with glossy displays, but the iPhone Duo will have a less shiny screen, making it easier to view in bright environments without annoying reflections.

The outer passport-size display on the iPhone Duo may be a little awkward for watching videos because of how it crops content to fit the new aspect ratio. Still, it’s handy to prop the phone up in tent mode and watch shows that way. You also have a large inner display to work with, but because of its passport-style design, even that screen has a different aspect ratio than the widescreen format people are used to on regular phones, so there will likely be some letterboxing in videos.

Try watching something with the phone set up in both ways to see if it bothers you enough to dissuade you from buying the phone.

Again, it’s not an iPhone Duo issue but a foldable phone issue — the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the same size and format. The aspect ratio of the display might crop the top or sides of videos, so it’s worth trying out if you expect to watch a lot of full-screen videos.

Like videos, apps on foldables can sometimes appear a little weird, and that could be the case with the iPhone Duo‘s aspect ratio. When you’re at the Apple Store, check out how your most-used apps look and feel on both the inner and outer displays, and make sure you rotate the inner screen to see how apps behave in this orientation, too — that wide screen could be great for watching vertical videos or scrolling through social media.

If some apps, such as Instagram, look a little different or are wonky, it’ll hopefully be just a matter of time until the developers make an update that optimizes the experience for this new design. Keep in mind that you can also have two apps open onscreen at once, making it easier to multitask.

If you want the best camera experience on an iPhone right now, you should be looking at the iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, but that doesn’t make the Duo a slouch for shooting photos, either.

Yes, the Duo is missing a third camera (telephoto), and if that’s important to you, then you probably shouldn’t even be considering Apple’s foldable. But still, if you’re going to shell out this much money for a new phone, test out those cameras — even if it’s in a controlled environment like an Apple Store.

Another thing to check out before you pull the trigger is your selfie shots with this new phone. There are two main ways to do this: with the phone closed, holding it up in the regular way you’d take a selfie using the outer screen’s 12-megapixel front-facing camera, or with the inner display open and shooting with the twin 48-megapixel rear cameras (the outer screen will show a preview of the shot).

There’s also a front-facing camera underneath the inner display, which is mostly for video calls — and which we suspect would produce the least-impressive shots from the device. Try them all and see what you think of the pics. And since you’re at an Apple Store, make sure you delete them afterward.

The odd but interesting aspect ratio of the front display on the iPhone Duo may be a little awkward for typing, so it’s best to do a typing test when you have one in front of you. While the inner display will provide a roomier and more comfortable typing experience, you probably won’t want to have to open up the Duo every time you want to shoot off a quick text to someone. If you have bigger hands, typing on the front screen could be a bit of a nightmare.

Typing one-handed on the small cover screen should be manageable, but try it out to see if it works for you. Some may find it convenient; others may find it cumbersome.

And when you’re typing on the inner display, try the Duo in both portrait and landscape orientations to see which feels better. You can also choose between a split keyboard and larger keys. It’s thoughtful of Apple to offer options that let you tailor the typing experience to your preferences, but you may find that none of them suit your style.

#3024. Cathie Wood Keeps Buying Archer Aviation Stock. Should You?

The tech-focused investor sees promise in electric vertical takeoff vehicles.

By Brett Schafer – Nov 18, 2026 at 4:30PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Archer Aviation ›

Archer Aviation (ACHR -8.24%) is down 72% from its highs. This is not deterring Cathie Wood from buying the dip. The founder of Ark Invest has kept scooping up shares of the electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) upstart, keeping it a sizable position in the defense- and autonomous-themed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) she manages.

eVTOLs as a theme have gone through a rough patch in 2026, but Archer Aviation is getting close to making a commercial debut with its Midnight aircraft. Does that make the stock a good buy-the-dip candidate today?

eVTOLs are a novel aircraft solution that combines the mobility of helicopters with fewer nuisances, such as dangerous landings and noise pollution. These are small vehicles propelled by multiple rotors and electric motors, designed to carry people over traffic in urban areas, such as for airport visits.

Archer Aviation has been pushing to get its Midnight vehicle approved by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), a slow process for a type of aircraft that has never flown commercial customers before. It is conducting numerous tests in California, including a recent test flight across the San Francisco Bay Area, and is setting up flight infrastructure in Los Angeles ahead of the 2028 Olympics, where it is a promotional partner.

The company hopes to start flying passengers in 2027, beginning in California and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Timelines can be finicky with FAA certifications, but this looks like the long road to certification is nearing its end, with a huge boost in marketing coming with the Olympics next year. Then, Archer Aviation will start generating real revenue.

In addition to commercial flying, Archer is now working with defense start-up Anduril to develop an eVTOL for military use, such as shuttling soldiers in and out of combat. The concept is in its early days, but this could help Archer Aviation diversify beyond its commercial eVTOL ambitions and bring reliable military revenue to its income statement.

Plus, it recently acquired some businesses from Boeing, including a company called Insitu that has $200 million in existing revenues from reconnaissance drones. This will play into Archer's long-term ambitions in commercial and defense autonomous eVTOL systems (along with other aircraft), and will immediately contribute revenues to the business.

Right now, Archer Aviation is not generating much revenue. However, with the start of its commercial eVTOL operations, along with the defense partnership and the Insitu acquisition, the company could see a meaningful inflection in sales over the next few years, which is perhaps what Cathie Wood is looking at when buying shares right now.

Because it is investing in airport infrastructure (its eVTOLs need to land and take off somewhere) and manufacturing its Midnight aircraft, Archer Aviation is burning a lot of cash. Free cash flow was negative $751 million over the last 12 months, with nearly zero revenue. Expect this type of cash burn to continue in the quarters ahead, even many quarters after commercial passengers start flying.

This could be a concern because of the dwindling cash on Archer's balance sheet. It had $1.35 billion in cash on the balance sheet at the end of last quarter. Unless it can turn around its cash burn, the company will run out of funds within the next two years. Cash burn has only worsened in recent quarters, I may add.

Continued progress on commercialization may help the stock price in the interim, allowing Archer to raise more funds. However, this will be a drag on long-term value creation.

Archer's market cap is already at $3 billion, pricing in significant future growth from its eVTOL network. These aircraft may be the future of transportation in cities, but the thesis will play out over decades. Archer stock does not look like a good investment at current prices.

#3022. Nvidia’s Earnings Calmed Markets, but AI’s Harsh Reckoning Marches On

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Jensen Huang's departure was only a symptom of a bigger problem in the AI economy.

Though Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday offered some reassurance to investors after Jensen Huang’s departure as CEO, it did little to resolve the political, regulatory and leadership questions hanging over the entire AI economy.

The semiconductor giant at the heart of the AI infrastructure boom saw its shares plunge by 35% from last month’s high following the scandal around Huang — wiping out nearly $2 trillion in market cap and triggering Wall Street panic around a broader AI reckoning.

Nvidia’s finance chief and interim CEO, Colette Kress, sought to project stability, telling investors it was “business as usual” and raising Nvidia’s fiscal 2028 outlook. Though the chipmaker’s stock price rebounded after reporting better-than-expected results, it’s likely to face a rocky future, as concerns linger around national security violations amid illegal export deals. Market confidence is also shaky amid supply chain backlogs for advanced chips and servers that remain critical to AI compute and the training of large language models.

In the lead-up to the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Huang issued a statement that he would return as CEO if the board of directors decides it’s in the “best interest” of shareholders and the country. Despite calls from President Donald Trump and other tech executives to reinstate the former GPU boss, Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia’s appointed first-ever chair of the board, said there is no intention to reinstate Huang, and no successor was named.

Prior to the call, The Wall Street Journal reported that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Huang over concerns that the company misled investors.

Huang maneuvered Nvidia into a linchpin role for frontier AI labs and data center firms, not just by supplying hardware but also by providing equity, credit and financial backing and by mobilizing third-party capital to secure investment for the AI buildout of data centers. Nvidia’s circular financing schemes — in which the chipmaker helps fund a hyperscaler like Meta or Microsoft, which then uses the funds to buy its products — were allegedly a source of contention for Kress and other executives.

Critics have warned that this kind of vendor financing inflated the AI bubble by inflating growth projections and buoying the market valuations of chipmakers and hyperscalers.

According to Reuters, Kress was expected to pull back from some of the riskiest AI financial deals, including investments in OpenAI and AI infrastructure companies such as Lambda. Already, Nvidia has significantly scaled back financing for a $250 billion OpenAI data center deal. During Tuesday’s call, Kress failed to announce a sweeping unwind of Huang-era financing arrangements, focusing more on continuity than retreat.

Kress mentioned that chip producer TSMC, a key Nvidia partner, will continue working with Nvidia despite Huang’s departure. The company also said it was assuming no China data-center compute revenue in its next fourth-quarter outlook.

Nvidia supplies the lion’s share of the hardware necessary for data center construction and model training, and the company has long said that the demand for chips exceeds supply. Shortages of RAM and high-bandwidth memory slow down the production of AI servers and raise prices for cloud companies and other buyers. In an attempt to buy its way out of the bottleneck, Nvidia has committed large sums of money to secure future memory supply.

If Nvidia distances itself too much from its GPU commitments, that could be a problem for the entire tech industry. Semiconductor production is an incredibly specialized field dominated by very few companies, and any changes to the supply chain could have ripple effects on global markets and vendors, including in consumer electronics and cloud services.

Huang’s affair with a Chinese executive connected to the Singapore-based Megaspeed — whom US intelligence claimed was a Chinese intelligence asset — complicated an already tight supply chain. Megaspeed was under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese firms obtain high-value Nvidia chips through channels that violated US export controls.

According to the investment research firm Culper, up to one-fifth of Nvidia’s fiscal-year 2026 compute revenues were driven by movement of some of the company’s most advanced chips into China through nonrestricted intermediary countries in a process called diversion. When advanced Nvidia chips or servers are illegally routed to Chinese buyers, those units are no longer available to legal customers in the US and allied markets.

Huang was influential in shaping the Trump administration’s chip export policies, pushing back against export controls that limited Nvidia’s sales to China. But the recent scandal prompted new Commerce Department restrictions on chip shipments through third countries.

While Kress cited improving supply and sustained demand in raising Nvidia’s outlook, stricter export rules and tighter controls could further constrain capacity by creating more obstacles to compliance and delivery.

Nvidia’s better-than-expected earnings may steady investors in the short term, but any company that supplies essential hardware for the AI buildout is at risk if investor confidence in the industry falters. When Nvidia reports strong growth, AI-focused stocks and funds with large technology holdings are likely to go up. When Nvidia’s outlook weakens, investors worry that AI spending is slowing or that companies have overcommitted.

A handful of big tech companies — colloquially known as the Magnificent Seven — make up a big share of major funds and indices. Five of them account for roughly 30% of the S&P 500 index, and AI overexposure in those businesses translates into overexposure in many individual retirement accounts and 401(k)s. Because index funds hold substantial positions in Nvidia and other large tech companies, an AI selloff could affect retirement balances even for people who don’t own Nvidia shares directly.

The Magnificent Seven are heavily affected by AI stock swings. Alphabet’s stock price sank as Nvidia news aftershocks reverberated through the markets, proving that top firms are not unassailable. Other tech companies heavily focused on AI infrastructure, such as Intel and CoreWeave, likewise saw their share prices decline.

Despite growing concerns about AI dangers, Huang was one of AI’s most aggressive promoters, framing the technology as an economic and national security imperative. In early September, the now-disgraced CEO said that artificial general intelligence, or AGI, had arrived, congratulating OpenAI on its GPT-6 Astra model, which was trained on Nvidia’s Grace Blackwell GPUs.

Huang pushed against recent warnings from AI researchers, calling for unrestrained progress on frontier models and repeatedly arguing against new laws and safety regulations.

Even before Huang’s business and personal scandals came to light, AI companies were gearing up for a post-midterm-election PR campaign, as the technology has become increasingly unpopular and the backlash against data centers has grown. Democratic Party politicians pushed a platform to shift the federal government’s lax approach toward the AI industry. Some Democrats are also poised to craft legislation to prevent an AI industry bailout in the event of a bubble pop.

Amid bipartisan calls for Huang to testify before Congress, many politicians are also seeking to investigate high-ranking members of US intelligence and the Commerce Department for allowing export loopholes or for failing to act on knowledge of Nvidia’s China-related deals.

Kress might be able to lead Nvidia with tact and diligence, separating the company from some of its riskiest deals. But the national security implications of her predecessor’s relationships have opened up a can of worms that no CEO can close on their own.

The federal government is ruled by inertia, but right now there’s some investigative momentum aimed directly at the major AI players. That will almost certainly ice out some investor hype. It’s clear the AI industry is facing a reckoning that was not in the cards just months ago.

#3020. 3 Energy Stocks With Dividends Built to Last the Next 10 Years

Chevron, Brookfield Renewable, and Williams are all reliable income investments.

Energy stocks can be volatile short-term investments, since commodity prices are cyclical. However, the biggest blue chip energy stocks can still be reliable long-term investments, since their scale insulates them from lower commodity prices.

Many of those top energy stocks also return a large share of their excess cash to investors through large dividends. Let's take a look at three of those high-yield energy stocks -- Chevron (CVX -3.95%), Brookfield Renewable (BEPC +1.57%), and The Williams Companies (WMB -0.34%) -- and see why they're worth buying and holding for at least the next ten years.

Chevron, one of the world's largest integrated energy companies, pays a forward yield of 3.3%. It's raised its dividend annually for 39 consecutive years, even as the U.S. economy endured three official recessions and five bear markets.

Chevron is resilient because it operates in 180 countries and owns a diverse mix of upstream, midstream, and downstream assets. That scale dilutes its operating expenses and allows it to easily cover its capex and dividends as long as the price of Brent crude oil -- currently at $92 -- stays above its corporate breakeven price of $50 per barrel. The last time Brent traded below $50 per barrel was during the darkest days of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Chevron expects to increase its oil and gas production by 2%-3% annually through 2030. It plans to hit that target by expanding its Tengiz Field in Kazakhstan, drilling for more oil in the Permian Basin, launching more deepwater projects in the Gulf of Mexico, and increasing its presence in Guyana, one of the world's fastest-growing oil regions. Therefore, Chevron is a great income-generating energy stock you can buy and forget for at least the next 10 years.

Brookfield Renewable Corporation, which was spun off from Brookfield Renewable Partners (BEP +1.43%) in 2020, builds hydroelectric dams, wind farms, solar power plants, and other green energy projects across 25 countries. It's raised its dividend every year since that spin-off, and it currently pays a forward dividend yield of 5.1%.

With an operational capacity of 51.4 GW and a pipeline of over 200 GW of renewable projects (including 85.7 GW of advanced-stage projects in active development), Brookfield is a great all-around investment in cleaner energy. Roughly 90% of its power generation is locked into long-term contracts with a weighted-average remaining contract duration of 12 years. About 70% of its revenue is also indexed to inflation, which insulates it from rising costs.

Brookfield easily covered its dividends with its funds from operations (FFO) last year, and it plans to keep raising its payout by 5%-9% annually. Those strengths make Brookfield a safe green energy play that will continue to generate stable income over the next decade.

The Williams Companies operates over 32,000 miles of pipeline in 24 states. It owns Transco, the largest natural gas pipeline in the U.S., which links the Gulf Coast to the Atlantic seaboard. It handles roughly a third of all natural gas produced in the country.

Williams is benefiting from the rapid growth of the data center market, which gets more than 40% of its electricity from natural gas, as well as other industrial markets. As a midstream pipeline company, it merely charges upstream and downstream companies "tolls" to use its infrastructure. That business model is well insulated from volatile commodity prices, since it merely needs those resources to keep flowing through its pipes to generate stable profits.

Williams has paid continuous dividends for the past 52 years, and it's raised its payout annually over the past nine years. It currently pays a forward yield of 3.1% and offers a good blend of growth and income, with some passive exposure to the booming AI market.

#3018. Fathom Forthcoming: First Battery Cells Roll Out of Ford’s Michigan Plant for Electric Pickup

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Ford's BlueOval Battery Park Michigan is shipping its first lithium iron phosphate cells to Louisville for Fathom prototypes, a key milestone for the automaker's next-generation EV.

This week, Ford began shipments of the first lithium iron phosphate electric vehicle battery cells from its new BlueOval Battery Park in Marshall, Michigan, to its Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky. There, the prismatic cells will power early Ford Fathom electric pickup truck prototypes and validation vehicles. The automaker invited me into the plant to meet the people who build the batteries and to see how the so-called “jelly roll” is made.

In 2025, consumers lost access to the clean vehicle tax rebates of the Inflation Reduction Act, but the program and its incentives remain in the law for automakers and suppliers. So bringing this US-based, domestically owned battery plant online is kind of a big deal for Ford. It’s an important milestone for the automaker’s plan to make its new Universal Electric Vehicle, or UEV, platform a reality and to bring the Fathom — its upcoming electric pickup truck — to market in 2027 at a price that EV-eager customers can stomach.

Ford expects to sell the upcoming Fathom at an estimated price of $28,350 (well, $29,945, including the $1,595 destination and delivery fee), with the first preorder expected to open early next year.

BlueOval Battery Park Michigan is a $3 billion, 2 million-square-foot facility with a targeted annual production capacity of 20 gigawatt-hours. That’s a whole lot of batteries. Ford is expected to employ 1,700 people at the site across two 12-hour shifts, running around the clock to reach that capacity.

The plant is a clean facility, so getting in meant donning a clean suit, mask, hairnet, gloves and two layers of shoe booties. I then crossed special magnetic and sticky floor panels designed to pull any metal particles off the bottoms of those booties, before passing through multiple air-blower airlocks that blasted my body clean of loose dust.

From the outside, the building is huge and difficult to take in completely. On the inside, the scale truly comes into focus as I stare down a massive hallway just under a mile long end to end. Raw materials — rolls of copper and aluminum sheet, plus the chemical powders that coat them — enter the plant at the eastern end, move in a straight line through the facility, and completed battery packs exit at the western end. The first 0.7 mile of the fab belongs to cell production, split between isolated cathode and anode lines that join halfway through for final cell assembly.

Ford engineers, battery experts and executives tell me that the automaker chose lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, chemistry in a prismatic (rectangular) format for its affordability and structural benefits. LFP uses no nickel or cobalt, which keeps costs down, and Ford found the chemistry well suited to bidirectional charging.

To keep costs low enough to deliver a reasonably priced car, Ford couldn’t use a Chinese supplier and still qualify for IRA manufacturing credits. So it licensed the technology from one, working with a company called CATL, which one Ford exec described as “the world’s leading battery manufacturer,” whose batteries power 30 million vehicles worldwide.

Despite working with a Chinese company, Ford says the plant is completely US-owned, staffed and operated and is totally IRA-compliant, with no foreign entity of concern, or FEOC, involvement beyond the licensing agreement.

Charles Poon, who leads vehicle hardware engineering, said Ford didn’t simply copy a catalog part.

“We designed a unique cell that does not exist in the CATL catalog, specifically for the UEV,” Poon said, adding that the taller and simpler cell delivers “the energy density, the affordability, the durability that [Ford is] looking for” and allows the automaker to more completely integrate the cells and battery pack into the vehicle’s design.

Ford also had to build the supply chain, Poon said, sourcing an IRA-compliant stream for a battery chemistry that is only just entering the mainstream in North America, and working with approved global partners and North American suppliers.

On the cathode and anode assembly lines, meter-wide rolls of copper and aluminum are first coated with a chemical slurry that is baked on. The large rolls are then split into 10 smaller rolls, with tabs notched into their exposed edges at set intervals. As the continuous rolls pass through multiple machines like gigantic cassette players, AI-powered vision systems watch the foil for coating defects, scratches and wrinkles, marking problem sections so they can be automatically removed.

Next, the cathode and anode foils are layered and rolled into a cylinder, then pressed flat into what Ford calls a jelly roll. Imagine a roll of toilet paper mashed in a hydraulic press, and you’ll have a good idea of what it looks like: a flat rectangle with rounded ends.

The jelly rolls are then gathered in pairs, and the previously exposed tabs are folded together and ultrasonically welded to more solid terminals, which are in turn laser-welded to a cap. The jelly roll couple is then laser-sealed into an aluminum box, about the size and weight of a masonry brick, to form a nearly complete prismatic cell. Engineers vacuum out the air, check for leaks by pressurizing the cell with helium, and fill it with liquid electrolyte. Bob’s your uncle: you have a finished LFP prismatic cell.

Ford says the assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, which plant manager Tracy Church says makes BlueOval Battery Park “among the fastest LFP prismatic lines outside China.”

From the cell line, completed prismatic cells would normally pass through a door and straight into pack manufacturing, where full battery packs with integrated “e-box” electronics, integrated cooling and wiring are built. That part of the plant is still undergoing validation, so for now Ford is shipping just the cells to Louisville, not complete battery packs. The company plans to have pack manufacturing up and running in Marshall ahead of Fathom’s launch, with full pack deliveries to Louisville planned in 2027. Church told me that the plant aims to produce 50 battery packs per hour.

Ford hasn’t officially specified the energy capacity of the cells or the completed battery packs and wouldn’t comment when asked about expected range for the Fathom. The automaker wouldn’t even confirm how many cells go into the EV’s pack, but I estimate between 90 and 108 cells based on a cutaway of the finalized unit I examined (but wasn’t permitted to photograph) during my tour. I expect Ford is holding off on finalizing details until closer to the EV’s 2027 launch window.

Battery Park Michigan isn’t just sending cells to Kentucky; it’s also sending expertise. Ford’s Glendale Kentucky plant — which used to build batteries for the F-150 Lightning full-size electric pickup — is currently being retooled to build LFP cells for Ford Energy for large-scale energy storage applications, and the lessons Ford learns in Michigan are already being shared with the manufacturing teams there.

Ford has been in the EV business for over 15 years. In 2011, it revealed the Focus Electric at CES. 2019 brought the debut of the Mustang Mach-E — which Ford recently found is holding up well after years on the road with minimal battery degradation — followed by the arrival of the F-150 Lightning in 2021. This isn’t the brand’s first electric rodeo, but executives tell me that the automaker has never had this much control and ownership over its battery production, and it’s hoping that will make the difference as it prepares the next-gen UEV vehicles.

#3016. Not Safe, Not Creative: 123456 Is Still the World’s Most Common Password

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Cybersecurity

Data breaches, hacks and cyberattacks. Guess what? Our passwords are still risky.

Our data keeps getting hacked, breached, stolen and exposed, and yet we’re still using the most predictable passwords.

For the seventh time in the past eight years, 123456 is the world’s most common password, and it’s got other uncreative companions on the list, according to the latest analysis by password and passkey manager NordPass, a division of Nord Security. The top three most used passwords in the US were: 123456, password and admin. Yikes.

In the 44 countries analyzed, the password 123456 was used more than 7.2 million times. The rest of the top 10 passwords: admin, 12345678, 123456789, 1234, 12345, password, Aa123456, Pass@123 and 1234567890.

NordPass said that even though many people prefer simple, easy-to-remember passwords, much more awareness of password safety is needed. The company recommends creating a unique password for each account that’s at least 15 characters long, including uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and special characters. Though it’s tempting to reuse the same passwords, hackers rely on that complacency.

NordPass suggests upgrading weak, old passwords to stronger ones. You can also add multifactor authentication, which requires an additional layer of security beyond a login password. That could mean entering a one-time passcode sent by text or email, answering security questions, or using facial recognition or fingerprint ID.

CNET managing editor Adam Benjamin said that the risk isn’t primarily from someone randomly guessing your password. The danger is from algorithms that collect data or bots that use credential stuffing (in other words, stolen username and password pairs obtained from a data breach).

According to Benjamin, using an obscure reference or a different language doesn’t make a password stronger. “A password is good when it’s too much trouble for an algorithm to crack,” he said.

You might remember the scene from the 1987 movie Spaceballs, where the combination to Planet Druidia’s air shield is 12345. Dark Helmet calls it “the stupidest combination I’ve ever heard in my life!” and says it’s “the kind of thing an idiot would have on his luggage.” The joke remains a staple reference for weak passwords and PINs, and yet, here we are.

Last year, two researchers hacked into McDonald’s hiring chatbot by guessing the password 123456 to access 64 million data records, including applicant names, email addresses and phone numbers.

In 2023, the Akira ransomware group hacked into KNP Logistics Group, a 158‑year‑old UK transportation firm, by guessing an employee’s weak password. The hackers locked the company’s data and demanded a $6.6 million ransom, forcing KNP to shut down and lay off 700 workers.

This year, suspected Iranian hackers gained access to US water supply systems due to internet-connected devices that used default passwords — or none at all.

The rise of the AI era has also made password hacking easier. One study even found that some AI systems could determine people’s passwords by listening to their keystrokes.

NordPass has conducted its Top 200 Most Common Passwords analysis since 2019. To compile its lists, NordPass and independent researchers examined passwords exposed in public data breaches and dark web repositories, then organized and categorized the data by country of origin.

NordPass has found that password habits are heavily influenced by current trends and culture. Over the last several years, some of the top three passwords have been Lebron0319 (in reference to NBA star LeBron James), Savage20 (musical group) and roblox.com1 (video game). In the 2010s, the top three were Lachimolala (meme), telegram (social media) and minecraft (video game).

But while these passwords might make us feel nostalgic for these time capsules of experiences, interests and entertainment, they don’t translate to strong internet security. “Unfortunately, fandoms make for terrible passwords,” the NordPass report notes.

Passwords based on pop culture, current events and sports can be easily predicted or cracked in seconds using automated tools, especially if your interests are visible on public social media profiles. Adding a number to the end of a password doesn’t help — attackers program their tools to test common number combinations and symbol swaps.

Given all the accounts we deal with — financial institutions, social media, stores, government agencies — creating dozens of unique passwords and remembering them can be exhausting and annoying.

“Inventing passwords that meet that criterion across hundreds of logins is virtually impossible, which is why we recommend password managers to create long, complex passwords and then store them all for you,” said Benjamin.

A password manager creates and updates passwords for apps, Wi-Fi networks and websites, ensuring that all your passwords are unique and resistant to bot attacks. Another plus is that you don’t have to remember them or write them down: They’re stored in an encrypted vault you can access by verifying your identity. Password managers can also auto-fill login credentials.

CNET senior writer Joe Supan said the best password managers also offer passkeys, which are ways of logging into apps and websites using biometric ID, such as facial or fingerprint scans, or PIN codes. “These are really the sign-in methods of the future, and I probably wouldn’t recommend a password manager that doesn’t include them at this point,” Supan said.

CNET’s top two recommendations for password managers are NordPass and Bitwarden.

#3015. Ray Dalio says Bessent move is sign that a debt crisis is getting closer; recommends gold and bitcoin

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's debt buyback announcement this week fits into a broader pattern that can signal a forthcoming crisis, according to billionaire investor Ray Dalio.

The Bridgewater Associates founder said Bessent's plan to increase government debt purchases may portend trouble for the U.S. economy. Coupled with the Japanese government reducing its U.S. bond market exposure and surging long-dated American bond yields, Dalio said investors may want to prepare their portfolios for increased risk by owning cryptocurrencies and gold.

"I am confident that the government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote in a LinkedIn post published Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Dalio noted that the Treasury Department has "only limited capacity" to buy back bonds. Bessent told CNBC on Thursday that his team was going to "make a market" and that the purchases would likely top $4 billion.

The U.S. is spending about 40% more than it's bringing in, resulting in the burgeoning budget deficit, Dalio said. The U.S. budget deficit topped $432 billion in July, but Bessent told CNBC that it's likely peaked under President Donald Trump's administration.

Bessent said in the interview that a team was looking at ways to shrink spending by hundreds of billions of dollars. But Dalio said there is "very little ability" to do so given that it is either committed or considered essential.

After years of overspending, Dalio said total debt now dwarfs what the U.S. brings in each year. If the U.S. government was a business, Dalio said debt service payments would come in at roughly $11 trillion — about 200% of annual revenue.

Dalio, 77, warned the cost of repaying principal and servicing the debt will only grow over time.

To solve this, Dalio said the U.S. needs to carefully employ a three-part strategy to get the budget deficit down to 3% of gross domestic product.

First, Dalio said the U.S. government needs to reduce its spending. Second, he said tax revenue needs to be raised. Finally, the New York native and Harvard Business School alumni said lower interest rates were needed.

"All three need to happen concurrently so as to prevent any one from being too large," Dalio said. "If any one is too large, the adjustment will be traumatic."

Dalio cautioned against ramming through these adjustments by "force." For instance, "it would be very bad if the Federal Reserve unnaturally forced interest rates down," he said.

Dalio said it's important to to take steps now, while the economy is healthy. An economy in recession requires increased government spending, he said.

Dalio said the exact timing of a debt crisis can be swayed by variables ranging from military conflict to political change. On its current trajectory, the U.S. could enter such a crisis in as early as one year or as late as five. "My guess, which I suppose will be a bad one, is that it will come in three years, give or take two, if the course we're on is not changed."

To prepare, Dalio recommended investors are underweight debt assets, such as bonds.

As much as 10% to 15% of a portfolio could land in gold, as well as "a bit" of bitcoin, the hedge fund founder said.

Dalio's post came at the tail end of a volatile week for U.S. financial markets. Rising long-term Treasury yields have pressured stocks, leading the S&P 500 to snap a a three-week-long advance.
