#3013. 5 Brokerage Features We’re Excited for in 2027 (And 2 Things We Could Do Without)

NerdWallet, Inc. is an independent publisher and comparison service, not an investment advisor. Its articles, interactive tools and other content are provided to you for free, as self-help tools and for informational purposes only. They are not intended to provide investment advice. NerdWallet does not and cannot guarantee the accuracy or applicability of any information in regard to your individual circumstances. Examples are hypothetical, and we encourage you to seek personalized advice from qualified professionals regarding specific investment issues. Our estimates are based on past market performance, and past performance is not a guarantee of future performance.

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. And while our site doesn’t feature every company or financial product available on the market, we’re proud that the guidance we offer, the information we provide and the tools we create are objective, independent, straightforward — and free.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us. This may influence which products we review and write about (and where those products appear on the site), but it in no way affects our recommendations or advice, which are grounded in thousands of hours of research. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews of their products or services. Here is a list of our partners.

Brokerages are vying for your dollars with truly helpful tools, expansive lineups of investment products and AI everywhere. Here are five features that we’re excited about — and two things we don’t love and are watching closely.

The investing information provided on this page is for educational purposes only. NerdWallet, Inc. does not offer advisory or brokerage services, nor does it recommend or advise investors to buy or sell particular stocks, securities or other investments.

Each fall, our investing team spends the latter half of the year hands-on testing a wide range of brokers, from legacy firms like Charles Schwab and Fidelity to newer, mobile-first firms like Public and M1.

This year, we opened or tested more than 15 brokerage accounts, funded them and placed real trades. We sent each broker a detailed questionnaire covering more than 65 data points and then verified, categorized and scored their responses using our proprietary scoring system. And finally, though our team is spread across the U.S., we met in person to compare the experience of using each platform.

While our updated reviews and final star ratings are still in the works, here is a preview of five things that really stood out to us this season — and two things we’re feeling a bit wary of.

Setting up buy and sell orders can be a pain point for some investors, especially beginners. Until recently, every platform required you to type in the ticker symbol, choose between dollars and shares, punch in the numbers and choose your order type. This creates opportunities for mistakes.

In recent months, AI has stepped in to help. Many platforms have launched agents that you can ask to set up trades for you using natural language. Beginners aren’t the only people who benefit; some trading agents can also set up automated strategies based on prompts, thereby saving advanced traders a lot of time and effort monitoring the markets.

Public’s “Agents” feature, which started rolling out in March and became available to all users in August, has become a trailblazer in agentic trading. It can place trades for you, set up recurring trades to automate a strategy (Managing Editor Chris Davis experimented with a “buy the open, sell the close” strategy for a while), and even sweep uninvested cash into one of Public’s high-yield cash management account options.

Robinhood also waded into the agentic trading space in early 2025 with the launch of its Cortex assistant, whose early iterations could place individual trades for you. In September of this year, the broker began rolling out Robinhood Agents, a more sophisticated natural-language interface that can build automated strategies based on a prompt, similar to Public’s Agents.

Interactive Brokers also offers a simple AI agent (IBot) that can set up trades for you, as does Cash App (Moneybot), but these are limited to one-time actions and cannot automate more complex strategies. Still, they can simplify the trading experience for beginners. That might be especially valuable to Cash App users, given the platform’s “My First Brokerage” ethos.

» Curious about trading with a text prompt? Compare brokers with AI trading tools

There’s been another profound shift in the past year that involves AI: agents that can actually help you manage your brokerage account. So far, some of the newer, mobile-first platforms seem to have an edge over the long-established financial behemoths. It’s also a mind-bending gray area: If an AI is giving you portfolio advice, who’s accountable for the advice it gives? Can you trust it? And how is it any different from a robo-advisor?

In our reviews this year, we looked into these questions. But here's a quick look at how one platform in particular is approaching this new frontier.

From my testing over the years, I was already a huge fan of M1’s portfolio-building system, and now that it's integrated an AI advisor into the app (to be specific, M1 bills it as an SEC-registered AI fiduciary investment advisor legally required to act in your best interest), M1 has created what I truly think is a one-of-a-kind product and service. I checked the forms M1 is required to submit to the SEC, and the company declares outright that the AI advisor looks at your entire financial situation and gives actionable recommendations. In my experience with the app, those recommendations are based on your balances, the knowledge you provide and the ongoing conversations you have. There’s a lot to discuss here, which we’ll cover in our full M1 review, but suffice it to say, this is very impressive.

Most brokers don’t charge many fees these days. Trading, inactivity and account fees have slowly but surely disappeared, making investing more affordable over the years. But there is one fee you still have to pay: an expense ratio.

Most of the time, brokers have little control over expense ratios, since they’re set by fund managers. The only way a broker could offer an index fund without an expense ratio is if it was big enough to eat the cost.

This is exactly what Fidelity did back in 2018, when they introduced their “ZERO” funds. These funds have no expense ratios and no minimums, meaning they’re totally free for investors.

Fidelity remained the only broker to offer this kind of fund until 2025, when E*TRADE introduced a very similar lineup of no-expense-ratio index funds. The suite of funds from both brokers is fairly broad — think large-cap, total market, international — which makes them especially attractive to beginners building a portfolio from scratch.

Now, you may be wondering why these brokers decided to stray from the industry standard and offer products that don’t make them money. The idea is that the free funds will get you in the door — since you can only buy them if you have an account with that particular broker — and you’ll spend money on some other product they offer.

But does that make free index funds any less great? No. I still think it’s a big step toward making investing more accessible for everyone, and I’m excited to see which brokers might add a similar offering in the future.

» Take a closer look: Compare Fidelity's and E*TRADE's free index funds

I'm a big believer in putting every dollar to work, but that goal can sometimes fall through the cracks. Idle cash sitting uninvested in your brokerage account is a common oversight. It can easily pile up if you forget to reinvest sale proceeds or dividends (something I do more often than I’d like to admit). Or maybe you leave it parked for too long in your brokerage’s default account while waiting on a good investment opportunity.

Thankfully, most brokerages offer some form of interest on that uninvested money. Some put the idle funds in a money market fund, which can offer yields that mirror market rates. Others “sweep” your unused cash into partner banks to take advantage of FDIC insurance.

In today’s environment, people with money in savings vehicles like high-yield savings accounts or new CDs are well-positioned to take advantage of high rates. What sets some brokerages apart is whether they operate similarly. That is, do they raise rates in response to larger economic circumstances? And if so, how quickly?

Robinhood and Public are two firms on our radar that are offering competitive rates in response to hikes, ranging from 3.6% to 3.75% as of this writing. Robinhood requires a premium subscription to unlock those higher rates, while Public’s already high base rate of 3.3% applies to all users and can be boosted to 3.75% with a Reserve membership. For investors who keep a lot of cash in their account, the extra fee can be worth it.

Interest rates, of course, shouldn’t be the main reason you pick one broker over another. Costs, the types of securities available and platform usability are better starting points. But when a company meets those expectations and also offers a compelling interest rate on your uninvested money, it’s worth taking a closer look.

» See which brokers pay the most on idle cash: Best brokerages for high interest rates

Direct indexing is a strategy in which you replicate an existing stock index (like the S&P 500, for example) but customize it how you like. The most popular reason people choose direct indexing is for tax optimization — but it’s not the only one.

Direct indexing can also be used to avoid overexposure to a specific company. For instance, if you work at Apple and get company stock, you probably don’t need even more exposure to Apple through the S&P 500. Direct indexing lets you replace that one stock with a similar company instead.

And then there’s the reason direct indexing appealed to me: it lets you avoid buying into companies you just don’t support. I’m sure we all invest in companies we don’t necessarily mesh with morally, but direct indexing can help you avoid that.

The strategy used to be available only to people with an advisor managing their investment account, and they had to have millions to get started. More recently, these minimums have dropped. And now, it’s not just for people with financial advisors — online brokers offer the strategy, too.

While some brokers still have steep minimums of $100,000 or so, others let you get started with less. Fidelity, in true Fidelity fashion, started offering direct indexing to clients a few years ago through a managed portfolio that has a minimum investment requirement of only $5,000.

I was pleased to see Public launch direct indexing with a minimum of only $1,000 a year ago. However, we should note that with a low investment amount, you can only track a portion of an index.

But even with those limitations, I think it’s great that these companies are putting out the message that there shouldn’t be a huge barrier to entry to customize your portfolio. As direct indexing continues to gain popularity, we’ll be watching whether more brokers start offering it, as advancements in AI undoubtedly make it easier to do so.

It’s hard to ignore the rise of prediction markets in the mainstream. These days, it takes just a few clicks to bet on who might win the Super Bowl or take home a Grammy. These markets, which operate on contracts with binary outcomes, are easy to access and use everyday language, making them all the more tempting to try — and now they are beginning to appear on many broker platforms and apps.

We’d like to be clear on this one: Our editors have no intention of telling you how to spend your extra discretionary money. If you have a solid financial foundation and have allocated a few bucks to bet on some event contracts, that’s all good. But as editors who view investing apps as vehicles for legitimate wealth-building strategies, we draw the line at these products being marketed alongside other investments, such as stocks, ETFs and mutual funds.

In fact, this year we’ve actually decided to dock points in our annual reviews and ratings from brokerages that offer unrestricted access to event and sports-style prediction markets. In our view, these products aren’t conducive to long-term investing, and they’re speculative without enough oversight — a troublesome combination. You can read more about our stance and why we’re taking it here.

I’d venture to say that since the dawn of social media, people have been talking about investing online. And nowadays, the online investing community is huge. The r/investing subreddit has more than 3.5 million followers, and even on a video-forward platform like TikTok, #investing has 4.1 million posts under it.

But is where people go to talk about investing online changing?

The first broker I saw incorporate a social media–style element into its platforms was etoro. When you scroll down on the app's “home” tab, you’re met with what looks like an X feed. And the CopyTrader feature lets you copy another person’s portfolio, with that section of the app highlighting “trending investors,” “market outperformers,” and more.

This wasn’t a huge surprise to me coming from a niche broker with presumably a large user base of active traders. What surprised me was when Robinhood added a social media-style section to its app, testing a beta version in March and expanding it to all U.S. users in October.

Robinhood Social is, again, much like an X feed but for showing people which stocks you’re buying or selling. When I created an account to see what it was all about, the app encouraged me to share my “stats” on my profile (my one-day and one-year profit and loss, and my profit rate). “Trading stats build trust and transparency on Social,” the app said.

You could argue that other, even bigger brokers promote social trading. Fidelity, for example, has a “customer orders” section that shows how many Fidelity users are buying and selling certain stocks (though, I’ll say, they don’t promote this feature and it’s buried in the app).

The huge difference, in my opinion, is that Fidelity leaves it up to you to research these stocks. There’s no feed or comment section. On etoro and Robinhood, people can say whatever they want about why they bought or sold a certain security — whether truthful or not — or worse, why you should or shouldn’t invest in something.

To me, the whole concept of social trading feels like the antithesis of long-term investing. It’s a trend that I hope we don’t see becoming more popular among big-name brokers.

#3012. Top Wall Street analysts believe in the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East and soaring bond yields weighed on global markets this past week. And investors are closely assessing the valuations of artificial intelligence stocks amid concerns about the sustainability of high spending on AI infrastructure.

Despite those continued challenges, top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the prospects of several stocks due to their long-run growth potential and exposure to lucrative business lines, including AI.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike Holdings (CRWD) is this week's first stock pick. The company is scheduled to announce fiscal second-quarter results on August 26.

Ahead of Q2 FY27 earnings, Truist analyst Junaid Siddiqui reiterated a buy rating on CrowdStrike stock and raised his price target to $245 from $187.50. Following CrowdStrike's impressive fiscal first-quarter performance and guidance raise, Siddiqui expects another strong quarter.

The 5-star analyst's optimism is backed by continued strength in Falcon Flex adoption and encouraging large deal activity. Siddiqui also cited continued momentum across emerging products. With the FY27 outlook assuming persistent strength in CrowdStrike's net new annual recurring revenue (ARR), Siddiqui is more focused on the longevity of key growth catalysts such as Falcon Flex adoption, platform consolidation and AI-led demand.

The analyst highlighted that talks with partners were encouraging, with pipeline generation and momentum in large deals remaining healthy in the fiscal second quarter despite tough, year-over-year comparisons.

"We continue to view CrowdStrike as one of the primary beneficiaries of platform consolidation, though we expect investors to remain focused on competitive dynamics and whether current growth levels represent a new baseline or a period of demand acceleration," the analyst said.

Siddiqui ranks No. 226 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 80% of the time, delivering an average return of about 40%. See CrowdStrike Financials on TipRanks.

Shares of personal computer maker Dell Technologies (DELL) have rallied 251% this year, driven by strong demand for AI servers. Recently, Evercore analyst Amit Daryanani reiterated a buy rating on DELL and raised his price target to $550 from $500.

The 5-star analyst contends that while Dell's AI compute segment is getting investors' attention, the company's Storage business is underappreciated and well-positioned to drive revenue and profit acceleration. Daryanani expects the storage business to see higher demand once enterprises start to bring workload back on-premises.

The analyst highlighted that Dell's Storage business, estimated to account for only 10% of FY27 revenue, is one of the factors that could help improve profit margins, given its higher profitability compared to AI servers. Daryanani estimates that the Storage business's operating margin is currently in the low-20% range, while margins for the AI server and traditional server businesses are in the mid-single-digit and mid-teens range, respectively.

Overall, Daryanani views the Storage business as an important catalyst for three reasons: Dell has one of the broadest storage portfolios in the industry; Storage has a significantly higher margin profile than AI servers; and the shift toward proprietary, software-defined storage and AI-focused platforms.

"We think DELL's storage business is becoming increasingly strategic as AI infrastructure deployments move beyond GPU procurement and toward full stack + AI-ready architectures," said Daryanani.

Daryanani ranks No. 19 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 38.70%. See Dell Technologies Statistics on TipRanks.

SanDisk (SNDK) is benefiting from AI-driven demand for its memory and storage products. Following the company's 2026 Investor Day event, J.P. Morgan analyst Harlan Sur resumed research coverage of SNDK with a buy rating (it was earlier, "Not Rated") and a price target of $2,250.

The 5-star analyst believes SanDisk is well-positioned to capitalize on a structural inflection reached in NAND demand, driven by strong growth in AI inference. Sur's bullishness is based on three key factors.

First, Sur believes that SanDisk's New Business Model (NBM) framework (or long-term agreements) has enhanced its margin profile and reduced cyclicality. SNDK's eight signed NBMs represent a total contract value of $94 billion and a gross margin of about 80%, even at the floor pricing.

Second, Sur highlighted the growing NAND market and expects the total addressable market to surge from about $70 billion in calendar year 2025 to over $300 billion in 2026 and about $500 billion in 2027. Importantly, the analyst noted that data centers are the largest driver of NAND growth, as hyperscalers increasingly deploy flash for AI inference workloads.

Finally, Sur is optimistic on SanDisk due to its technology dominance. The company's BiCS10 technology is sampling ahead of schedule and has 65% more bits per wafer than BiCS8, the analyst said. Also, Sur expects SanDisk's High Bandwidth Flash to become a differentiated memory platform for AI inference.

"Layered on top, mgmt's commitment to returning 100% of excess cash flow to shareholders should drive an aggressive share count reduction trajectory that further amplifies EPS growth on a per-share basis," said Sur.

Sur ranks No. 15 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 43.20%. See SanDisk Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#3010. Stock Market Today, Nov. 18: CoreWeave Slides as Nvidia's Blowout Earnings Fail to Ease Debt Concerns

Booming demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure is doing little to alleviate investor concerns about the financial costs of keeping pace with the industry's rapid expansion.

By RJ Fulton – Nov 18, 2026 at 4:45PM EST

CoreWeave (CRWV -4.13%) fell 4.13% on Wednesday, November 18, closing at $47.83. Strong quarterly earnings from Nvidia (NVDA -2.90%) initially lifted CoreWeave shares in premarket trading, but those gains quickly evaporated as investors shifted their attention back to the company's substantial debt burden and ongoing financing needs. Despite booming demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, Wall Street remains increasingly concerned about the financial costs of sustaining that growth.

Trading volume reached 58.9 million shares, approximately 28% above its three-month daily average of 45.9 million. Despite recent selling pressure, CoreWeave shares remain up approximately 20% since the company's initial public offering in 2025.

The broader market delivered mixed results on Wednesday. The S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.23%) fell 0.24% to 7,323, while the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +0.42%) gained 0.42% to 24,430.

Despite modest strength in technology stocks, AI infrastructure providers remained under pressure. CoreWeave's peer IREN (IREN -3.58%) fell 3.61% to $15.24, underscoring growing investor concerns about the substantial capital requirements and financing costs associated with expanding AI computing capacity.

It is clear that demand for AI infrastructure remains exceptionally strong. Last week, CoreWeave reported year-over-year revenue growth of 168% and raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to between $13 billion and $13.3 billion. However, the market's reaction to Nvidia's earnings suggests investors are becoming less concerned about the strength of AI demand and more concerned about the financial costs of meeting it.

CoreWeave is targeting profitability in 2028, leaving the company with a considerable period during which it must finance its expansion. With the 10-year Treasury yield above 5%, elevated borrowing costs present a significant headwind for a business that relies heavily on debt financing to acquire computing hardware and expand data center capacity.

Looking ahead, investors should pay particularly close attention to CoreWeave's financing arrangements, capital expenditures, and ability to convert contracted customer demand into cash flow. Long-term customer contracts and prepayments provide some financial stability, but the timing of those cash inflows relative to infrastructure spending remains critical.

While CoreWeave's revenue growth is impressive, the investment thesis increasingly depends on whether the company can generate sufficient returns on its substantial capital investments. Until there is greater visibility into sustainable profitability, strong revenue growth alone may not be enough to restore investor confidence.

#3009. 5 Student Loan Scams to Avoid in 2026

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Student loan scams use pressure tactics and make false promises. Here’s what to watch out for.

Student loan scams can be costly, but they usually leave clues. Scammers will often try to hook victims with tempting claims of “act now or miss out” and “we promise to get you student aid."

The communication might seem realistic, but unexpected fees, unknown contacts and big promises are usually red flags. The age-old adage is true: if an offer sounds too good to be true, it probably is.

Here’s a breakdown of common student loan scams and what to do about them.

» MORE: How to spot student loan repayment scams

The scam: A fraudulent private company offers to manage your student loans and help you get them relieved or even fully forgiven. These services can cost more than $1,000, and there’s no guarantee that you’ll actually get the help you’re looking for.

How to avoid it: You can manage your federal student loans for free. According to the U.S. Department of Education, you never have to pay for help with your federal student loans[1]U.S. Department of Education. Avoiding Student Aid Scams. View all sources . You can work with your loan servicer to adjust your payment plan, consolidate loans and apply for loan forgiveness at no cost to you.

If you’re being promised immediate student loan forgiveness, are asked for personal identification information like your FAFSA login credentials or asked to authorize a power of attorney, proceed with caution — it’s likely a scam.

» MORE: How to get help with student loans

The scam: A company charges you an upfront fee to combine multiple student loans into one new loan to reduce your monthly payment. The company may be illegitimate and is likely to pocket the fee without actually consolidating your loans.

How to avoid it: You can consolidate federal student loans for free. There is no fee to consolidate your loans through the Department of Education at studentaid.gov. If you’re looking to reduce your monthly payment through consolidation, start by contacting your loan servicer. And if you get unsolicited communication from a company promising federal student loan consolidation, it's probably a scam.

The scam: Scammers use transitions in federal loan programs to take advantage of borrowers. For example, the Education Department was set to resume wage garnishments after a long pause, but in January 2026 announced a temporary delay implement repayment reforms.

When federal decisions go back and forth like this, it creates a gray area for scammers to make wage garnishment threats. For borrowers who may not know if wage garnishment restarted, it can be hard to know what to do. This goes for other federal changes, too; any uncertainty can be an opportunity for bad actors to take advantage of the confusion.

How to avoid it: If your wages are truly being garnished, the communication will come from the federal government and not a private company. Likewise, if a company offers to stop your wage garnishment for a fee, you’re probably getting scammed.

The scam: Criminals impersonate a real person and apply to colleges in their name. Then, they can collect financial aid, take out loans and use their college admission to net discounts on goods and services. This is known as a “ghost student” scam.

How to avoid it: Follow the steps on identitytheft.gov to report fraud and get a recovery plan. There are a few safeguards you can put in place to prevent this form of identity theft, such as setting up a credit freeze and monitoring your FSA ID activity.

How it works: You might receive a call from someone claiming to be from your school’s financial aid office saying you have unpaid tuition. The caller may threaten that you cannot start your classes until your tuition bill is paid in full. Scammers can be creative and convincing, even going so far as to replicate a school’s phone number to display on your caller ID.

How to avoid it: The Federal Trade Commission warns that schools will not call and pressure you to pay tuition[2]Federal Trade Commission. Got a call about unpaid college tuition? It could be a scam. Accessed Nov 16, 2026. View all sources . Rather than trust the caller, use your school's secure student portal to check your account balance. Know for certain what you owe and to whom before sending money. You can also call your financial aid office to confirm the legitimacy of a phone number that has called you requesting tuition funds.

Realizing you’ve been scammed is stressful, and it’s natural to feel overwhelmed or embarrassed. But acting quickly can make a real difference. The sooner you report what happened, the better your chances of limiting the financial damage and getting your accounts back on track. Here’s what to do:

If you’ve already paid a scammer, report the problem to the bank that issued the payment. If you paid with a credit card, for instance, contact the company and tell them what happened. They may be able to freeze your account or reverse the transaction.

Reach out to your federal student loan servicer as well and report what happened. They can check to make sure no changes have been made to your account and, in the case that changes did occur, they can help you get your loan back on track.

File complaints with the Education Department, the Federal Trade Commission and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Filing complaints with these agencies helps hold scammers accountable, can result in enforcement action or business shutdowns, and in some cases may help you recover lost funds.

#3006. Beyond Token Counts: A Framework For Measuring AI ROI

Monica Bajaj is the Senior Vice President of Engineering at Okta.

Engineering leaders are facing an uncomfortable AI reality. Token consumption is soaring, while true business impact often remains unclear. Companies want their teams to embrace AI, but there’s growing pressure to demonstrate a return on that investment. Engineering leaders want to see greater velocity. Security leaders want to ensure that all systems are safe. Finance leaders want to know how dollars are spent and if they are getting the proper return. It’s a three-edged sword, and that tension is building every day.​

Part of the problem is that our systems, architectures and workflows were designed for humans. AI agents are the new kid on the block. Humans find workarounds when processes aren’t working. Agents can continue looping, consuming resources without producing meaningful results. We need to rethink how we measure AI’s value, distinguishing between consumption and outcomes.

In my opinion, token consumption measures system activity, not business value. It tells you what you’re spending, not what you’re getting in return. A sharp increase in token volume can reflect inefficient system design, bloated prompts, repetitive trial and error or agents caught in unnecessary loops. Someone might repeatedly prompt an AI tool because the output isn’t useful, consuming more tokens without improving productivity.

That’s why I believe we need to shift our mindset from cost per token to cost per successful outcome. Instead of measuring consumption alone, evaluate the cost per resolved task, quality and defect rates, task completion velocity and caching efficiency. Evaluate whether a use case needs AI or would be better served by traditional automation.

We should always be asking whether we’re getting meaningful outcomes at a reasonable cost.

To evaluate AI investments, I’ve developed a framework called SQUAD. It looks at five dimensions engineering leaders should consider together.

Security: Is AI introducing systemic risks or vulnerabilities? We need to measure how many vulnerabilities are detected before code is merged and what proportion of AI-generated code requires security remediation.

Quality And Reliability: Is the codebase getting healthier, or is it degrading because of AI-generated work? Faster code generation doesn’t mean much if we’re introducing more defects. Change failure rates, bug density, code churn and test coverage help us understand the actual impact.

Unit Economics: Does the output we’re getting justify the per-seat and compute costs? Instead of focusing exclusively on token consumption, measure cost per merged pull request, cost per successful task completion and whether we’re using the right models for the right tasks.

Acceleration And Velocity: Are our teams shipping business outcomes faster? Look at pull request review cycles, lead time for changes and whether we’re actually delivering more value rather than simply generating more code and PRs.

Developer Experience: Are these tools helping engineers be more productive or creating additional pain? Consider developer sentiment, review fatigue and time spent correcting AI-generated work.

Evaluate these dimensions together. The substantial improvement in pull request throughput isn’t considered a win if the number of security issues or quality failures has risen. It’s also crucial to look beyond code acceptance rates. What is the gain if the engineer accepts AI-generated code and then spends an hour refactoring it?

SQUAD helps us understand whether AI improves engineering rather than simply accelerating individual activities.

Experimentation is extremely important. With AI, it’s faster and easier to experiment, fail fast and learn. But we have to balance that freedom with responsible spending.

Build innovation sandboxes separate from production pipelines, giving developers reasonable testing quotas. Give developers reasonable caps or quotas for freeform testing. When someone reaches that limit, don’t automatically shut down the project. Instead, evaluate the prototype’s validity and whether it can graduate to a production-level budget.

Another important practice is what I call model-conscious engineering. People often use the most powerful model for the simplest tasks. But you don’t need a frontier model to generate boilerplate code or format JSON. Use dynamic model routing to match the task’s complexity with the appropriate model, balancing quality, cost and latency.

Architectural hygiene is equally imperative. Caching, better prompt design and limiting the tools available to agents can reduce unnecessary consumption.

We’ve asked teams to adopt AI; now we need to educate them on using it effectively and efficiently.

My philosophy is to regulate the data, not the tool. Models and tools are continuously evolving, but organizations can establish consistent policies around their information. I use three categories: green for public information, yellow for internal proprietary information that requires approved enterprise environments and red for restricted or confidential information that shouldn’t be exposed to unauthorized AI systems.

Human accountability is equally vital. When you commit code, you own it. The responsibility doesn’t belong to the agent. Developers must be able to justify their work, including its security, performance and edge cases.

We also need to be enablers, not blockers. If you tell a team of problem solvers they can’t use the sharpest tool on the market, they’ll find a workaround. Providing secure, enterprise-approved access is far more effective than creating unnecessary barriers.

As AI adoption expands into product and design, we need to rethink how value is measured across teams. For engineering, we’re looking at velocity, quality, security and how quickly we’re shipping features.

For product teams, we should measure discovery cycle time, not how many product requirement documents people are generating. AI should help teams validate problems, gather customer insights and reach cross-functional alignment faster.

For design teams, the focus should be on broader exploration, testing different workflows and reducing the back-and-forth before engineering begins.

Engineering, product and design need to work together rather than operating in silos. Otherwise, we risk generating more AI slop that creates additional work downstream (when that happens, the net ROI can actually be negative).

Ultimately, we want to deliver better outcomes at a reasonable cost. With the right framework, guardrails and mindset, we can encourage innovation while guaranteeing our AI investments create meaningful business value.​

#3004. Survey: Gen Z Loves a Winter Challenge, but Money Goals Often Fizzle

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Gen Zers are apt to try cold-weather challenges like “winter arc.” But they’re also the generation most likely to say they generally quit challenges before finishing and set the same money goal more than once due to not sticking with it.

It’s not technically winter yet, but depending on where you live, it may feel like it. For many of us, this is a time of hibernation, but for others, it’s prime time for a glow-up.

“Winter arc” is a popular social media challenge through which people aim to improve themselves before the new year. It typically runs from October through December, but can be started any time during the cold months. The aim is to jump-start the “new year, new me” season before the ball even drops.

Whether they call it a winter arc or not, plenty of Americans are working on self-improvement as the chill sets in. According to a new NerdWallet survey, conducted online by The Harris Poll, 75% of Americans say they’re working on their physical health, and 69% say the same about their finances.

Popular as it is, winter arc isn’t the only cold-weather challenge out there. The survey found that half of Americans (50%) say they’ve tried some sort of winter improvement challenge. And no one likes a challenge like Gen Z: Nearly three-quarters of Gen Zers (74%) have tried a winter challenge, compared with 64% of millennials, 42% of Gen Xers and 29% of baby boomers.

Note: The survey defines Gen Zers as those 18-29; millennials, ages 30-45; Gen Xers, ages 46-61 and baby boomers, ages 62-80.

But there’s a difference between starting a challenge and successfully completing one. Gen Zers reign supreme as those most likely to hop on a winter challenge. But they’re also the most likely to say they generally quit challenges before finishing, buy products they saw on social media in an effort to stick with the challenges and set the same financial goal more than once.

Gen Zers are more likely than any other generation to say they:

Have tried a winter financial challenge other than no-spend January (21%, vs. 11% of millennials, 5% of Gen Xers and 2% of baby boomers).

Generally quit challenges before they finish them (59%, vs. 42% of millennials, 36% of Gen Xers and 22% of baby boomers).

Expect to spend more on at least one discretionary expense this winter than they would during another season (90%, vs. 83% of millennials, 61% of Gen Xers and 48% of baby boomers).

Put off dealing with money until after the holidays (60%, vs. 47% of millennials, 35% of Gen Xers and 15% of baby boomers).

Aren’t currently working on improving their finances, but want to make it a priority (15%, vs. 8% of millennials and 6% each of Gen Xers and baby boomers).

“Embracing the winter arc trend can be a great way to find motivation to make progress on a goal over the slower winter months,” says Kimberly Palmer, personal finance expert at NerdWallet. “Pick a winter challenge that aligns with a longer-term goal for the coming year.”

Winter challenges popular with Gen Z include diet- or fitness-related challenges (29%) and self-improvement challenges, like winter arc or 75 Hard, a mental toughness challenge that runs for 75 days and includes two workouts every day, a strict diet and daily nonfiction reading (25%).

While winter arcs typically focus on physical, mental and intellectual self-improvement, Gen Z is game to try a financial challenge as well: One long-standing financial challenge — no-spend January — is more popular among younger Americans (22% of Gen Zers and 20% of millennials) than their older counterparts (12% of Gen Xers and 6% of baby boomers). As for other types of financial challenges, Gen Z is more likely than any other generation to have tried at least one: 21% compared with 11% of millennials, 5% of Gen X and 2% of baby boomers.

Of course, it’s one thing to try a challenge, during wintertime or otherwise. It’s another thing entirely to follow through and complete it. That’s the hard part for many Gen Zers.

When taking on a self-improvement challenge, the beginning tends to be easiest. You’re motivated and excited to reach goals and better yourself. But as time goes on, it’s easy to slip back into old habits or for the shine of a brand-new challenge to dim. And Gen Zers report that they are most likely to quit early.

According to the survey, nearly 3 in 5 Gen Zers (59%) say they generally quit challenges before they finish them. That compares with 42% of millennials, 36% of Gen Xers and 22% of baby boomers.

Along with challenges in general, money goals can be difficult to follow through with, especially for younger Americans. Around two-thirds of Gen Zers (64%) say it’s been hard to stick to financial goals they’ve set in the past, compared with 52% of Gen Xers and 34% of baby boomers. Gen Zers are more likely than any other generation to say they’ve set the same financial goal more than once because they didn’t stick with it — 33%, compared with 20% of millennials, 15% of Gen Xers and 7% of baby boomers.

This isn’t for lack of desire, though. Seven in 10 Gen Zers (70%) say they’re working on improving their finances. All generations show high levels of effort here: 76% each of millennials and Gen Xers say the same, along with 59% of baby boomers.

So why is it so hard to stick with money goals? One possibility is that it’s difficult to see meaningful progress on finances, particularly when you’re young. According to the survey, 65% of Gen Zers say it’s harder to see progress on financial goals than on physical goals.

This makes perfect sense for this age group — for those light on money but rich in youthfulness, desired physical changes may show up faster than financial progress. On top of that, the current job market is tough for younger Americans. Recent college grads now have a higher unemployment rate than workers in general. Even if you’re still on the job hunt, your 20s are a great time to start taking steps, however small, toward building future wealth.» MORE: I’m 25. Here’s How I Got Started Investing

“To increase your chances of success, try coordinating winter arc plans with a friend or giving yourself smaller goals along the way,” Palmer says. “Leaning on the support or coaching from a loved one can make it easier to keep going, as can celebrating incremental progress.”

Self-improvement is a noble pursuit. But as with most things in life, it’s easy to lose sight of the ultimate goal in favor of buying things to help you reach it.

“It’s easy to feel like a quick purchase can help us meet our goals, and sometimes a product can be a useful tool, but the reality is that true winter arc progress comes from putting in the hard work. There’s no option for ‘purchasing’ it instead,” Palmer says.

According to the survey, more than a quarter of Gen Zers (26%) say they’ve bought a product they saw on social media to help with a personal goal or challenge. This is more than any other generation: 17% of millennials, 11% of Gen Xers and 7% of baby boomers say they’ve made social media buys for self-betterment.

Some self-improvement purchases may be billed on a monthly basis. More than 1 in 5 Gen Zers (23%) say they're still paying for a subscription or membership they signed up for during a past goal or challenge. This is also true for 17% of millennials, 9% of Gen Xers and 2% of baby boomers.

These challenge purchases may pile onto already higher winter expenses. A majority of Gen Zers (90%) say they expect to spend more on at least one discretionary expense this winter than they would during another season, more than any other generation. Top expenses include food delivery (38%), entertainment at home (35%) and indoor family entertainment (30%). A quarter of Gen Zers (25%) expect to spend more on fitness or wellness apps this winter compared to other seasons.

Some may be spending more to make themselves feel better during the cold, gray months. Nearly 1 in 5 Gen Zers (18%) say they tend to combat winter blues by spending money, compared with 10% of Gen Xers and 3% of baby boomers.

The holiday season is an expensive time of year for many of us, and it’s easy to sweep finances under the rug until the new year. According to the survey, 3 in 5 Gen Zers (60%) say they generally put off dealing with money until after the holidays. This is more than any other generation: 47% of millennials, 35% of Gen Xers and 15% of baby boomers say the same.

Even for those taking on financial challenges before the new year hits, it’s easy for the resulting “savings” to disappear. Nearly three-quarters of Gen Zers (74%) say money they save by cutting back in one area usually just gets spent somewhere else instead of staying “saved.” This is also true for 68% of millennials, 63% of Gen Xers and 45% of baby boomers.

For some, the holidays are just one thing competing for their money. Over half of Gen Zers (52%) say they’d rather spend money on how they look now than save it for their future financial security. This compares with 26% of Gen Xers and 13% of baby boomers.

We don’t begrudge anyone for their desire to look and feel their best this upcoming season. But that doesn’t have to mean you can’t level up your money at the same time.

More than 2 in 5 Gen Zers (43%) say they’re putting consistent work into improving their finances, and 27% are putting some work into this, but not consistently. Moreover, 15% of Gen Zers aren’t working on improving their finances but want to make them a priority. No matter your age, here are some ideas for a financial glow-up before the spring thaw.

Start small if you tend to quit. Nearly 2 in 5 Americans (38%) say they generally quit challenges before finishing them. Early-challenge motivation can make it easy to overcommit. If you often take on challenges impulsively then peter out a few weeks later, try starting small. For example, maybe no-spend January is a stretch, but you can still save by intentionally creating two no-spend days a week.

Move money the day you save it. Over 3 in 5 Americans (61%) say money they save by cutting back in one area usually gets spent somewhere else. If you’re cutting back, transfer the difference to savings that same day, so it can’t leak out elsewhere.

Make money progress measurable. Half of Americans (50%) say it’s harder to see progress on financial goals than physical goals. There’s a saying that what gets measured, gets managed. Choose one number to track. This might be down payment savings, debt payoff progress or an investment milestone. It may not move much month to month, but you’d be surprised at the difference a year can make, even without a ton of money each month to dedicate toward your goal.

Begin before January. More than a third of Americans (37%) say they put off dealing with money until after the holidays. Facing your finances during the often busy and expensive final months of the year can be daunting, but don’t put your head in the sand until after the holiday credit card balances come due. Put a cap on your winter spending before the new year to avoid going overboard during the tempting sales this time of year.

“If you’re trying to choose a winter arc, pick one that’s realistic but also a stretch goal, so it’s satisfying to accomplish while not being completely out of reach,” Palmer suggests. “Chances are you’ll be glad with what you got done over the colder months when springtime hits.”

#3001. The 'debasement trade' returns after Bessent bond maneuver. Crypto and gold are back in style

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

The conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

Gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

Bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department said last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the plans.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "big toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

"Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold said in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah said. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah said in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining."

Coltman at 21Shares said the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh said in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

"The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, said Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

#3000. AI Delivered The Savings, But Can Your Business Sustain Them?

Kelvin Cheema is a Global CIO and transformation executive advising boards on technology, AI, transformation and enterprise value creation.

Imagine two businesses each reducing the cost of processing a transaction by 20%. Both report a legitimate improvement. In one, AI helps employees resolve difficult exceptions, captures specialist knowledge and strengthens the organization’s ability to improve. In the other, it performs work through which employees once developed judgement, leaving the business increasingly dependent on a supplier or a shrinking group of specialists.

The saving is identical. The future economics may not be. The figures are illustrative. The distinction is real.

I believe boards risk treating an immediate productivity gain as proof of sustainable enterprise value. Reducing the cost of today’s work matters. But it does not tell us whether the business is better equipped to deliver tomorrow’s performance. For that, we must examine what happens to the knowledge, judgement and operational capabilities behind the saving.

Research by Tania Babina, Alex He and Renhao Jiang associates AI investment with productivity growth through the accumulation of organizational capital: durable, firm-specific knowledge developed through learning by doing. Their findings suggest that AI can make an organization more capable rather than merely less labor-intensive.

That is the favorable outcome: lower costs accompanied by stronger capabilities that support future performance. But the same technology can change how those capabilities develop.

A controlled 12-week study involving more than 200 chess students offers a useful warning about the design of AI assistance. Students with additional help available on demand improved by 30%, compared with 64% among those receiving structured assistance. Chess is not corporate finance, and the experiment does not establish an effect on enterprise profitability. It illustrates a narrower point: Making assistance more convenient does not necessarily produce better independent learning.

Consider finance. Automating reconciliations can release capacity, strengthen controls and give teams more time to investigate anomalies. That is an attractive investment. But what if automation also removes the experience through which future finance leaders learn to recognize an unusual transaction, challenge an unexplained balance or understand why a control failed? Transactions may be processed faster while the organization becomes less able to investigate the exceptions that matter most.

I would not preserve inefficient manual work simply to train people. That would mistake a development method for a commercial objective. I would redesign how judgement is acquired, tested and retained while allowing automation to perform the work it does better.

The question is not whether AI should replace tasks. It is whether management has accounted for the capabilities those tasks once developed.

When AI changes how work is performed, it can also change where critical expertise resides and who controls it.

One business may embed knowledge in reliable workflows, accessible systems and employees who can improve them. Another may achieve the same cost reduction while becoming dependent on proprietary technology, external specialists or processes its people can no longer meaningfully challenge.

Neither arrangement is automatically superior. Buying external capability can be more economical and resilient than maintaining everything internally. But dependency has a price, even when it is absent from the original productivity calculation. What happens when a supplier changes its commercial terms? When an automated process fails under unfamiliar conditions? When the business must adapt a workflow that nobody internally fully understands?

These are not arguments against automation. They are questions about the cost of sustaining it. A serious investment case should account for switching costs, recovery capability and the consequences of losing control over critical knowledge.

This is where an operating model question becomes an investment question. Two businesses can report identical reductions in operating costs while warranting different assumptions about future margins and cash generation. One may have strengthened its ability to scale, adapt and resolve problems. The other may need recurring remediation, expensive supplier support or scarce specialist intervention to maintain its reported performance.

Those are different economic propositions.

A saving that creates reusable capability can support operating leverage. A saving that creates fragile dependencies may carry costs that emerge long after the initial benefit has been recognized.

The uncomfortable possibility is that both investments could pass the same financial approval process and subsequently be reported as equally successful. The business case captures the reduction in operating cost. The benefits dashboard confirms its delivery. Yet neither necessarily tests whether the organization has retained the ability to challenge, recover or adapt. That is a governance weakness, not merely a technology risk. Management may have delivered exactly what it promised while leaving the enterprise less capable of sustaining it.

Capability is not the only determinant of AI returns. Demand, implementation economics, reliability and competition also matter. But a board cannot judge the durability of a saving without understanding what the enterprise can still do, what it must buy and what it may struggle to recover.

A productivity dashboard measures what became cheaper. It does not necessarily reveal what became more valuable, more fragile or harder to replace. That is why I would challenge an AI business case that stops at hours released, headcount removed or cost per transaction. Can the enterprise still investigate exceptions, recover from failure, challenge its providers and develop the judgement required for decisions it remains accountable for?

AI can deliver exceptional operating leverage. It can also build organizational capabilities that compound beyond the original investment. But neither outcome follows automatically from a reported saving.

Before approving an AI investment, I would ask three questions: 1. What capability will this investment create, transfer or stop developing? 2. Where will that capability reside? 3. And what will it cost to sustain, recover or replace?

Productivity can be measured this quarter. The consequences of lost expertise, concentrated dependency or stronger institutional knowledge may emerge years later. The real test is not simply whether AI delivers the saving. It is whether the enterprise can sustain the value.​

#2998. AI Agents Reward-Max. Your Enterprise Needs To Govern The Path To The Goal

AI agents are designed to work toward a goal. Give one a task, the tools to act and broad enough permissions, and it will find a way to achieve its objective. Their intentions aren’t always malicious, but that doesn’t mean they don’t create enterprise risk. Agents don’t naturally understand a company’s internal norms, security policies or the difference between an efficient shortcut and an unacceptable one. They’ll do whatever it takes to achieve their goals.

Agents relentlessly pursue the reward embedded in their task. If the task is to resolve a support issue, generate a report, find a revenue opportunity or optimize a workflow, the agent will seek the actions most likely to achieve that outcome. The problem arises when its path crosses systems, data or actions that sit outside the authority it should have.

Enterprise leaders need to not only rethink authorization before they scale agents across the business but reevaluate whether the objectives they’re setting for their agents are achievable through a governed path.

For two decades, identity programs have largely centered on a durable question: Who is this person or system, and what access should it have?

That model was built for people working at human speed. An employee authenticates, receives a set of permissions and uses applications throughout the day. Security teams can review access periodically, investigate exceptions and revoke privileges when roles change.

AI agents operate differently. They can make thousands of requests in minutes, call multiple tools in sequence and move across systems without opening a dashboard or filing a help desk ticket. An agent may be authorized to access customer data, for example, but that doesn’t mean it should export records, alter permissions, invoke a financial workflow or use an unrelated internal tool to finish its assignment.

Authentication is still important. Every agent needs a unique, accountable identity that can be traced to a responsible owner. But authentication is the starting line, not the security program. That lies in the question “Should this agent be allowed to take this action, against this resource, on behalf of this user or process, for this task, right now?”

Organizations have learned that standing privilege creates unnecessary exposure. The same principle applies to agents, with higher stakes because the rate of execution is much faster.

Every agent should have a defined mission, a human owner and access that maps to the work it’s been asked to do. Its permissions should be narrow, time-bound and revocable. Access to a CRM doesn’t mean permission to change account ownership. Read access to a document repository doesn’t automatically create the right to download a large dataset or share it externally.

Agents need unique identities, clearly scoped job descriptions, short-lived credentials, logs and controls that evaluate their actions in context rather than accepting a one-time permission grant.

Leaders can begin with a practical set of controls:

• Assign every agent a unique identity and a named human owner.

• Document the agent’s purpose, permitted tools, data domains and expected outputs before it’s deployed.

• Once a task has been completed, nullify any credentials required for the agent to perform that task or follow that workflow.

• Separate read access from the ability to take consequential actions, like changing records, moving money, publishing content or sharing sensitive information.

• Require step-up authorization or human review when an agent requests access beyond its defined mission.

These controls aren’t an argument for adding manual approval to every agent action. That would recreate human bottlenecks in an environment built to operate at machine speed. The goal is to give agents room to act autonomously inside well-defined boundaries, then escalate only when the action is novel, sensitive, irreversible or outside the authority originally delegated to them.

Succeeding with agentic AI requires treating exceptions as a design requirement.

Consider an agent being asked to prepare a quarterly sales forecast. It may need to pull data from approved systems, analyze trends and/or produce a draft for sales leaders. Those are ordinary actions within the mission. If the agent attempts to modify compensation plans, export customer data to an unapproved third party or create a new OAuth connection, that’s a different category of action. The system should pause, deny the request or bring a human into the loop.

The human role is changing, not disappearing. People increasingly define the objective, establish the boundaries, evaluate the output and make the judgment calls when the work crosses into high-risk territory.

This hybrid model requires enterprises to improve their observability. Security and technology teams need to know which agents exist, who owns them, which credentials they use, what systems they can reach and what actions they’ve taken. If an organization can’t reconstruct an agent’s decision path and authorization context after an incident, it can’t govern that agent effectively.

The answer to reward-maxing isn’t to block agents until every risk has been eliminated. That approach will push employees toward shadow AI, unmanaged credentials and tools that security teams can’t see. Security teams need to create a governed path that’s easier than working around the rules.

Give employees approved tools, self-service access within policy, clear boundaries and fast escalation for legitimate exceptions. Build the controls into the infrastructure, not into a long list of manual processes. Likewise, agents should be empowered to achieve their objective, but it’s up to humans to give them the resources they need to succeed without putting the enterprise at risk.​

#2996. When Construction Professionals Retire, Their Knowledge Shouldn't Retire With Them

Ronnie Sheth is the founder and CEO of SENEN GROUP.

A CEO with three decades in the field once told me he can tell whether a project will succeed within its first few weeks. He looks at two things: the project manager and the client. A head of engineering at another firm told me he can look at a design and know what will work in the field. ​

I’ve seen what happens when people like them retire. What they know leaves with them. ​

Many experienced construction professionals are now close to retirement age; according to a 2025 report by The Center for Construction Research and Training, in 2024, “1 in 5 construction workers were 55 years or older.” Additionally, the Associated Builders and Contractors explained that “In 2027, the industry will need to bring in 456,000 new workers to meet demand as construction spending growth is poised to resume for the first time in years.”​

When that CEO knows a construction project is in trouble, he isn’t guessing. He is matching what he sees against past projects, such as a project manager stretched too thin or a client who keeps changing scope.

Many of those signals already sit within schedules, cost reports, change orders and daily logs. The issue is that they’re scattered across various systems, so finding them can take hours each week. ​

​AI can help construction teams by learning the patterns a firm’s best people carry in their heads and putting those patterns in front of the entire team across projects. While AI models can’t fully replicate the intuition, context and judgment that come with years of hands-on experience, they can recognize and surface some of these patterns. Experts should still make the hard calls, but AI can enable the rest of the team to see what the experts see. ​

The Associated General Contractors of America and Sage surveyed 951 firms for their 2026 outlook. Out of the respondents, 61% indicated that “their firms use AI or plan to increase investments in it,” compared to 44% a year earlier. The survey also asked how respondents use AI. The majority (45%) said they “deploy AI for office and administrative functions.” Other use cases included estimating (23%) and design or preconstruction (20%). Additionally, 16% said they use AI to recruit and train employees, as well as for other HR tasks.

AI can help with work that occurs in the office. But in my view, AI can play a bigger role in the field. Specifically, AI can benefit projects in various ways, but three stand out to me for construction companies.

​In 2024, construction accounted for 1,034 worker deaths.

AI can help safety directors keep workers safe. Specifically, computer vision can spot certain visible hazards and unsafe behaviors in real time, and predictive models can identify upcoming work that may carry higher incident risk so supervisors can intervene earlier.

​Experienced buyers know which suppliers tend to run late and when to order materials earlier. Translating that knowledge into a system can be hard.

AI-enabled procurement optimization can leverage machine learning to forecast material and equipment needs from a firm’s schedule, inventory and supplier history. ​Agentic AI workflows can then check stock, prices and lead times and draft purchase orders for a person to approve.

Using their gut instincts, construction CEOs can often tell which project is slipping and which machines are sitting idle.

Using computer vision, schedule and equipment intelligence can compare site imagery against a plan. Predictive models can flag delay risk while there’s still time to recover. AI-powered equipment monitoring can also help firms identify machinery that’s sitting idle or being underutilized.

First, I recommend that leaders start with the business problem they’re facing, not the technology. They should name the KPI they want to move, such as ​incident rate or days of delay.

Then, leaders should bring in stakeholders who will have to use AI, such as superintendents, project managers, safety leads and IT, from day one, and let them shape the work.

From there, leaders should have the right experts pick the technical path. Data and AI specialists should check whether a firm’s data is ready and decide what to buy versus build.

After that, leaders and their teams should integrate AI into existing workflows. They should make sure the insights AI generates inform day-to-day decisions and actions.

Finally, leaders should invest in their people. If workers worry AI will negatively impact or take away their jobs, silence from leadership can make those concerns worse. ​Leaders should tell their teams early on how AI will be used and what will change in daily tasks. They should train their teams on projects and share early wins. Leaders should give every AI project a small squad, such as a business owner accountable for the KPI, field experts who test the tool, engineers who build it and a change lead who drives adoption. In my experience, AI projects with defined owners move much faster.

​AI usage comes with risks. Construction leaders shouldn’t treat AI as a catch-all solution. Based on my observations, three implementation challenges can increase those risks.

​The first challenge is building on weak data. ​If schedules, cost codes and incident logs are incomplete or don’t match, the model learns the wrong lessons.

Then there’s skipping governance. Leaders should decide who can use which AI tools and which data points they can feed into them. ​I recommend leaders adopt this policy: no proprietary project plans in public AI tools.

Finally, there’s taking people out of the loop. An AI model may suggest a schedule based on past projects, while a project manager with 20 years on similar jobs knows this site needs more time. Leaders should task people with relevant expertise to make final calls.

Many construction firms have at least a few people whose years of experience give them an intuitive understanding of how projects work. I believe the construction firms that pull ahead will teach their systems to see what those people see before they leave.​

If you’re a construction leader, ask yourself: ​If your best project executive retired tomorrow, which of their calls could your company still make?​​

#2993. I Listened to MP Materials' Earnings Call. Here's the 1 Thing That Stuck With Me.

MP Materials has a budding relationship with one of the biggest companies in the tech sector.

By Keith Noonan – Nov 18, 2026 at 5:05PM EST

10 stocks we like better than MP Materials ›

MP Materials (MP +3.13%) published its third-quarter results and hosted an investor conference call on Nov. 6, and the company had some promising results and updates to share with investors. The company recorded earnings per share of $0.04, which beat the average analyst estimate's call for a loss of $0.01 per share. Meanwhile, sales rose roughly 176% year over year to reach roughly $147.7 million and beat the average Wall Street target by $28.8 million.

Along with promising generalized updates on progression for the production and sale of its neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) rare-earth oxide, the company also shared some specific updates about expectations to begin delivery to Apple next year. Here's why that stood out to me.

MP Materials has secured a 10-year offtake agreement with the U.S. Department of Defense with pricing floors, and the relationship should help support the sustainability of the business, but sales to commercial customers are also important to the company's future. MP is already scaling its deliveries of magnets to General Motors, and comments from management during the company's earnings call suggest that rare-earths mining and processing specialist is on track to begin making deliveries to Apple in 2027.

MP has already been receiving prepayments from Apple, but it expects to actually begin deliveries to the tech giant in the second half of next year -- and that this will become a much bigger sales driver. The company said that it expects an additional $120 million in prepayments over the next one-to-two years, which points to an encouraging demand outlook and a relationship that has the potential to continue scaling from there.
