#2974. ​Your AI Workforce: Hiding In The Software Budget

Rotem Alaluf | Founder and CEO of Wand AI, an enterprise AI software provider delivering AI solutions and accelerating AI transformation.

​Companies can measure what AI costs. Most are less prepared to measure the work their agents perform.

Ask a CFO what the company spent on AI last quarter, and there is usually a report: model fees, cloud consumption and software licenses. Ask how many exceptions its agents resolved, or which business outcomes they improved, and the answer is harder to find.

That isn’t a reporting problem. It’s a management problem.

In a previous Forbes article, “AI Stops Being A Tool The Moment It Owns An Outcome,” I argued that an AI system changes organizational status when it receives an ongoing responsibility rather than an isolated instruction. An agent tasked with keeping unreconciled transactions below 0.5% needs defined authority, escalation rules and a manager. It also needs to be measured against the objective it owns.

Companies have systems for managing people: organizational structures, compensation, performance objectives and functional budgets. Their AI agents, meanwhile, appear in technical dashboards showing token consumption, API calls and error logs. Both are useful but don’t reveal how humans and agents perform as one workforce.

A department can reduce labor costs while increasing the human effort required to review faulty AI output. Neither outcome is visible in a cloud invoice.

The operating question isn’t whether an agent costs less than an employee. It’s which combination of human and agent effort delivers the required result, at what cost, quality, speed and risk. To answer that, both forms of work need to appear in the same management picture.

Human labor has long been budgeted in hours. It’s an imperfect measure. A timesheet tells you how much time someone worked, not what the work accomplished. The hour gives organizations a way to plan capacity and compare the cost of delivering work.

In my book, The Agentic Age, I describe the agent-hour as a basic unit of AI labor: a measured hour of an identifiable agent operating under a defined mandate and governance controls. Unlike a bare compute charge, a governed agent-hour can be connected to the agent’s identity, assigned objective, authority, actions, escalations and audit trail.

That distinction matters. An hour is still an input, not an outcome. Two agents can consume the same number of hours and deliver different results. A company should measure agent-hours alongside verified output, quality, human supervision and total cost. It requires treating AI labor as something that can be managed, not merely purchased.

Consider a reconciliation team. Knowing that its agents consumed 2,000 governed hours gives the CFO an indication of capacity and spending. Knowing how many exceptions were resolved, how many were escalated and how many reopened tells the CFO whether those hours were productive.​

A dangerous shortcut is using an agent’s own completion message as evidence that it succeeded. “Task complete” may mean the agent produced an answer, not that a payment cleared, a claim was settled or a discrepancy disappeared from the system of record.

Verification has to come from evidence beyond the agent’s assertion: the reconciled ledger, the completed transaction, the policy-compliant decision or an independently checked sample. A second model can assist with evaluation, yet its judgment should not substitute for the underlying business evidence where that evidence is available.

The more useful scorecard operates at the level of the business function. It combines cost per verified result, turnaround time, error and rework rates, escalation frequency and the human effort still required. Those measures show whether adding agents improves the operation and where authority should or shouldn’t expand.

AI ROI asks how many employee hours the technology saved. That misses an important category: valuable work that organizations left undone because the cost of performing it was too high.

Agents can expand the coverage and frequency of this work, provided the results are verified and exceptions receive oversight.

There may be no historical labor cost to eliminate because the work was never performed. The benefit could appear as fewer unresolved exceptions, earlier detection of risk or better service, not a reduction in headcount.

If AI is measured only against jobs it replaces, companies will miss the value it can create.

Official GDP includes economic output regardless of whether it was produced with help from people, software or machines. What national accounts don’t separately show is the contribution made by autonomous AI agents within that output.

I use the term agentic GDP for an analytical view of the economic value attributable to agentic labor. It’s not additional GDP to add on top of existing output, and counting agent-hours alone cannot establish it. Measuring it would require connecting governed work to economic results while avoiding double counting in operations where people, agents and conventional technology collaborate.

As agents take on more work, the relationship between output, employment, wages and tax receipts may change. Governments will need better evidence to understand where productivity gains accrue, how income is distributed and whether fiscal rules need to adapt. The data cannot begin with an estimate invented at the national level. It must begin with what organizations can observe.

Start with one business function, not a companywide transformation program. Give every agent a named business owner and a defined objective. Put its governed hours and fully loaded costs on the same page as verified results, quality, escalations and human review effort. Use the same business outcome metrics to evaluate the combined human-agent operation.

​The first scorecard will be imperfect. That’s acceptable. What’s not acceptable is declaring an agent productive because a dashboard shows it was active or because it says the job is done.

Companies need to stop confusing deployment with performance. Before giving an agent more responsibility, leaders need to answer a question: When it says the work is done, what independent evidence proves it?

A workforce you cannot measure is a workforce you cannot manage.

#2973. What You Can Pay for with Scholarship Money

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Scholarships are usually restricted to the necessary costs of attending college, but some scholarships let you apply the money to more than tuition.

Scholarships are meant to pay for the cost of attendance to study at a college or university. This often includes required bills and purchases, such as tuition, textbooks and on-campus living expenses.

Some scholarships restrict the funds to specific costs, such as tuition. How you can apply the money may depend on the scholarship’s requirements.

Here are the most common college costs you can pay with scholarship money.

Scholarships commonly pay toward the tuition and fees your college charges.

Tuition usually covers only the cost to enroll in classes. Your college will also charge fees for a variety of reasons, such as attending a lab portion of a class, access to on-campus technology, facility maintenance and student activities. You’ll have to pay many of these fees regardless of if you use those facilities or participate in campus activities. Fees are often charged with tuition on the same bill so that you pay them together.

Tuition and fees cost students at public four-year institutions an average of $32,730 for the 2026-2027 school year, according to College Board’s 2026 report. If you use scholarship money to pay for these costs upfront, it can help you save a good chunk of money.

Scholarship money also pays for textbooks and supplies you need to complete your courses. These can include physical books, e-books and software licenses to access online content.

Depending on the scholarship, the cost of additional supplies that are required for certain courses might be covered as well. For example, nursing students might have to purchase scrubs with their college’s logo or medical supplies such as stethoscopes for clinical shifts.

Some scholarships will pay for the purchase of a laptop because you’ll likely need one to complete your coursework; however, you’ll want to confirm that the money can be used for that purchase before buying one.

Your scholarship might help cover some of the costs of living on campus, including paying for a dorm room and meal plans (often called room and board). To apply the funds, you usually have to live in university housing, which might be in a dormitory or even university apartments.

Many students can purchase meal plans to eat meals in their college and university cafeterias. These plans are usually for a set number of meals each week and might be required for first-year students. Because meal plans are part of college expenses, some scholarships will let you apply the funds to purchase a meal plan.

Some scholarships might also allow money to pay for campus parking fees because those are paid directly to the college or university.

» MORE: What is need-based financial aid for college?

Scholarships are generally intended only for educational expenses such as those explained above, but there are some scholarships that want you to use the money for specific expenses. If your scholarship has this type of restriction, your award letter should outline how the funds must be used, such as paying for tuition and fees only.

If you aren’t certain whether there are restrictions on how you can spend your scholarship money and the scholarship was paid directly to your college, you can call your financial aid office to ask. But you’ll want to contact the organization that awarded you the scholarship to ask about restrictions if the scholarship money was sent to you instead.

Even if a scholarship is open to most educational costs, expenses that are rarely allowed to be covered by a scholarship include:

Some transportation costs such as car payments.

Non-essential supplies such as clothing or entertainment.

Scholarships can be paid directly to your college or to you, depending on the individual scholarship. If the money goes to your college, it’s applied to your account based on the scholarship’s requirements. For example, if the funds are only allowed to pay for tuition, the financial aid office will apply the money to your tuition bill to reduce how much you owe.

Scholarships work the same way for room and board. If your scholarship will pay toward the costs of living on campus, the money will reduce how much you owe or cover the costs entirely so that you don’t owe anything.

In some cases, you might be able to use your scholarship money to pay for books or supplies. If that’s allowed, the funds might be available on your account through the college bookstore. Instead of paying the entire cost of your textbooks with cash or your student loans, you can pay with the scholarship money.

If your scholarship sends you the money instead of giving it to your college, you’ll be responsible for using the funds to pay for eligible costs instead of your university automatically applying it toward your bill.

On Nov. 18, 2026, Recursion shares climbed after regulators aligned on its lead familial adenomatous polyposis trial, though investors are watching for more detail.

By Josh Kohn-Lindquist – Nov 18, 2026 at 5:20PM EST

Recursion Pharmaceuticals (RXRX +3.86%), an AI-enabled clinical-stage drug discovery company, closed at $2.83, up 3.86%. The stock rose after the company said it reached FDA alignment on the REC-4881 Phase 3 design, and investors are watching for further regulatory detail. Trading volume reached 39.4M shares, coming in about 65% above its three-month average of 23.8M shares. Recursion Pharmaceuticals IPO'd in 2021 and has fallen 91% since going public.

S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.23%) closed at 7,323, down 0.24%, while Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +0.42%) finished at 24,430, up 0.42%. In biotechnology: AI-enabled drug discovery and clinical-stage therapeutics, Schrödinger (SDGR +6.00%) closed at $27.20, up 6.00%, and Relay Therapeutics (RLAY +0.24%) closed at $16.51, up 0.24%.

Recursion shares are up 4% today after it aligned with the FDA on a Phase III trial design for 200 adults with familial adenomatous polyposis. The disease currently has no approved therapies, making Recursion's REC-4881 one of the first AI-enabled treatments to advance toward a Phase III trial.

Recursion believes there are over 50,000 patients with familial adenomatous polyposis in the U.S. and E.U., representing a $15 billion market opportunity for the $1.7 billion company. The FDA accepted 10 mm or larger polyp excision as part of its primary endpoint of event-free survival, which could be a win for RXRX stock, as it shouldn't have to run a longer, costlier trial waiting for adverse events to develop further.

While today's development is great progress for the stock, the results of the Phase III trial itself remain paramount, as success with REC-4881 would serve as a proof of concept not just for Recursion but for its AI platform. The Phase III trial won't begin until the second half of 2027, however, so interested investors need to be uber-patient and risk-tolerant before considering this stock.

#2967. Billionaire Bill Ackman Sold 2 Million Shares of Microsoft Stock. But Here's Why He Says He's Still Bullish

Pershing Square's latest filing shows a big cut in its Microsoft stake, but Ackman says it omits what he bought instead.

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 18, 2026 at 5:22PM EST

At first glance, Pershing Square's latest quarterly holdings report might suggest that billionaire Bill Ackman soured on Microsoft (MSFT +0.41%) stock. But he says that's the wrong read, and his reasoning makes perfect sense.

The filing shows his firm held 4,064,779 Microsoft shares on Sept. 30, down from 6,206,730 three months earlier. That's a cut of about 2.1 million shares, or roughly a third of the position.

On Wednesday, Ackman explained on X what the filing leaves out. In July, Pershing Square bought 2 million "deep-in-the-money" options on Microsoft, with a strike price of about $310 a share and a term of two and a half years. Those options were bought over the counter, which excludes them from the quarterly filing.

"We remain bullish on Microsoft and believe the stock remains undervalued," he wrote.

Count the options, and Pershing Square's bet on Microsoft is about the same size as before: roughly 4.1 million shares plus options on 2 million more, compared with 6.2 million shares in June.

A deep-in-the-money option behaves much like the underlying stock. With Microsoft at $506.24 at Tuesday's close, an option to buy at $310 rises and falls nearly dollar-for-dollar with the shares. But it costs less up front than buying the stock outright, which frees up cash for other ideas. Ackman said only that the firm occasionally makes the swap "for portfolio management or other reasons."

That said, if Microsoft were to fall below $310 before the options expire, they could end up worthless, a risk that owning the shares doesn't carry.

Microsoft wasn't the only move. Pershing Square opened new positions in Alcon (ALC +1.55%), worth about $954 million, and Intercontinental Exchange (ICE -0.24%), worth about $1 billion. It sold its small remaining stake in Hertz (HTZ -3.70%).

It also trimmed several of its biggest holdings. The firm sold about 11% of its Meta Platforms (META -0.40%) shares, 11% of its Mastercard (MA -0.36%), 12% of its Visa (V -0.37%), 11% of its Brookfield (BN -0.51%) and 15% of its Restaurant Brands International (QSR +0.07%). The one big addition was Netflix (NFLX +0.23%), where it raised its stake by about 18% to 15.4 million shares.

Its largest positions by value at the end of September were Uber Technologies (UBER -0.07%) at $2.35 billion, Amazon (AMZN +3.82%) at $2.12 billion, Microsoft at $2.08 billion and Meta at $2.05 billion.

The lesson is to be careful with 13F filings. They show only the stock and listed options held at the end of each quarter, and they are released weeks later. Private options deals, short positions, and anything bought or sold since then don't appear. Simply comparing filings might yield a headline saying a famous investor "dumped" a stock, when in reality, the conviction hasn't changed.

Ultimately, Ackman's Microsoft bet hasn't really shrunk, and long-term investors can still consider this a vote of confidence from one of Wall Street's best-known stock pickers.

#2960. Invesco QQQ Is 14% Below Its October Record. Here's Where I Think It Will Be in 2030.

The Nasdaq-100 fund trades around 14% below its October record. Can it pass that peak by the end of 2030?

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 18, 2026 at 5:23PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Invesco QQQ Trust ›

The Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ +0.39%) closed at a record $759.66 on Oct. 6. Since then, the exchange-traded fund that tracks the Nasdaq-100 has fallen to roughly $654 as of this writing, about 14% below the high.

It's still up about 6% in 2026, but the drop has erased most of the year's gains.

Even so, I think QQQ will end 2030 at roughly $890 per share. That would put it about 17% above the October record and about 36% above today's price -- a rise of close to 8% a year, before the fund's small dividend.

That would also be a slower pace than the fund's recent run. The Nasdaq-100 itself climbed around 12% a year in the five years through October, according to Siblis Research. And my number rests on one assumption more than any other: how fast the index's companies keep growing their profits.

Showing how much profit growth has powered the Nasdaq-100, the index's total earnings climbed around 50% in the last year, according to Siblis, which removes big accounting gains. That was up from about 28% a year in the past three years and about 19% a year in the past five. In those five years, earnings outpaced the index's price by more than 6 percentage points a year. That means the valuation dropped even while the index rose.

At the end of October, the Nasdaq-100 traded at about 33 times earnings, and QQQ has slipped roughly 5% since then. By my math, this leaves the fund near 31 times earnings now.

That's a bit under where the index finished 2024 and 2025 (about 32 times earnings both years). But it's well above the 24 or so times earnings it hit at the end of 2022.

The fund isn't cheap. Still, its price-to-earnings ratio is arguably more reasonable than its recent gains would suggest, because earnings have carried most of them.

I started with the earnings. Going by the end-of-October numbers, every QQQ share represents about $21 of its holdings' earnings in the last year.

I'm assuming these earnings rise about 12% a year through the end of 2030, well below the five-year rate and a fraction of the past year's. That still puts them about 60% higher, near $34 a share.

The other piece is what investors will pay for these earnings at the end of 2030. I'm assuming 26 times earnings, about what big U.S. companies as a group sell for today. It's also under the Nasdaq-100's average of about 29 times earnings at its past 10 year-ends.

In other words, my estimate assumes the Nasdaq-100 winds up valued about like the broader market is now, with its normal premium gone. At 26 times earnings of about $34 per share, QQQ would trade at about $890 a share. Its dividend, which yields about 0.5%, could add a bit on top.

The earnings growth rate worries me more. I've already set the final valuation multiple under the index's recent average, but part of the past year's profit surge came from companies whose earnings can swing hard.

Micron Technology (MU -1.00%), one of the fund's 10 biggest holdings, is the clearest example. The memory chipmaker's revenue more than tripled to around $133 billion in its fiscal year that ended Sept. 3.

Its net income was around $85 billion, almost 10 times its net income a year earlier. But Micron's own annual report says that in the past five fiscal years, yearly changes in the average selling prices of its memory chips ranged from a rise of about 200% to a drop of about 50%.

Profits that climb so fast can fall quickly if the supply of memory chips catches up to demand, as Micron itself warns.

At 8% growth, though, the fund's earnings would reach only about $29 a share by 2030. Even at 26 times earnings, it would trade near $760. That price would just bring QQQ back to its October record after four more years.

All told, I expect QQQ to finish 2030 around $890, over its October peak but at a slower pace than investors have gotten used to. The forecast doesn't need this year's profit surge to repeat. It just needs the Nasdaq-100's earnings to keep growing at a double-digit rate once the memory chip boom cools.

Compared with the last five years, that's a modest outlook. But I think roughly 8% a year from a fund trading 14% below its record would still be a decent return.

By RJ Fulton – Nov 18, 2026 at 5:25PM EST

Cryptocurrency markets extended their recent sell-off on Wednesday, November 18, as deteriorating liquidity conditions and weakening risk appetite continued to weigh on digital assets. Bitcoin is once again approaching its recent lows near $62,000, while a rare breach of a long-term technical indicator is drawing considerable attention from investors.

As of early evening, Bitcoin (BTC -2.68%) was down 3.84% to $62,386.56, while Ethereum (ETH -2.30%) fell 3.80% to $1,753.33 and Solana (SOL -1.88%) declined 2.88% to $72.94. Although near-term downside risks remain elevated, historical market cycles suggest that periods of comparable weakness could present compelling opportunities for long-term investors.

Selling pressure intensified on Wednesday as investors awaited further insight into the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook. With Treasury yields remaining elevated and liquidity continuing to deteriorate across cryptocurrency markets, investors appear increasingly reluctant to take on additional risk. The ongoing unwind of leveraged positions has compounded selling pressure, while subdued spot market demand has made it difficult for cryptocurrencies to sustain meaningful rallies.

Spot Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs extended their recent losses on Wednesday, reflecting continued weakness in the underlying cryptocurrencies. The iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT -2.16%) and Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC -2.16%) both declined 2.16%, while the iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (ETHA -2.63%) fell 2.63%.

Despite deteriorating conditions in the cryptocurrency market, one historical indicator offers a potentially encouraging perspective for long-term investors. Following last week's 12% decline, Bitcoin broke below its 200-week moving average, a long-term pricing benchmark that has historically helped identify periods of extreme market weakness. According to CoinDesk, comparable instances in 2015, 2020, and 2022 were followed by positive returns over the subsequent three months. However, Bitcoin experienced further declines before recovering each time.

Before becoming more constructive on the broader cryptocurrency market, investors should look for signs of stabilization. One relatively straightforward way to gauge whether broader market conditions are improving would be to monitor Bitcoin's ability to reclaim and sustain a price above its 200-week moving average.

While historical precedent suggests cryptocurrencies could be approaching attractive long-term valuations, lower prices alone are not necessarily indicative of a market bottom. Until liquidity conditions improve, capital flows stabilize, and major cryptocurrencies demonstrate renewed price strength, the risk of further declines across the digital asset market remains elevated.

#2941. 6 Stocks Set to Cash In on the Grand Theft Auto VI Launch Boom

Take-Two Interactive is the obvious winner, but it's not the only company that will benefit.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 18, 2026 at 6:04PM EST

Grand Theft Auto is one of the most iconic video game franchises on the planet, and its newest edition, Grand Theft Auto VI, or GTA6, has been called the most anticipated video game in history. All five previous versions of the game have been hits, and it's been more than 13 years since Grand Theft Auto V was released in September 2013. With an estimated $1 billion budget, a lot is riding on the game, and early signs are that it is set to deliver.

A day before its launch, the game had nearly $1.7 billion in preorders, and it was already drawing rave reviews. The game was already atop Metacritic's all-time gaming leaderboard with a score of 99, which had only happened one other time back in 1998, with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

With excitement building, let's look at six stocks set to cash in on Grand Theft Auto VI.

As the developer of the game, Take-Two Interactive (TTWO +6.22%) is the biggest winner. It's already closing in on $2 billion in orders, and management has projected Q3 net bookings for its fiscal Q3 to reach $3.35 billion to $3.5 billion, about double from a year ago.

The key going forward, though, will be how the company monetizes the game over the long term, through online multiplayer extensions and recurring consumer spending. The up-front sales are great, but that is just part of the story.

Sony (SONY -0.04%), which makes the PlayStation gaming console, is also set to be a big winner. About 75% of preorders have been for PlayStation versions of the game. The success of the game could not only drive sales of its PS5 and higher-margin PS5 Pro, but also give it a take rate on all digital software downloads and in-game microtransactions made through the PlayStation Store.

Both Walmart (WMT -0.13%) and Target (TGT +4.01%) should also benefit from the launch of GTA6. Now, these retailers will not be selling physical discs; instead, physical boxed copies of the game will contain a digital download code. However, collectors still like to get boxed copies for the artwork and physical inserts like maps, while it's also a better gift presentation for the upcoming holidays.

Importantly, it can increase foot traffic to their stores, which can also lead to other impulse purchases that typically don't happen online.

Big video game launches are also often accompanied by strong sales of gaming peripherals. This can be a revenue growth driver for a company like Turtle Beach (TBCH +1.55%), which holds a roughly 40% share of the U.S. gaming headset market. It has also expanded into other accessories, such as controllers, chargers, and simulation gear.

Gamers tend to upgrade or replace equipment during big new game launches. The company also has strong retail distribution, with its items placed near popular games.

While all these companies could see a lift from the sales of physical items, Reddit (RDDT -0.41%) could see a strong benefit from increased community engagement on its platform around GTA6. It's common for its platform to have dedicated gaming communities, and with the launch of a game the size and scope of Grand Theft Auto VI, millions of users will likely flood gaming subreddits to share clips, potential easter eggs, map theories, and gameplay discoveries.

Young, predominantly male gamers are a highly desirable demographic for many advertisers, and brands that cater to this segment will likely be looking to spend to capture their attention for what is not just a video game launch, but a true cultural phenomenon. Reddit, meanwhile, is in a unique position to command strong ad prices, given the concentration of hyperengaged eyeballs on its gaming subreddits.

#2935. Palo Alto Networks: Accelerating Growth and a $4.5 Billion Bet on the Future of Cybersecurity

Demand has never been stronger for the cybersecurity specialist.

By Danny Vena, CPA – Nov 18, 2026 at 6:14PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Palo Alto Networks ›

A quick look at the headlines is all it takes to understand the unprecedented need for robust cybersecurity. The emergence of next-generation artificial intelligence (AI)-powered threats has emboldened hackers, and the frequency of attacks has risen to new heights.

With that as a backdrop, investors watched closely as Palo Alto Networks (PANW +9.90%) released its quarterly financial report. Shareholders were pleased to find that the company has risen to the challenge, as robust demand has fueled record growth. Palo Alto also made a sizable investment to ensure that enterprises can adopt AI securely, regardless of what models they use.

For its fiscal 2027 first quarter (ended Oct. 31), Palo Alto Networks delivered record revenue that grew 39% year over year to $3.44 billion, driven primarily by robust growth in its Next-Generation Security annual recurring revenue (NGS ARR). The company also generated adjusted net income of $881 million and adjusted earnings per diluted share (EPS) of $1.05, up 33% and 13%, respectively.

To give those numbers context, analysts' consensus estimates called for revenue of $3.31 billion and adjusted EPS of $0.97, so Palo Alto Networks easily scaled expectations.

It isn't just the current quarter that looks strong. Remaining performance obligation (RPO) -- contractually obligated revenue that hasn't yet been earned -- grew 35% year over year to $21 billion, building a strong foundation for future growth.

Palo Alto Networks' customer metrics were equally compelling, as its net retention rate remained above 120% for its platform customers. Put another way, existing customers are spending 20% more than in the prior-year quarter.

Not only did Palo Alto Networks surprise to the upside, but it also signaled strong growth ahead, as evidenced by its robust outlook. For the fiscal second quarter, management is guiding for revenue of roughly $3.53 billion, or year-over-year growth of roughly 36%.

Investors were particularly inspired by the company's full-year guidance. For fiscal 2027, management is guiding for total revenue of $14.5 billion, up about 26% year over year, with NGS ARR of $11.5 billion, also up 26%. Given management’s tendency to underpromise and overdeliver, that forecast will likely rise over time.

In a surprise announcement, Palo Alto Networks revealed that it will shell out $4.5 billion to acquire Applied Compute, a leading platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models. This will allow Palo Alto to "help enterprises adopt AI securely, whether they choose open-weight models, closed frontier models, or both," according to the announcement.

Even as demand remains high, cybersecurity stocks have swooned as technology issues have fallen. Ahead of its Q1 report, Palo Alto Networks shares declined nearly 19% from their early October peak.

However, some investors will still balk at Palo Alto Networks' premium valuation, as the stock currently sells for 82 times forward earnings and 70 times next year's expected earnings. Historically, investors tend to reward high-growth stocks with premium valuations thanks to their consistently above-average, uh, growth.

I'm a firm believer in the old adage "You get what you pay for." Management has shown an uncanny knack for stoking Palo Alto's impressive growth, and recent technological advances make cybersecurity more important than ever.

That's why I'm confident in saying Palo Alto Networks is a buy.

#2930. Thinking About Buying Anthropic’s IPO on Nov. 19? Here’s an AI Stock I’d Consider First (Hint: It’s Not Nvidia or Broadcom).

ASML’s impeccable fundamentals allow investors to rest easy amid AI stock volatility.

By Daniel Foelber – Nov 18, 2026 at 6:15PM EST

Artificial intelligence (AI) stock investors have been on a roller coaster in recent weeks, with far more drops than pops.

The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +0.42%) is now in a correction -- which is a drop of more than 10% from the highs. The iShares Semiconductor ETF -- which closely tracks the semiconductor industry -- is in a 35.3% drawdown, and leading chip stocks Broadcom (AVGO +3.65%) and Nvidia (NVDA -2.90%) are both down over 30% from their all-time highs.

Red-hot AI spending has pushed once-cash-cow businesses like Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta Platforms into negative free-cash-flow territory. Rising interest rates are making capital more expensive. And Jensen Huang's sudden resignation as CEO of Nvidia leaves the industry without one of its biggest champions.

The timing is bad for Anthropic, which is set to hold its initial public offering (IPO) on Thursday, Nov. 19. Reports indicate Anthropic was eyeing a valuation as high as $2 trillion. But a Nov. 10 press release by Anthropic prices its 825 million shares between $70 and $78 per share. At the midpoint of $74 per share and based on its total share count of 13.09 billion, Anthropic would have a valuation around $968 billion.

Given the downward pressure on AI stocks, some investors may be eyeing Anthropic's IPO as a great buying opportunity for the company behind one of the leading frontier models. But I think semiconductor equipment manufacturer ASML (ASML +0.88%) is an even better way to buy the dip on AI stocks.

Huang's resignation exposed Nvidia's key-person risk. So much of the company's identity, strategy, and even its organizational structure centered around Huang. And his sudden departure is undoubtedly challenging the investment thesis.

Similarly, the frontier models like Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's ChatGPT, Alphabet's Gemini, and xAI's Grok, owned by Space Exploration Technologies, have shaky moats, as a single upgrade can challenge one model's competitive advantages in a heartbeat.

Meanwhile, hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet are spending so much on AI so quickly that it's difficult to discern whether those investments will pay off in the long run or prove wasteful.

Uncertain profitability road maps, paired with Nvidia's scandal, have made me even more confident that ASML is the best all-around AI stock to buy for the long term.

Ultimately, ASML doesn't really care if Advanced Micro Devices takes market share from Nvidia or Anthropic grows its lead over OpenAI. Rather, its long-term growth runway depends on increasing demand for next-generation AI chips that must be manufactured on ASML's machines.

ASML has a virtual monopoly on extreme ultraviolet (EUV) machines that are used in the lithography step of chip manufacturing. These machines are needed to mass-produce both logic and memory chips at commercial scale. And the most advanced version of these machines, called high-numerical-aperture (high-NA) EUV, will be needed to make next-generation AI chips.

EUV is making up a larger share of ASML's revenue, but the tech company remains heavily reliant on its deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography systems and aftermarket servicing on existing machines. In its latest quarter, EUV system sales accounted for 35% of net sales -- which puts into context the sheer size of its non-EUV and servicing segments.

ASML being in the relatively early stages of its EUV and high-NA system rollout is music to the ears of long-term investors. ASML spent over 6 billion euros researching and developing EUV over a 17-year period. But many chip fabs have yet to widely adopt high-NA. On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, ASML said that Samsung Electronics will be using high-NA in high-volume manufacturing starting in 2028 -- joining Intel. ASML is also working with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing to unlock the full efficiency benefits of high-NA EUV by 2033.

In the meantime, ASML can't keep up with 2027 or 2028 demand. On its recent third-quarter 2026 earnings call, the company said it is now taking orders for 2029 and 2030 and increasing production to meet customer needs.

If there is an AI spending slowdown, ASML's near-term results will definitely cool off. But it's still incredibly well positioned to capitalize on AI innovation over the long term because chip fabs will need to upgrade their equipment to EUV and high-NA to support advanced-node manufacturing. In the meantime, ASML generates steady revenue from its DUV business, and high-margin cash flow from services for its existing installed base. What's more, ASML isn't dependent on an expensive research and development (R&D) budget because it has already cracked the code on high-NA and is now in the stage of fine-tuning the commercial manufacturing process with chip fabs. Its operating costs are reasonable, and its balance sheet is in impeccable shape -- with ASML exiting its latest quarter with 8.03 billion euros in cash compared to just 1.96 billion euros in long-term debt.

ASML is the exact company long-term investors can rest easy holding during an AI slowdown. The business is extremely high-quality and will produce strong earnings even during a downturn -- albeit at a slower growth rate. ASML can also generate high cash flow to buy back its stock, even if the price gets discounted. And with the growth stock down 23.7% in the last three months, ASML no longer commands as lofty a valuation -- with the price-to-earnings ratio now sitting at a premium but more reasonable 34.7 compared to over 50 a couple of months ago.

ASML is a company built around the strength of its technology, rather than a single key feature or product upgrade. It sits upstream of the AI value chain, making it the perfect bet for investors who believe in a sustainable, gradual AI innovation cycle rather than those looking to capitalize on a boom in a particular bottleneck, such as memory chips.

ASML presents a far more attractive risk-and-reward profile than an Anthropic IPO or setting sail into uncharted waters aboard Nvidia -- a ship that suddenly finds itself without its veteran captain.

The entire market is very aligned in the fact that lithium demand is growing and growing robustly. However, prices are not driven by demand. They're driven by this low-cost supply coming out of regions that are not necessarily formal. So the challenge for us producers is to remain resilient to match those prices. And this is what Sigma has demonstrated throughout this presentation. When you look at the impact of African production, there are 3 key variables. First is vertically integrated with the supply chain. So it continues to produce and deliver even during price downturn, almost in price agnostic.

Then you have the phenomenon of low-cost DSO or low concentrate DSO where the material gets to the client almost at cost given that the client is financing the production. So the only curbing is the downward pressure of high logistics costs. And then you have the full concentrate production coming out of countries like Zimbabwe and Mali, those are formal and they're integrated into the supply chain. So they come at an LCE equivalent of $7,000 to $13,000 [indiscernible] per ton. In other words, very competitive pricing. So here at Sigma, as we described, we are the floor.

So these prices don't worry us because even with this pricing environment, we can compete and we can deliver significant cash flow. Today, for instance, prices are about $1,200, which gives us ample room to deliver cash flow. So that's the importance of resilience is the fact that going forward, lithium pricing will continue to remain volatile as demand demonstrates tremendous growth throughout the next couple of years. Now we go into the production capacity and what we see as the 2026, 2027 operational outlook. This slide demonstrates how Sigma will deliver the forecast.

What we are forecasting for the 2027 year is not different than what we have already delivered since the upgrade of our industrial plant in the fourth quarter of 2024. The plant has 2 circuits, the reprocessing circuit and the main circuit. The total production capacity amounting to approximately 82,000 tons. In the fourth quarter '24, we delivered 77,000 tons. So that's industrial capacity. From then onwards, we delivered approximately 68,000 tons every single quarter. And if you annualize the third quarter when we decommissioned the contractor, it was the same exact number. Then in 2026, we entered the primarization phase, and we quickly reached the targets on the second quarter. The third quarter, we were stopped.

But again, we demonstrated tremendous resilience to just bounce back and pick up when we left off twice. We remobilized and demobilized our entire contingent twice. So when you look at the picture of the third quarter, it's essentially a company motion because we have 21,000 tons of inventory and 7,000 tons of production. Now entering the fourth quarter, we have an additional 11,000 tons of production of high grade. Going forward, as we catch up with removal of overburden, we're going to be well on our way to deliver on our projections.

This page gets further into the details of the reprocessing circuit we talked about on the previous page, where we've shown that we can deliver approximately 15,000 tons of high-grade material coming out of the circuit. This is a circuit that's separate from the main high-grade circuit. It has its own dedicated cyclones, its DMSs, and it essentially upgrades the fines into higher-grade material in an automated process so that we achieve 100% circularity, but more importantly, we deliver more lithium with the same mining footprint. That was the key to the upgrade of the lithium industrial facility, going from an average of 60,000 tonnes per quarter into 77,000 plus up to 82,000 tonnes per quarter, the reprocessing circuit.

That is the 100% circularity we strived for, making us able to meet the recycling criteria of the European Union because our lithium has recycled material, same mining footprint, more lithium. This page essentially shows how the Cleantech plant upgrade enables 100% circularity. The amount of concentrate is essentially larger with just that one plant. In other words, in the fourth quarter '24, the plant delivered 920 tonnes a day. What we're forecasting going forward is kind of in the same magnitude at 950 tonnes a day. So nothing different than what we've been delivering. And that's again, the 15,000 tonne extra coming from the reprocessing circuit is more lithium concentrate with just one plant. Here is the mining.

So we're focusing now on increasing volumes during the fourth quarter to compensate for unremoved overburden that stay put during the third quarter. We're going after the same section of the pit shell design in order to access this larger amount of high-grade material. So this is the south of our South pit. In other words, there's approximately 200,000 tons of concentrate equivalent over here, a volume of approximately 1.1 million tons of ore. And that's the goal for us in the next month or so, getting to that material, processing and converting that into concentrate. On this page is how we plan to deliver it.

We're doing a second round of fleet upgrades, bringing in larger excavators and larger trucks. The excavators deliver an additional 40% ability to load up the trucks and then the trucks deliver a 25% increased ability to haul material. So the second stage deployment of large equipment is essentially a result of the primarized and upgraded mining operations. And again, we do more haulage with fewer amount of equipment, less diesel, more efficiency. And that's a result of our partnership with SANY China and our equipment provider. We have decreased lead times for equipment availability and larger equipment available for us.

Wrapping up this section on operational delivery, we want to delve into achieving the landmark victories of our impeccable environmental and social credentials. Minas Gerais delivered the verdict that Sigma is too big to stop. We achieved this institutional visibility to our economic impact of Vale do Jequitinhonha. Rule of law has upheld our licenses and operations. So it was the institutional strength of Minas Gerais in Brazil. Rule of law swift resolution to the stoppages. We were awarded the TAC in record time, and we were awarded a classification of too big to stop and then limited financial exposure given that we didn't have any additional royalties or any essentially burdens levied on the company.

But more importantly, we came out of this with a positive engagement with the state administration and with the federal courts, demonstrating the number of jobs at risk and the number of family members that would be vulnerable if Sigma wasn't operating. We have over 19,000 jobs connected to us directly. It's a shared prosperity business model. And out of these jobs depend 80,000 people. So this is essentially the too big to stop. These are Sigma fuel jobs. Half of them come from our social engagement, social inclusion programs. Here is the object of one of the conversations, the TAC.

Ultimately, we demonstrate here that we adhere to the highest global mining standards with our Quintuple Zero fully traceable lithium. If you look at other G7 countries, you can see there are high standards. There's a tailing dams to high standards in a country, and there are overburden rock piles to high standards in another country, both G7s. When you look at Sigma and our rock piles, they have the same standards of a G7 country rock pile and they have grass -- active germination, which was our element of delivery in concomitance with the TAC. We agreed to $1 million of active germination to be delivered throughout the next year. Concluding the presentation, here are our priorities.

We plan to continue to execute and achieve the re-rating. First, the milestones for 2027. We're going to continue to ramp up mine 1. We're going to deliver on the growth, and we're going to unlock the full potential of Phase 2 in stages in a disciplined organized execution. First, continuing ramp-up of Mine 1. We plan to deliver 240,000 tonnes in the next 12 months. We're going through a second round of fleet upgrades to enable more haulage, and we plan to deliver 330,000 tons in the full year of 2027. Second, growth. We plan to resume Phase 2 growth plan with a new mine opening.

In other words, we're going to resume Phase 2 bottom-up, opening a new mine. We're fully funded for the CapEx of opening a new mine by the current cash flow generated by the existing industrial line. Why did we start by the mine? Because it's the largest job creation. That's how we bring the most amount of prosperity to Vale do Jequitinhonha. A new mine means another 25,000 people connected to Sigma, 6,400 indirect jobs, and that's without the social programs attached to it. Then we will resume Plant 2 construction. So with that, we would plan to get to 580,000 tons of capacity, which will bring in more job creation in the region.

So unlocking the full potential of Phase 2. If we start the mine, if you would add this number of jobs to the current jobs we have, we would essentially following opening a second mine, have 100,000 people connected to our operation at Jequitinhonha -- Vale do Jequitinhonha. In other words, the potential for prosperity is tremendous, and that is why we have tremendous support from the newly elected government of Brazil and Minas Gerais. And here, we have the magic. It's low cost plus cash generation. So we're very well positioned for re-rating. There are companies that have the same production that we have and that trade at double our value.

We do believe that as we continue to execute, the re-rating will come gradually. And this is why we're so focused and we maintain our discipline. And with that, I'll conclude and shall pass on to Q&A.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first 3 questions comes from Ailing Chen from Hotwind. With Q3 production falling to just 7,293 tonnes, how did unit cash costs remain so low? Were shutdown-related fixed costs excluded or capitalized? This is the first question. The second question is regarding the USD 120 million convertible notes, are there any provisions that allow the company to redeem or repurchase the notes earlier to avoid shareholders' dilution? If so, could you please explain these provisions in detail, including any conditions, restrictions or early redemption penalties? And that's it.

Ana Cabral Gardner: So I'll answer questions one by one. First, it was regarding the costs. They were neither capitalized nor excluded. They sit as an expense line together with other operating expenses. There's a note specifically dealing with this, which is Note 24. So those costs amount to $13,376. And essentially, these are what we call idle capacity costs. The note provides quite a lot of detail about it. And that's how IFRS would dictate us to account for these costs. The second question is related to the convertible bond. Yes, there are provisions for early redemption and for early payback. It's a non-call, non-put 3. So by year 3, we could actually call the convert and redeem the bonds.

But the actual intention is to let them convert because we have not diluted since 2021. We're very calibrated in the way we plan dilution. So investors can start converting after month 12. And we believe that given where the shares were, where the shares are, the investors perhaps will convert these bonds into equity, which will relieve the balance sheet as we've shown in one of the slides where we simulate leverage ratios with the conversion. Again, investors can start doing that after the first 12 months, and there is a put on year 3 by investors for the bond. The same way we have a call on year 3 for the bond.

Operator: We have one more question from Ailing Chen from Hotwind. Sigma Lithium has been listed on the ASX for more than 2 months, but there appears to be virtually no trading activity or meaningful share price quotation. What is your view on this situation? Why has the Australian listing failed to attract trading activity so far? And what specific steps will the company take to improve liquidity and attract Australian investors? So without active trading, how can the ASX listing achieve its intended purpose?

Ana Cabral Gardner: Absolutely. And the convertible bond note that I was just referring to in the previous answer is the answer to the question. When we listed in Australia, our commitment was to deliver or to execute in the ASX every single issuance the company would do thereafter. So the convertible bond is converted into CDIs, which are the ASX listed shares. So we do believe that when conversion takes place, initially beginning 12 months from now, that ticker, that CDI security will begin to have quite significant liquidity resulting from the converted shares of the bond. Again, the dilution was approximately 14%.

So there's going to be a number of shares that when and if the bond is converted, will flow into the ASX market, hopefully beginning the trading activity you referred to. We're doing our part to act on that listing in order to foster the liquidity and the trading and the note was a demonstration of it. Our first instrument issued was already in Australia.

Operator: The next question comes from Katie Lachapelle from Canaccord Genuity. I want to clarify your comments regarding debt. Is the plan to repay the Synergy debt before year-end instead of in 2027, but then also bring the additional debt?

Ana Cabral Gardner: Katie, well, thanks for the question. Good to see you. Yes, that's exactly the plan. We decided to do the conversion because the refinancing of the debt saves us quite a lot of cash. With the debt reset and the interest rate increases of SOFR, that debt would end up almost in 14% following the reset in December. So our decision is to pay the debt immediately -- immediately after the issuance of the convertible bond closing. We'll pay the debt immediately after the convertible bond closes, which is imminent. So essentially, Synergy will be completely repaid and removed from our balance sheet. And therefore, the balance sheet becomes unencumbered because Synergy is a secured creditor.

The plan going forward, as we've mentioned a few times, is to releverage the balance sheet for the growth strategy. And that will be done with what we call adequate type financing. In other words, as we bring in more debt for growth, we plan to bring in long-term low-cost debt along the same lines of the BNDES debt that we have. So most likely, once we begin this new stage of growth in 2027, we will bring -- we will unlock that credit line in order to tap from it to deliver the growth.

Operator: We have one more question for Katie. Hi Ana, can you provide more specific time lines around the planned growth at Phase 2? When will we open the mine? When you plan to construction commence? Or procurement for the Phase 2 plan components?

Ana Cabral Gardner: Yes. We plan to start opening Mine 2 shortly, very shortly. Most likely, it will be first quarter of next year or later this quarter. Now that will be the foundation of planning for the second plant. We have initiated the construction of the second plant in December 2024. We used quite a lot of our liquidity on it. We continued throughout the first quarter of '25. So what's remaining is procuring for equipment. We've had a procurement sheet, and we estimated based on that procurement sheet updated that there's approximately USD 80 million left of equipment to be ordered. We do not plan to do it now.

We do plan to do it most likely early in the year of 2027. There's a transition of governments here, both in the state and in some of the key positions in federal government. So once all of them are installed in the posts in their positions, we then will proceed on recommencing Mine 2 and Plant 2.

Operator: Next question comes from Rock Hoffman from JPMorgan. First, can you speak to the market dynamics around lithium tailings right now given lower lithium pricing dynamics? It is still a liquid market and would it be possible to sell the full 15,000 tons in the fourth quarter? Or will this material [indiscernible] need to be reprocessed to high grade to be sold?

Ana Cabral Gardner: Both things. It is possible to sell it. The lithium tailings market now looks a lot like it did almost a year ago when we made the decision to go and primarize the mine. Ex Works price for that material now hovers between $30 to $50 -- so that's a net profit. I would say, depending on the lithium quantity of the material, you would have a different Ex Works price. What we got on the plant probably will command a higher price of around $50-ish, perhaps even higher. We typically do not sell tailings against a falling lithium price as we've been seeing, observing in the last 2 weeks.

So we'll stay put and wait further into contract season to make a decision about the tailings. Even though ironically, this is when we get the most amount of offers because that product is very profitable for the client. Essentially, the client just transports it out and throws it into a flotation plant, converting it into very high-grade lithium concentrate. And an example is what's happening with a lot of the African content, which comes out in similar format and becomes very profitable on a fully integrated basis for the battery makers.

Some of these producers being able to live with numbers as low as the equivalent of $500 a ton, which for us, if you convert it back into the lithium content of the tailings benchmarks to approximately USD 30 to USD 50. So it triangulates well with lithium coming out of Nigeria, for example.

Operator: The second question from Rock Hoffman from JPMorgan is, how should we think about your offtake strategy after the main offtake is completed in a few months? Any discussions with partners for additional offtakes or prepayments agreement?

Ana Cabral Gardner: We do have a number of discussions with several partners because we're one of the few large producers with uncommitted material into 2027. We typically strike our offtakes on an annual basis. We strike contracts on an annual basis, and we are considering doing a multiyear offtake agreement into the 2027 year. But typically, for us, we've been achieving very successful commercial results by selling the material on maximum what we call a quarterly contract. For instance, the previous quarter of the third quarter, we achieved a $1,485 realized price, which was very robust if you were to take into account the falling lithium price environment. And we have been over the peers when it comes to achieved realized prices.

Why is that? As we're not hostages to an offtake, we don't price our products on formula. We use the market quote straight out of Shanghai Metals Market for concentrate, which essentially provides a more beneficial financial condition. But we are considering to do a multiyear offtake into 2027, but it's not something necessarily we have to do. We can perfectly survive continuing to do what we always do with selling material on a 1-year basis.

Operator: I'm returning to our CEO, Ana Cabral, for her final remarks.

Ana Cabral Gardner: Felipe and I and the entire Sigma team would like to thank you for your support throughout this quarter. We are very proud of how we came out of the third quarter into the fourth quarter. We came out stronger with tremendous visibility into our business, visibility such that the new governor of Minas Gerais has announced that he's going to take office from our region. So in January, he's actually going to become governor in our region in Vale do Jequitinhonha, which fills us with tremendous pride because we were able to shed the light in the transformational shared prosperity work we have been doing there for almost a decade.

And that has culminated in Sigma becoming this key company in the Western and Eastern global supply chains, delivering large scale, low cost and traceability. Going forward, that decision by the newly elected government has filled us with enthusiasm to full on continue on our growth strategy. And again, starting bottom up because the mine is what brings the most amount of jobs. And as a result, we plan to bring in another 25,000 people into the prosperity fold of Sigma. So working in an endeavor such as this is a partnership between the public powers, between society and between the company.

And as a good citizen company, we're really looking forward to contributing to lift the people of Vale do Jequitinhonha. And for that, I want to thank all of our stakeholders and our shareholders for being with us on this journey.

Operator: The third quarter of 2026 conference call of Sigma Lithium has concluded. For further information, please visit the company's website at www.sigmalithiumresources.com. You can disconnect now.

#2922. Alphabet vs. Apple: Which Warren Buffett Stock Is the Better Buy?

Both are major positions in the Berkshire Hathaway portfolio.

By Adria Cimino – Nov 18, 2026 at 6:25PM EST

Warren Buffett is known for selecting quality stocks and holding on to them for many years. And he's proven that this strategy works: For 60 years as chief executive officer at Berkshire Hathaway, Buffett helped deliver market-beating returns. Buffett retired at the beginning of this year, but he remains involved at Berkshire Hathaway and now holds the title of chairman emeritus.

Greg Abel, who took over from Buffett as CEO, has maintained the investing giant's principles and continues to hold many Buffett favorites. Two in particular remain among the company's top holdings: Apple (AAPL +0.15%) and Alphabet (GOOG +0.58%) (GOOGL +0.80%), in the No. 1 and No. 4 positions, respectively.

Which of these Warren Buffett stocks is the better buy today? Let's find out.

Warren Buffett. Image source: Getty Images.

This year marks a 10-year anniversary for Apple and Berkshire Hathaway: Buffett initially bought Apple shares in 2016. And over the years, it's become a cherished position, with Buffett on multiple occasions praising Tim Cook, who held the CEO role until September of this year.

Cook, who recently retired, helped the company's market value soar 1,000% to $4 trillion and revenue almost quadruple to $416 billion in the 2025 fiscal year. Now, with John Ternus at the helm, there's reason to be optimistic about more growth ahead. Ternus, formerly the company's senior vice president of hardware engineering, has the product experience and knowledge to lead Apple through new waves of innovation. Products are Apple's strength, with the iPhone the global smartphone leader, so a product focus is key for future growth.

Apple stock has climbed more than that of fellow tech giants this year, as it isn't as heavily linked to artificial intelligence (AI) -- and therefore is less sensitive to AI-related risks. Though Apple stock isn't cheap, it still could have room to run.

Buffett opened a position in Alphabet last year, and Abel added to it this year, showing clear commitment to this Buffett selection. Alphabet climbed earlier this year but has been under pressure in recent times, along with other tech giants that are investing heavily in AI. Some investors worry that these players are overspending and that the revenue opportunity will be disappointing.

Still, Alphabet's Google Cloud business hasn't faltered; in fact, that unit's revenue has been soaring amid strong demand for its AI products and services. In the recent quarter, Google Cloud revenue jumped 103% to $30 billion. The company has also begun selling its own chips, known as TPUs, to certain customers for use in their data centers. Though this is a small source of revenue right now, it could grow in time.

Meanwhile, Google's search business continues to hold 90% of the search market worldwide, and this has been its ticket to enormous revenue year after year. This is through advertising, with advertisers eager to place ads across the platform to reach potential customers. In the recent quarter, Google ads brought in $82 billion in revenue for the company.

Alphabet stock today looks cheap, particularly compared with that of Apple.

There's a clear reason for this, however, and this goes back to the point I made above: Some investors are turning away from AI big spenders. But this opens up an opportunity to buy Alphabet at a fantastic price.

This depends on your investment style and priorities. From a valuation perspective, Alphabet clearly stands out. Today, this tech giant is a great deal for growth investors looking for a bargain. Though current market sentiment may continue to weigh on Alphabet stock, this doesn't change the company's long-term story.

Alphabet's search business remains solid, and the company's cloud business is well-established and growing -- and doesn't rely uniquely on AI. So investors may benefit if they buy now and hold on as the storm passes.

However, Apple, less linked to AI spending and a long-term Buffett favorite, may be a better buy for the cautious investor. Though the stock has climbed, the release of new products just recently could boost revenue and lead to more gains ahead.

#2919. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for steady income

Stock markets remain volatile as investors weigh uncertainty in the Middle East, rising interest rates and concerns about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking a stable income stream can enhance their portfolios with the addition of dividend stocks. In this regard, tracking recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks that are backed by strong financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is the first dividend pick. Earlier this month, the company paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12 per share, CVX offers a dividend yield of about 3.5%.

After a meeting with senior leadership, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on CVX and raised his price target to $240 from $225. Among the key takeaways Mehta emphasized was that Chevron is building a solid pipeline of promising international exploration projects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. In particular, he mentioned the focus on Venezuela, where Chevron expects to more than double gross production to 600 kbd from about 280 kbd by 2031, using three joint ventures.

Mehta also noted Chevron's efforts to deploy new technologies, especially in shale and tight-oil operations. CVX is focused on boosting productivity and efficiency to maximize free cash flow, he added.

Initiatives such as artificial lift optimization, AI and machine learning, and advanced chemical treatments are expected to improve recovery by about 10% in new wells. Consequently, capital spending per barrel in U.S. shale is projected to fall 25% in 2026, with total Permian spending dropping below $3.5 billion.

Mehta also said that Chevron sees power as a growth opportunity and is using its U.S. natural gas portfolio, key equipment and partnerships to meet rising demand. Notably, Chevron recently signed a 20-year power purchase deal with Microsoft (MSFT) to supply 2.67 GW of behind-the-meter capacity. This project, called Kilby, is expected to see its first power delivery in 2028 and generate mid-teens returns and long-term cash flows.

Mehta ranks No. 536 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.3%. See Chevron Statistics on TipRanks.

Enterprise Products Partners (EPD) is a master limited partnership (MLP) that provides midstream energy services to producers and consumers of natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), crude oil, refined products and petrochemicals. With a quarterly cash distribution of 56 cents per common unit ($2.24 per common unit annualized), EPD offers a yield of about 6%.

Following a recent call with the company, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on EPD with a price target of $42. The analyst slightly lowered her estimates for the second half of 2026, citing margin and volume normalization, though demand dynamics remain strong.

While the 5-star analyst expects a sequential decline due to normal seasonality and normalization following high spreads in the first half of the year, she still expects EPD to report another solid quarter (Q3 2026) and enter 2027 with a favorable setup. Ahead of Q3 earnings, Scotto expects investors to focus on export demand durability, EPD's ability to profit from spot cargo sales and growth in Permian volumes.

Scotto continues to expect $150 million of common unit buybacks per quarter in the second half of 2026. She expects buybacks to increase to $200 million per quarter in 2027, as capex spending declines and free cash flow improves.

In total, Scotto is bullish on EPD and views it as a core MLP holding that has both offensive and defensive characteristics. The analyst praised EPD's diverse asset base as ensuring stable cash flows. "Furthermore, the partnership's multi-year organic growth backlog helps provide visibility on long-term distribution growth," Scotto said.

Scotto ranks No. 199 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 15.9%. See Enterprise Products Partners Financials on TipRanks.

Brookfield Infrastructure Partners (BIP) operates a diversified portfolio of high-quality utilities, transport, midstream and data assets. The company declared a quarterly distribution of 45.5 cents per unit, payable on September 29. At an annualized distribution of $1.82, BIP offers a yield of 5.2%.

Recently, BMO Capital analyst Devin Dodge reaffirmed a buy rating on Brookfield Infrastructure with a price target of $47. The analyst cited improved visibility into BIP's growth and views its corporate simplification as a potential catalyst.

"Layering in the benefits from the proposed corporate simplification, a multiple well below historical levels and an attractive yield, we believe BIP offers a compelling risk/reward and it remains a preferred idea," said Dodge.

With more organic growth projects in the pipeline and new partnership investment opportunities, Dodge believes that BIP has clearer visibility into where it will deploy capital. That should support continued double-digit growth in funds from operations (FFO) per unit.

Dodge said the semiconductor foundries that BIP is developing with Intel (INTC) are expected to be fully commissioned by the end of 2026, with returns improving through Q4 2026. Dodge expects the joint venture to boost FFO by 300-400 basis points.

#2918. Blackstone Digital Infrastructure: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Amazon keeps a 25% stake in the joint venture, a structure that ties the tenant's fortunes to the portfolio's performance.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 18, 2026 at 6:26PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust ›

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 16, 2026, Blackstone Digital Infrastructure (BXDC +0.18%) announced a deal to acquire a 75% interest in a $5 billion portfolio of 13 powered shell data centers (facilities where the landlord owns the building and power connection while the tenant supplies equipment) leased to Amazon. The deal would transition the trust from holding cash to generating steady rental income backed by an investment-grade technology titan. For long-term investors, this initial purchase establishes the template for how the company plans to scale its portfolio. Three things management said stand out.

Management committed its initial capital to acquire a 75% majority interest in a $5 billion data center portfolio. Amazon retained the remaining 25% minority stake as a joint venture (a cooperative business partnership) under a triple net lease (an agreement where the tenant pays property taxes, insurance, and maintenance costs), ensuring the technology titan remains aligned with the property's performance.

Powered shells have fewer ongoing landlord responsibilities than turnkey facilities. The transaction delivers a 7% going-in capitalization rate (cap rate, the initial annual rental yield on a property investment), along with 2.75% annual rent increases that protect against inflation.

Hyperscalers (large-scale cloud providers requiring vast computing capacity) face massive infrastructure spending demands to support artificial intelligence. Purchasing existing assets through sale-leaseback transactions (where an owner sells property and immediately leases it back) doubles the company's addressable market (the total market opportunity) to over $2 trillion by 2030.

Data center demand is expanding into power-rich regions such as Indiana and Mississippi, where early positioning offers a distinct advantage. Blackstone's platform scale and sourcing pipeline give the trust access to a wide range of on- and off-market deals.

Management is evaluating an expanding pipeline of upcoming asset deliveries while focusing on disciplined capital allocation and tenant alignment.

#2916. Federal Reserve Board finalizes changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements

An official website of the United States Government

Secure .gov websites use HTTPSA lock (LockLocked padlock icon) or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 9:00 a.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday finalized changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements. The two final rules are largely similar to the proposed rules from 2025. The Board also requested comment on a proposal to better capture differences in banks' business models to generate fee income.

The Board conducts stress tests to ensure that large banks are sufficiently capitalized and able to lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. In December 2024, the Board announced it would modify the test to improve its resilience.

"The stress test is an essential component of our regulatory capital framework," said Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman. "Today's changes preserve its resilience by ensuring that it is transparent, granular, and risk-sensitive. The public will now have greater assurance that the risks banks take will be reflected appropriately in their stress test losses and their capital requirements."

The first final rule requires the Board to invite public input annually on the stress test scenarios and any material model changes. It also updates the framework that guides the design of the hypothetical scenarios and adopts the models that will be used for the 2027 stress test. In addition, the final rule makes several adjustments to the stress test calendar. The final rule also updates the global market shock component, which is a set of shocks to specific market components applied to banks with large trading books. These banks will now be tested against two global market shock components each year, and the Board will use the shock that produces the largest losses for each firm to calculate the firm's stress test results.

The second final rule requires the Board, when calculating stress capital buffer requirements, to average the results from the two most recent annual supervisory stress tests for firms subject to the stress test in both years. The Board will begin averaging stress capital buffer requirements in 2028 to ensure that only models incorporating public input are used in the calculation.

The proposal would request public comment on a revision to the Board's noninterest income model that would improve the stress test's ability to capture business model diversity across firms. If adopted, these adjustments would replace the current noninterest income model that projects each bank's fee income under stress. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Together, the changes are likely to reduce year-over-year volatility in capital requirements by approximately 50 percent and are not expected to materially affect aggregate capital requirements.
